div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.

"WHAT is your idea of a gentleman, Yellowly ?" 44A true gentleman always laughs at the joke of a story, and never says that he heard it before." IT is well enough to say that 13 is an unlucky 'Jambes, but America started in business with 13 States, and seems to be still holding her own. "You'RE the most curious woman I ever heard of," said a boy to his mother; "yon tell me that I have a bad temper, and yet blame me for losing it." TAILOR—" The fashionable spring coat, sir, has but three buttons." Old Customer—" Put on the usual number; they will get down to three soon • enough." "IT is a solemn thing to be married," said Aunt Rachel, a grave spinster, to her niece. "It's a good deal more solemn not to be," said the merry • girl. FRANKLIN, 0., is excited over a new-born babe whose head is seven times the normal size. Chicago is the only city in which the child can be success- fully reared. SMIT a (a physician)—" I tell you doctors are a necessity, but lawyers are ric t." Briefs—" They are not? How do you make that out r Smith—" Be- cause necessity knows no law." " YOU'VE been riding a bicycle, 1 hear," said one clerk to another. "Just for esercise, you know." . "It hos reduced your weight, I tiaink." "Yes, I have fallen off a grent deal.' JOHNNY, I have discovered that you have taken more maple sugar than I- gave you." "Yes, grand- ma; I've been making believe there was another little bey spending the day with me." "HARRY, dear, do you smoke?" she asked sweetly. "Why ?" queried Harry, in doubt. "Because," she answered, "papa has just got a box of cigars, and I known where he keeps them." CARRIE—" I know George loves ma and wants me to be his wife." Hattie (her bosom friend)— "And how do you know ? " Carrie—" Because he has taken such a strong dislike to mamma." A WESTERN paper kindly supplies this beautiful simile :—" You might as well try to shampoo an elegant with a thimbleful of soapsuds as attempt to do business and ignore advertising." DURING the performance of a tragedy, a bald- headed gentleman, looking up into the gallery, said—" My dear madam, I respect your emotion, but the truth is you are shedding tears on my head."

DESPAIRING LOVER (bitterly)—"l dare say it would rejoice you to see me blow out my brains right here?" Mocking Maiden—"No, it would not rejoice me, Louis, but it would certainly sur- prise me." "WHY, I thought you were in the railroad acci- dent ?" was." "I heard the engine ran over you." "It did." "And that the baggage car fell on you." "Yes. "Well, you're a wonder." "No ; I'm a football player." LITTLE Dor —" Mamma, didn't papa say General Greely predicted high winds for to-day ?" Mamma —" Yes, my dear; he read it in the paper." Littla Dot—" Well, they isn't high at all. They is so low down they 'most blowed me over." A DEVOTEE lamented to her confessor her love of gain Wing. " Ah, madam," replied the priest, "it is a grievous sin. In the tirst place, corndder the great loss of time." "Yes," replied the fair penitent. "I have often grudged the time that is lost in shuffling _ _

and dealing:" - BERTIE BRILLIANT (driving home from the club, after having taken rather more champagne than he ought)—" I say, how much pleasanter it is to ride in a cab and think how much pleasanter it; is to ride In a cab than to walk, than it is to walk and think how much pleasanter it is to ride in a cab than it is walk."

" WELL, well," mused the love lorn youth, "I'm In a fix. If I marry Mabel people will say that I married her for her money; and if I suddenly give her up from conscientio,:s motives people will say that she jilted me because I am poor. I guess I'll brave opinion and propose at once." THE minister was a great handshaker—shutting down like a vice. One day he shook a boy's hand, and, forgetting, gave it an awful squeeze, as he said —"My little fellow, I hops you are pretty well to- day." With tears in his eyes, the bey answered— "I was till you shook hands with me." SMART GIRL—" Mr. Nicefellow, this is my little sister, Miss E.la. What do ycu wish, pet? Why are you regarding the gentleman so intently ? " Little Sister—" I was looking for the strings—that's all." " Strings ? What strings ?" "Why, mamma said you had always two strings to your beau." ' "Do you know," said Algernon, "your face reminds me of a mirror, for I can see nothing in it but the truth." "Oh," said Gertrude, "I thought you were going so say that when you looked in my face you expected to see your own." "BM" said Algernon, and then a great light came into his eyes, and he cried, "If you would be my own ! " and Gertie said "I will." AT a Perisian restaurant a patron complains of the amount of his bill :—" But what am I to do " says the host, with a sweeping gesture. "You can't have magnificent mirrors and rich ornaments like these unless you pay for them. You can't have frescoes and genuine gilt for nothing." The cus- tomer responds, phlegmatically—" Let the waiter remove them. I didn't order them." " AH I dearest," sighed a young man, kneeling at the feet of his ownest own, "do you know what of all things is nearest to my heart ? "—" Really I cannot say," she sweetly replied, " but in this cold weather I should think it was a flannel vest." She was too practical, and it broke the engagement. IN a debate on the leather-tax, in 1795, in the Irish House of Commons, the Chancellor of the Exchequer observed with great emphasis, that, in the prosecution of the present war, every man ought to give his last guinea to protect the remainder. A memb,tr said that however that might be, the tax on leather would,be severely felt by the bare•footed peasantry of Ireland. To which another replied, that this could be easily remedied by making the underleathers of wood.

A LAW-SUIT between Foote and Ross, respecting the Edinburgh Theatre, let by the latter to the former, came by appeal before the House of Lords. The matter was terminated in favour of Mr. Ross, and Foote was saddled with the costs. Whea Foote had paid the bill to Mr. Ross's solicitor, who came from Scotland, he said to him—" Now, when do you return to Scotland ?" "To-morrow." "And how do you travel? I suppose, like the rest of you countrymen, you will do it in the most economical manner." "Yes," replied he. "I shall travel on Foote I" IT is said that on one occasion as Miss Words- wo7th, sister of the poet, was passing through a wood, which the stock-dove was filling with its soft music, she fell in with a country-woman, who exclaimed, "I am so fond of stock-dove QI" ti Oh!" thought Miss Wordsworth, "At last I have come on one of nature's poets, with a Foul to appreciate the beantiful music of the birds." Very ru•hlessly was 022 dream disenchanted by an explanatory remark of the woman's—" Some likes them in pies, and some likes them roasted, but for my part I think there's nothing like them stewed with onions l" "CAN I see your father for a few minutes before :I go, Miss liendericks ?" he asked. "I want to speak to him V -en. a Taqqr Pf importance." irtainlzJr. Bauvton,h-replied the girl, with a blush. Atter 7::.r!": Zampson had taken his departure with a happy smile upon his face, Miss Hendricks found her way to her father's shoulder, and, 'steal- ing one arm about his neck, whispered—" What did he want, papa ?" "He is an agent for a patent gas burner," said the old man, "and I've agreed to give it a trial. A SCOTCH proclamation for holding a fair:— "Oh yes! and that's e'e time; Oh yes! and that's twa times; Oh yes I and that's third and last time. All manner of person or persons whosoever, let 'em draw near, and I shall let 'en t ken that there is a fair to be held at the muckle town of Langholm, for the space of aught days, wherein any hustrin, enstrin, land-lopper, clubs-kouper, or gang-the gate- swinger, shall breed any hurdam, durdam, rabble- ment, babblement, or squabblement, he shall have his lugs tacked to the ruuckle throne, with a nail of twa-a-penny until he down on his hobshatiks, and pray to been nine times God bless the king, and thrice the muckle laird of Relton, paying a groat to me, Jemmy Ferguson, bailey of the aforesaid manor. So you've beard my proclamation, and I'll gang .hame to my dinner. MINISTER (making a call)—" And do you always do as your mamma teiis you to, Flossier Flossie (emphatically)—l guess I do, and so does papa."

div.head: " CAPITAL " CHAT.
div.p: " CAPITAL " CHAT.

The famous electrician Edison is writing a novel in conjunction with Mr. G. P. Lathrop, who will probably put in the necessary sentiment. Mr. Lathrop is a well known writer in America, and is married to Nathaniel Hawthorne's second daughter Rose.

The arrangements are now complete for the establishment of the naval pigeon service. Dove- cotes have been erected at all the naval ports on the south coast, as well as at St. Mary's, in the Scilly Isles, and the carrier pigeons will be utilised in the naval manceuvres of 1892. The " homing" station in the Scilly Isles has already four hundred pairs of birds, and two men are engaged in looking after them.

A hundred times Mr. Balfour says in one speech, "Very well, sir." He marks his divisions of sub- jects by it, his sub-divisions and the progress of his oratorical paragraphs. " I hope I have made it clear to the house. Very well, sir,' is said over and over again. Sir Charles Russell's catchword is, " Let that pass" ; Sir William Harcourt's " A-ah " Mr. Gos- chen clears his throat, Mr. Oladstone takes a drink. But Mr. Balfour produces his pocket handkerchief and exclaims "Very well, sir."

M. Pasteur is now entitled to style himself Baron von Pasteur, the Emperor of Austria having sent him the Order of the Iron Crown. There are some doctors and savants who have a right to wear it, The Paris " Liberte " is curious to see whether M. Pasteur will cause himself to be announced as M. le Baron de Pasteur when he -goes to dine at great houses. There is practically no hindrance to Frenchmen in France going by foreign titles or wearing foreign orders.

The Emperor William has repeatedly and earnest- ly invited the Queen to visit Germany next year, and, all being well, her Majesty will probably com- ply with his wish, as she told him when he went to Windsor Castle to bid her farewell on the 14th of July. Nothing, howeVer, is yet settled about the arrangements for the visit, except that the Queen will stay for at least ten days at Cronberg, in the Taunus, with the Empress Frederick, whose magni- ficent new chateau will be finished very shortly.

The Women's Liberal Federation, of which Mrs. Gladstone is president, reports a year of continued progress and good work. The federation, although only four years old, renders the Liberal cause im- portant service in country districts by sending round lecturers among the villages, more especially to edu- cate the women in Liberal principlPs. Attention has also been paid to the registration of women voters, and the selection of women candidates for municipal school board, and board of guardian elec- tions.

I do not believe in the truth of the announcement that the Queen is going to have a railway carriage made expressly for her use when travelling abroad, because her Majesty already possesses a large dou- ble saloon, which she has used for many years past on her Continental journeys, and which is kept at Brussels. The Prince of Wales also has a spacious railway carriage of his own, which he always uses when travelling abroad, and it,tou, is kept at Brus- sels, and it can go on any line, being fitted with bogie-wheels.

The travelling company representing " The Mikado " at Aberdeen, were " commanded " to give a performance on Friday night at Balmoral before ths Queen. The manager, overwhelmed by the honour, submitted that they were sufficieutty well paid by being allowed to afford her Majesty enter- tainment, but he received a cheque in the usual course without any acknowledgement of his fine compliment. It is not commonly known that when the Prince of Wales visits a theatre he invariably pays ten guineas for his box.

A lucky mother as the c orld reckons luck, is the Dowager Duchess of Marlborough, not so much in respect of her sons, the present duke and Lord Ran- dolph Churchill, as of the marriages which her daughters make. The eldest is Lady Wim borne, the second is Lady de Ramsey, the third is Lady Fanny Majoribanks and will be Lady Tweedmouth, the fourth is the Duchess of Roxburgh e, the fifth is Lady Curzon and will be Lady Howe, and the sixth, Lady Sarah is just engaged to My. Wilson, son and heir of Sir Samuel Wilson, the present tenant of ilughen- den Manor.

Mr. George Fox, the gifted young baritone and rising composer, has completed an English opera, the libretto of which is founded on the late Lord Lytton's novel," The Last Days of Pompeii." The composer studied at the Royal Academy of Music, and carried away from that institution many prizes and certificates. Mr. Fox first made a reputation as a composer by a musical setting of Thos. Ingolds- by's legend, "The Jackdaw of Rheims," which al- though conspicuous here and there for remini- scenes, was a work of great credit for a first intro- duction to the public.

Mrs. Besant, I learn, was not sought out by the Theosophical Society, as has been stated in some quarters. It was she who sought out the society. A friend was sitting with Madame Thavatsky one afternoon when Mrs. Besant was announced. It was the first time these two women had met. 1 have come to ask you to let me join the Theoso- phical Society as a student," Mrs. Besant said, with her usual directness, She went on to tell Madame Blavatsky that she had read her books arid others bearing on theosophy, and that she had devoted more than a year to these studies.'

Says a lady correspondent at Homburg :—" At every town one comes upon a statesman or Minister, past, present, or to be. The grave features of Lord Hartington, heightened by the wide-spreading brim of his sombrero, and the tawny beard of Lord Spencer attract the attention of all near them, Sir Charles Russell, looking business-like, as though he had weighty briefs to attend to even during his holiday, stalks along with head bcwed down, followed by Lord Justice Bowen, and his pensive face and mild scholarly smile and with Mr. George Lewis bringing up the rear of legal luminaries.

It is rumoured that Dr. Angus is about to retire from the presidency of the Regent's-park Baptist College, after occupying the chair for forty-two years. Dr. Angus was born near Morneth in 1816. He was educated at the Old Grammar School, Newcastle-on-Tyne, whence he remcved to King's College, London. His conscientious objection to subscribing to the Articles of the Church of England precluded a university career. So he entered the Stepney Baptist College as a student for the Baptist ministry, He afterwards went to Edinburgh University, where he carried off most of the prizes and the gold medal of his year.

As in Mid-Devon, so in the Lowestoft Division of Norfolk, the Conservative rank and file will not, work for a Liberal Unionist candidate. Mr. Jackson was first forced upon the East Anglican Conserva- tives. Ile had not been long in the field, however, before he found out that the Tory workers enter- tained their own views, and that there were not 200 Liberal Unionists in the division. 31r. Jackaon complained that he had been deceived, and retired, and now Mr. Dawson wants to do the- same. The lesson of Wisbech has had apparently no result,. and so angry are the Conservative workers, that they declare they will not accept any candidate who comes from the central office here.

Mr. Parnell keeps up his Sunday entertainments in Ireland. He admitted for the first time on Sun- day that" their strength was undoubtedly to some extent broken." He objected to be called " the champion of Mr. Balfour " or the Tory Government, but expressed a curious readiness to support ths Tory Local Government Bill before he has seen it. The Unionists build great hopes on tboir alliance with Parnell in Ireland. They have arranged to contest about a dozen seats, and, acting in conjunc- tion with Parnell, they hope to split the Nationa- list vote and oust a few Home Rulers. The result of the union of Balfourism and Parnellism will be the strengthening of the Nationalist cause.

The little island of St. Helena, hitherto famous for its associations. with a great name, has now secured a second claim to the notice of the world i by being almost, f not quite the first Crown colony to overcome the reluctance of the Colonial-office to a divorce law. There is now by proclamation, by and with the consent of her Majesty in Council, instituted in this.small Atlantic island a court for divorce and matrimonial causes, wherein any of her Majesty's subjects may file a petition tor the small sum of 25., and for a grand total of less than 30s. in court fees may go through all the varying stages of a suit for dissolution of marriage, down to the Pronouncement of the decree absolute. Other -colonies similarly situated will now, it may be

presumed, seek from the Colonial-office a revision of those decisions which in the past have denied to subjects of her Majesty resident in Crown colonies.

A new evening paper is to be started in Man- chester towards the end of this month. It will be issued from the office of the " Examiner " and "Times," and be called the" Evening Times." The editor of the new venture will be Mr. Arthur B. Chamberlain (no relation of Joseph's) until recently a member of the editorial staff of the " Standard.' Mr. Chamberlain is a young man of great promise, who, after a brief journalistic experience in Hull, of which town he is a native, and on the London edition of the " New York Herald," was a special correspondent and sub-editor of the "Times." In politics he is a Tory Democrat. Mr. Chamberlain, who II not more than twenty-five, was educated at Edihburgh, Cambridge, Nit'. 11114 1i Germany. His acceptance of the editorship of this new journal is said to be connected with his appearance at the , general election as a candidate in a Lancashire con- stituency.

The Report of the Education Department issued on Monday, is not so interesting as will be next year's one, when the effect of the recent revolution in education will be known. The number of scholars on the registers of all schools is reported to be ,4,825,560. For these there is an army of teachers of nearly 100,000. As usual, the Voluntary schools compare badly with the Board schools. The average grant earned by the Church schools was 17s. sid. per scholar, as compared with 18s. sid. in Board schools. The London Board schools are fourth highest on the list of large towns—Liver- pool, Leeds, and Bradford being before it with a grant of 19s. Ofd. per scholar. Voluntary schools in Loudon earned a grant of 18s. sid. Voluntary school pence have been increasing-11d. Oid. per scholar in 1888 to us. LW. in 1889 and us. 2id. in 1800; but the subscriptions are diminishing. The hope of the clerical party, while loweridg the fees, is to get the subscriptions increased.

div.head: ACROSS THE ATLANTIC.
div.p: ACROSS THE ATLANTIC.
BY "TOWNSMAN." XII.-THE QUEEN CITY OF THE WEST.
ITS AREA-ITS STREETS-CABLE CARS-JUR BUILD- INGS-THE HOTELS-A HUGE CONCERN-THE
SHOPS.

Among the many wonders of a wonderful coun- try, are the number and size of its cities. Cities which to-day are not, are to-morrow peopled, with thousands of inhabitants, laid out, built up, and carrying on business with all the agencies of old time places. When you think that a few short years ago, the sites of world-renowned American cities were rolling prairie, over run with buffaloes and Red Indiane, you are filled with wonder and amazement at their growth and development, and with admiration for the people who design and build them. Especially is this the case with cities Of stleh magnitude as Chicago, the Queen City of the West. Fifty years ago it wa* a mere Iniian trading station_, and twenty years ago it was burned to the ground, to-day it bids fair ere long to be the largest city on the American continent. It al- ready shelters a population of over a million souls, land it is considered the most go-a-head city in the United States. It owes its development largely to its situation. Located at the foot of Lake Michigan and almost in the middle of the continent, it occupies a most commanding position. All the great railways have a terminus in the city, and a railroad map of the district resembles more than anything a great spider's web. Chicago covers an area of 175 square miles, the greatest length of the city being, from north to south, 24i, miles, and the greatest width from east to west 14i

div.head: ITS STREETS
div.p: ITS STREETS

are broad and noble avenues, which intersect the city at right angles. Some of them are of great length, one being 18 miles on the straight, and no- thing seems to reduce the perspective. If you ride for an hour on the cable cars you seem no nearer the end of the street than you were at the start. The chief streets are Fifth Avenue, Clark-st, Dear- born-st., State-st., Madison-st., Washington-st., Sze. These are mostly given over to commercial pur- poses, while others, such as Michigan Avenue,. are reserved foil pleasure driving. On the latter are to be seen the best turnouts the city can boast, and on Sundays they greatly resemble Rotten Row, by reason of the numerous vehicles that are driven rapidly along their course. Americans have a fail- ing for buggy driving, and every city boasts a driving course. The first thing a man does when he's "got on," is to rim a buggy, and as a "one horse" affair is apparently looked down upon, the. box-like arrangement that seems all springs and spokes is usually drawn by what our American cou- sins call "a team." Such, is the passion for driving that, it is asserted, if a man fails in business the next thing you'll hear is that he owns a buggy and team ; and, indeed, such men were pointed out to me on the streets. Most ofthe streetsare traversed

CABLE cAs3, whiCh• run along the main thoroughfares like trains. It is a sight to see the cars in the evening when the business people are making for their homes; A train of five or six cars will come along loaded to its utmost capacity with people hanging on to the foot boards. Still.every per- son the cars pass, who wants a ride; makes a grab at the vehicle and feels happy if he can but find a place for the sole or his' foot. Talk about overcrowding !;—never was such a sight seep in England. The cars—or rather trains —follow each other in quick succession,and as-they are all provided with gongs to warn the people of theirwpproach an incessant clanging is kept up• all the claT It so happened that Mr. H. H. Barker chose an office Eg a point where-el the cars passed, andithe ringing of the gongs and the rumbling of the cars as-they rounded the curve was aomething awful. The pace of the'curs, too, is somewhat alarming at first. Thepseem to go like the wind ! Just to give an instance. Mr. J. F. 136te axid' / were out together, and we decided to "take the car " home. We arranged to jump on as it came along,.and we made the attempt—but the car left us in the road. Mr. Bate made a grab and I grabbo,.but, oh !:we might as well have tried to board the " Flying Duchman." The cars simply flew past us. When the trains get on,t into the suburbs the ears are detached and taken to their I various destinations by horses. The fare •is -ths same i (2P.) for long or short rides,and somegood long ler,gths can be coveredlor the popular 5 cents.

div.head: BUILDINGS.
div.p: THE BUILDINGS.

Magnificent and palatial structures adorn the com- mercial portion of the city. The Chicagoans are malting the best of their way heavenward with their buildings,, and every new erection seems to be higher than, its predecessors. The buildings in Boston • are dwarfs eotnpared to • those- of Chicago. Twetvs,•.and fourteen storeys, and higher, is the order of the new erections-in, the Pork City,,and the many storied, many windowed. buildings that are being erected look more like immense factOries than stores and offices. The highest building in the city is the Auditorium Hotel Tower Balcony, v2hlch is in storeys, 0r..?,60 feet. From this tower a grandview can be obtained of the city and Lake Michigan. The other aspiring structures include the Board of Trade Tower Balcony ',22'fft., Grand Central PaSsenger Station Tower 200 ft., Owings Buildings (top, of 14th storey) 158 ft., Chamberof Commerce Buildings frkft., Tacoma Bailding 1641 t:„. Rookery Building- 159 ft., and the Pullman Buildiag.:l4oft. All these are noble buildings,-. elaborately carved and beautifully finished, and vie 'with anything there is to be seen in Londen. Then there -ape the General Past °lice, the Palmer-House Hote4:the Auditorium lietel.:•,.• a great granite warehouse, bullt by Messrs. Marsh'ali itield and Co., and the Railroad dep4ts, while of 'quite, a-different stamp are the miles of ware-. hotses,- factories,. and grain elevators. The barbees shop in the Palmer nOuse-is- an elegant appartment, and the fi'dor.is inlaid with silvertlonar pieces. But perhaps the-largest and best of thebotels is the Auditorium, vvhioh is a huge concern. Asl write a picture-of it lies before me, and it resembles-an immense factory, with its square • tower and flag-staffs. It covers an area of one and a half acres, and has a total street frontage of 110 feet. The main buiitling is ten storeys high, with a tower. eight floors above that, and a lantern tower Voo floors stilt higher., The weight of the entire building :3110,001' tons. Several mammoth establishments have a Prontaga- on State Street, and the most popular of these is appropriately called "The Fair."- It swarms all day long with bar- gain hunters, who glide up and down to the various floors in elevators that are found in nearly every corner. Anything can be‘purchased here from a yin to a house stove, from a reel of thread to a complete outfit- The proprietor of this" big thing "in stores—quite a young man—made such a big lit, that It turned his brain and he is now in a lunatic asylum' doubtless wishing his success had nat been so great. Besides these" Dry Goods ". stores, there are great tailoring emporiums, and vast furnishing houses, where your every want can be sup-. plied. The store-keepers of Chicago are quite alive to the advantages of good window dressing, and the die, plays7made by the jewellers, tailors, and drapers are very enticing. div.head: IT WAS MARY SHERLOCK'S WAKE.
div.p: IT WAS MARY SHERLOCK'S WAKE.

"There lays a hundred years o' peace and happiness." It was the wake of Mary Sherlock, who had died of old age; and it took place on the night of Thursday, March 19th, 1891, in the City of New York. The room was crowded with men and women, old and young, and an aged junkman, who sat on a keg in the middle of the room, said to every new-comer, "There lays a hundred years of peace and happiness," to which the party res- ponded in chorus, •‘ Faith, Mike, niver truer words did ye speak."
For Grandma Sherlock had come to America frem Ireland before any of them, and, no doubt, was at least 105 years old when she ended her long journey.
But she was one of the old stock, and never knew what illness was.

How different is such a story as this, for instance, told by a woman ! "I was never well in my life,T she says, always weak and ailing, constantly sick, and troubled with giddiness and swimming in the head. Pew; le who did not know me would at times think I was tipsy. I always had a poor appetite, with bad taste in the mouth in the morning, and pain after eating. I had great pain and tightness in the chest and side, and was languid'and tired after the least exertion, so I was unable to do any work or get my own living. "As te sick headache, I was seldom free from it, and often my heart would palpitate, so I had to stop and hold myself, for fear of falling. I was nearly always under the doctor, and when I was so, something formed in my mouth that the doctor called eranula 'and I was confined in the Exeter Hospital I? weeks with it. "From that time I was worse than ever; and after eating the least morsel of food I heaved at the stomach and would spit up a sour fluid. "Better and worse I continued until April, 1889,when I became much worse,. and my abdomen swelled until it reached a great size, and a pain in the side and back made me scream out. Indeed, I was in such agony I could not stir hand or foot. Just then my neighbour, Mrs. Harris, wife of Joshua Harris, the read contractor, came in, and I had to be carried' to bed, So dreadful was the pain that I broke out into a heavy sweat, and a faintness came. over me. Mrs. Harris stayed with me and poulticed me; but as I gat no better my mother, who-lived at Rousdon, was-sent for; She came at once, I and sent fora doctor, as r was- in terrible distress, and fighting for breath:. The doctor said he could not tell what was the matter, and a second doctor was sent for from.Seaton by the clergyman, who thought I was dy- ing. So critical was my condition considered that prayers were made for me at the church. "The swelling of the bowels increased,, and the doctor said if this swelling did not go down I could not get better,.as it must be a tumour. He seemed puzzled by my ease- and kept changing my medicine, but I got no relief. My brother and ethers wf.o• came to see me all believed me to • be dying:

"After two months of this as lady named Mrs. Stockem.who lived at Rousdon. came to see me and told me about a medicine called Mother Seigeles Syrup, and said, Ybu try it, for it once saved my life." "I sent to. Mr. Gage,,the grocen-at Seaton, and got a bottle, and before I had taken the contents 1 felt better, the painwas easier, and the swelling I's have spoken of gradually went away. After having taken three bottles I was able to move about, and now feel better than I ever did in my life before, and am stronger than when I was agirl. But, oh,,if I, had known of Mother Seigel's Syrup soonorit would have saved me years of misery. (Signed) "-MRSI.MARY HOARE,
" Combpyne, Axminster, Devon,Yeb. IS, 1891."

This was a case of chronic indigestion and dyspepsia, with terrible constipation;: the swelling was caused by matter in the intestines•which had probably been slowly acommulating for months: In the -meantime this fester- ing mass-filled the whole system, with poison, causing aU the other symptoms described. Women are subject t, this far more than men, on account of their eareleris ' habits. It occasionally. happens -that surgical interfer- ence is necessary. There was no t mrour of course, Nit in the end there might have, been, had not Seigas Syrup removed the loathsome-deposit before it was tno late.
What a pity that women (and men too) will not check the first symptoms- of disease and thus, like Nary, Sherlock, enjoy a hundred years of peace and happiness.
MOLLY BUSHELL, AND, " EVERTON TOFFEE.'

Another ofthe links 'which connect the Liverpool of the present with that of the past, has been, severed by the death of James Bushell, of the fish- ing village of Firkgate7. Cheshire. Born in 1811-in Everton-crescent, he had: thus attained the patrian. chal age of 80(years. He:was-the only grandson of old Molly.Bushell,the originator of the famous toffee, which has made the name ofiEverton so well-known throughout the length and breadth of the land. in the early days-of Mr. Bushell, Everton was a very. different place fromcwhat it is now. At that time it was a beeatiful saburhoornmanding an uninter- rupted view of the estuary of the Mersey, grom which the merchants-of Liverpool in their mansions perched on its eminence,, could watch the fleets of vessels arriving at and leaving the port. It is, how- ever, in connection with the ancient village—now known as Village-street—that Mr. Bushell's recol- lections are principally interesting. It was in this street, near the top en the left hand (where now. stands the Wesleyan (Chapel) that his grandmother first made in 1753: the toffee with which the names of Bushell and Everton are inseparably associated. Subsequently Molly built for herself a new house and shop a little lower down the village,which still remains there, and where she continued to carry on the toffee and confectionery business, together with that of a small farmer. James Bushell leaves behind hint two sons (one of whom takes up his father's career as a Dee fisherman) and one daughter, who sincerely mourns his loss.

div.head: DARING IMPOSTOR.
div.p: A DARING IMPOSTOR.
THE STORY OF AN INNOCENT CONN-Tr"'
BY ALFRED R. CALHOUN.
CHAPTER VII. IN NEW YORK.
"You must not follow me," said Allen Gilbert, coming to a halt near his cabin in Pine Place, and facing the ex-convict, who called himself "Mingo Pete."

"Well, blow me, but this is a nice way to treat an old chum," blurted out the ex-convict; and his face at d manner all showed the most unmistakable surprise. This was not the kind of a reception he had been accustomed to receiving from his criminal associates, for there is a fraternal feeling among these men who are banded against the law, and they am always generous in helping, with their ill-gotten gains, a friend in distress. . "You must keep away from me. Ido not know you. I do not want to know you," said Allen, hotlf. "And what if I shouldn't keep away from your sneered Mingo. "Then I shall make you." "How will you do that I" "I will thrash you first, and hand you over to the police afterwards," said Allen, again turning away; but there was no mistaking his determina- tion.

Mingo watched him till he entered the cabin, then he gave a long whistle to express his amaze- ment, and slouched away to a shanty, about which the children, goats and old tin cans were particularly thick.
This meeting with the ex-convict disturbed Allen greatly, for it not only brought up all the horrors of the past, but he saw in it a danger that might shadow its future.

But when he caught sight of Florence, who dropped her sewing and hastened to kiss him when be appeared, in the door, the good news he had for her and the mother, made him forget all else, and so he embraced them by turns as he narrated the events of the day. " To-morrow ! " he exclaimed, joyously, when the lamp was lit, and the little blinds drawn over the eight panes of glass that made up the two windows, "we shall be away from this wretched place. I wish, mother, that you and Florence had been along to help me select rooms; but I think you will like the four I have rented. They are in a tenement, but I think the people are of a better class than is. usually found in such places. But, be that as- it may, it will be a change for the better." "No change can be for the worse," sighed the old lady, adding, after a pause': "We have sounded the lowest depths of poverty and suffering; it is a. comfort to think that any movement at all must be upward." "-Ali, mother mine!" cried Florence, as she knelt beside her mother, and kissed the thin, tremb- hands, "10 us thank God for the light ahead, and let it comfort us to know that poverty has brought no stain, and suffering left' no hate in our hearts."

Having decided to move to New York, Allen set to work with that energy that distinguished him of old. He found the landlord who owned the cluster of shanties at Pine Place, and paid hire the rent in full till the end of the month. Early the next morning all the furniture was placed in a waggon, and sent over to Masters-street, where rooms had been secured.
Then Allen hastened over with his mother and Florence, reaching their destination a short time before the furniture.
All that day Allen ad his sister worked like beavers, and as a consequence their new quarters were as cosy by supper time as if they had been lived in for months.

During his much coming in and going out that day, Allen discovered that the tenement was occu- pied by a dozen or more families, men andmomen who did sewing at home, for the continued whirr a sewing machines made the place sound like a factory, to which, even at the noon hour, there was aever an instant's stop. After supper, and when IVir.s Gilbert had gone to bed wearied with the lab6urs and excitements of the day. Allen and Florenoe• sat in the darkness, with the doors and windows open, for the night was hot; but still, like the hum of a swarming hiva; they heard the machines going; and the beating oThease- less feet along the bare .stairs. _ _ _

It was a familiar sound to Florence. During the tong years of her father/1s illness and her brother's 'imprisonment, she and her mother had kept their sewing machine going for sixteen hours out of the twerZy-four, day in ad day out; and them, were times when even on Sunda,- they had to work in order to get money for bread-, rent, or medicine. Until far into the ni;;:kit they discussed the future, turaing, despite their resolution not to do so, to that past which they vainly tried to forge '4 or at least to leave unmentioned.

"-Yen ha' e been a brave„ noble sister," said Ailen„ as he kissed her-before retiring that night. "Thewonder is that yondid not go down in the struggle. But the future is full of promise, and if yonand the dear mother are not happier from this time on., it will be becauselove and duty havefied my. heart." "And that can never be, dear Allen; while. your heart continues to beat," she said, with a sob of joy. , The next morning, in a modest but beooming business suit, Allen was about to start off and begin the work of collecting, when, to his surpriSei his good. friend, Doctorr Patnami, appeared at the lodgings. "1 called to sae you, Mr. Gilbert," said the diucteer, after Allen < liacl introduced his, mother and: sister, "and to, say that I shall ble away from my office far some weeks, business, and pleas-we calling ma •to Canada. I shall, leave the keys of my. office with you, and. r shall be glad if you maze it your headquarters, Indeed, even when not away, I only use the office 'for; a, few hol -c, ecich daick;, for, as you. may know I have to lecture at the Univer:nty wiring the regular ternushand then I have clinicsin a num- ber of the hosiitals, so that the will be practically yotlrs) and I will I,ave the satisfaction oilknowing it is in good han3." Allen Gilbert) like all men enyable ledingpro- fonadly, was afters at a loss for words, to express his feelings, and: so he coubl only btuali awl stam- mer a few short sentences ; hut the doctor under- stood them, a:ad,to him ti 3 were clot:neat with a manly gratitcdo:. liet the doctor was himself ova:used, and without being able to give him&;if: a reason for it.

From the..frnsit instant he, looked :littte Florence Gilbert's e:vs, and hearth her sweet, low voice, his heart was touched with n strange per, and ex- perienced the sensation. of a new and thrilling emotion.

Skilled, thowgh he was, in medicite4z,nd anatomy, and expeionced as he was beyond most men of his years in the physical ilis—real and imagined—that trouble Namanity, yetiohe was notable for many a. day to Ziagiaose rightly the heart trouble—perhaps " trouble "is not tin correct word—that came to him thaa and there.

And,when he wenb, away he tried to explain to himse:fwby he had,such a desire to go back; Led he re4,ioned himself:into the balief that his inte7est in ttpkgentle, Madonna-like sister was due to the intermt he alreadz felt for the brave but some-tthat mystatious brother,.
Tbat is my friend, Florrie ; :what do you Akink of h:ua r asked Allen, whe.a Doctor Putnarl had left,.
"-Your frienal must be.my friends," she replied, our list ia so limitei, Allen, that we can give thana all the regard we might distribute e4aong a thwsand friends if we wore 80 favoured."

It was und% these fa-Aourable circumstances that Allen Gilbert began tho new fi,fe. From the -AerffirFit sour he went to wctic.succeas 'atecamie his attendant,and,goodlortune ihminated all his walks..

_ . No matter how ready and anxious pople may be to pay their bills, W4ey are never rejoiced at seeing a collector, for such a man is generally a reminder of a dut,y, neglected; but Allen Gilbert did his work wi..411, so rare a tact as to give entire satisfac- tion to his patrens, and to win the esteem of the people whom LA dunned," or witose biZs he re- ceiptel. At irst he hared eat Mingq. Pete, tr some of those who lind seen him in prison, or who knew of his trial and conviction, would meet him and WI his employers of his identity with the convicted forger, Allen Lee.

The doubt, the dread, the constant watchfnlaess, and .the uncertabaty of his position, were at first tryilag in the extreme ; but gradually, as the current of what promised'to be a successful vareer flowed on.without a break, Allen came to Teel more and mitre secure, and with this sense of securly the confidence with which he faced the word also increased.
The rooms in the tenement house graduaily took on a cosier aspect, atd as Florence persisted in adding to the revenue with her needle, taey soon paid off the money. advanced. b.: Dr. Putaam. and

With the precaution that had been Increa3ed by long years of poverty, they laid by from their earn- ings, and the second most interesting book in the family was the one in which the joint savings of the brother and sister were recorded by the receiving teller in a neighbouring savings bank. The fall had come, and with it the wealthy and fashionable ; and the many who, without the means to be either, would have the world believe they were both, came back from villas in the mountains and cottages by the/ shore to the deserted city mansions.
Mr. Allen caught sight of the Lefferts's carriage, with Irene and her father on the back seat, and he reasoned that they had returned to their home on the Avenue.

Although he had never given himself much credit for saving the young woman's life, yet he often thought of her, and particularly of that meeting at Greenwood the day his father was buried. The picture then presented was destined never to fade from his heart; but, though often recalled with delight, it was always to be set behind the curtain of his memory agAin with pain. The name " Lefferts " always brought to his mind the imprisonment and consE quent disgrace endured through the climes of Frank Lefferts and his associates.

One bright afternoon, when the keen, exhilarating breath of winter was in the air, Allen's business took him to the Avenue, and as he was hurrying on, intent only on the collections he was about to make, a clear, musical voice called out, "Mr. Gilbert ! Mr. Gilbert !" and turning in the direction of the sound, he found himself lace to face with Irene Lefferts.

"You have never come near me," she said, blushing, and reaching out her hand; "but the fact that I still live must be the proof that I have not forgotten you for a day." "I am glad to see you again, Miss Lefferts," he stammered. "But you over-estimate my services. There were a thousand men ready to go to your rescue—"

"Yet only one man went," she interrupted; then added quickly: "Both my father and myself have tried to find you, and now that I have un- expectedly succeeded, will you do me a favour?' "A hundred, if in my power," he replied. " Come and dine with us to night, at half-past six."
Irene Lefferts took a card from her wallet, and writing the hour on it, she added: "Brave men never break their promises." "If you would permit a compromise, Miss Lefferts—"

"In what way ?"' "Let me call after dinner." "This evening,?" "Yes." " Very well. A half loaf is better than no bread. Till then, good-bye."' Again she gave him her hand, and with such a glad, frank manner, that Allen had to turn away to hide the confusion manifest in his face.

Neither Mrs. Gilbert nor Florence expressed any pleastare at Allen's Proposed visit. Both knew that all hia troubles were due to a member of that family, and the fact that he had unconsciously returned good for evil did not reconcile them to an asBo3iation so suggestive of pain. But Allen kept his promise. •

He was respe-ctably-clad, and months of labour in the open air had kronzed his cheeks, and given strength and elasticity to limbs cramped by long years ci prison routine. He was now a decidedly handsome man of the intellestual type, though, in repose, his face had a tinge oflsadness such a 5 one often sees in the faces of yorng theologians who are given to thinking more of the world's suffering than of its joys. Irene Lefferts met Allen with a. warmth and an artlessness that put him once at his ease. _ _ _

"My ther i; in the library, waiting to welcome you," shs fdaid, as she led he guest back through the spacious parlours; "and he is surprised to think that he has never had an opportunity to thank in 2erson the man who saved his daughter's life."

Mr. Le3brts, a fine-looking niiigentleman, with white hair and beard, both inclined to curl, greeted Allen witha manner that showed profound emotion. "Mr. C-abert," he said, as he held Allen's hand, "I thank you for coming to-night. Till I could greet you and express my gratitude I have felt that I had a grsat duty undone. God bless you, sir— God bless you—for having saved to me the one thing thatima!ies life worth. the lining !" And his voice becoming husky, he coughed, and motioned Allen to a ohair.

Allen cculd enly thank Mr. Lafferts for his kind expressiwast and to altempl, modestly to under- estimate what he had done by c;aiming that others would have done the same th'.ng if he had not chanced tc,be a little the fiNt.

There can be me doubt abont that. ladeed, the cheque was paid, fog- I saw it caly to-day when the bank sent back my can- celled cheques for the past quarter. Do :zon. know this. Dr. Putnam, Mr. Gilbert 2" "-I do, sir.' "And what do you ixnow about him 7" 'That from the day when he roused nte bAck tc. consciousnoss, after I was taken from the water at, Long Branch, he has. been to me a neble friend. Indeed, I owe to him the position tha.t has lifted, miy mother, sister and myself above want" said Allen, with great earnestness. Mr. Le/erts wrote down the cloctor''*acidress, then ' asked :
" IVoral you object to my looking lath this matter, Mr. Gilbert 7"
"Not, at all, sin!'
"And now will you permit me, for I am moved by interest and laot by curiosity, to ask you,3, few questizns about yourself?" "Certainly," replied _Allen.

And at th-ought- of the hated past which these quesions might bring up, but which he co.uld not reveal, "he roved uneasily in his chair." • "How old, are you ? " "Going 027, twenty-eight." 'Where born 2" 'ln this city." __

" I judae you are well edacatesir "In a business way—yea; but, beyond that, I can only claim to be fairly well informed. well-read might ezpress my acquirements." "What has been your business?" "I have been an accountant." "For whom?"
"Far the past four years I have been ix the service of the State," said Allen, the cold sweat beading his brow, and his eyes down- cast.

"Ahi a political office, /ost, no doubt, through a change of party?" Allen did not attempt to explain, and the obi gentleman went on, evidently believing that he was right in his surmise. "Thousands of our best young men are wrecked In politics. Such a life unfits one for actual business; and its associations—unless where one has unusual force of character—are apt to lead to, unsteady habits. But it is evident you have bravely resisted the temptation. Now, call at my office any morning you may choose, and, if you are the man I take you to be, I will find you a place with a future in it and a good present living. What say you I" What could Allen say, but "Thanks." Here was an opening that, were he unrestrained, might result in his rising as had been his ambition. But, like an echo to the offer, he beard the clank- ing of the prison chains and the gloomy doors of the penitentiary swinging on their hinges.
After some further talk, a visitor to see Mr. Lef• ferts was announced, and the old gentleman excused himself and went out. - "Mr. Gilbert 1' said Irene, when they :were_ alone.

"did you ever hear a sentence uttered that stuck tc your memory, and could not be banished night not day ?" Again he started, and the cold sweat covered hiE face, and his neart rose up in his throat and throbbed like a funeral drum. Yes, he had the memory of a sentence that was ever with him. Could it be pos. sible that she was thinking of the same thing? Not daring to trust his voice he nodded his head and compressed his lips. "The sentence I have in my mind is the one you shouted in my ears when your strong arms wen battling for my life, after you had brought me up Can you recall it, Mr. Gilbert 2" Again he shook his head, this time with a sense of great relief. "It was: Courage, and I will save youl'" "I surely meant it," he said. "And you as surely kept you word. Now, dare say that if you applied these words to yourself that there might be a great future before you ?" "I am afraid, Miss Lefferts, that my ambition is a thing of the past. If I can care for myself and those dependent on me, I shall feel that I am ac- complishing my mission." _ _

" A.h, how I wish I were a man. I should win success for its own sake. I should want to stand high among men, without any regard to the wealth that my efforts should command. I should try to make my life such that fathers would point theii sons to it as a model for their imitation ,-" and Irene Lefferts's eyes glowed, and ste looked radiantly beautiful in the light of her own enthusiasm. "It is not apathy with me," said Allen, with forced calmness. "But, by no fault of my own, I carry on my shoulders, as did Sinbad, an Old Man of the Sea, whose hands rest on my head and press it down when I try to look up." He rose to his feet and added: "I thank you and your father for your kindly interest. I hope you may find me worthy O. its continuance."

"That we shall do so I have not the slightest doubt," Irene hastened to say. "And if you will permit me to call on your mother and sister, I shall be happy to pay my respects." "We live in a place you would hardly care to visit—"

"But," she interrupted with a manner that showed a trace of annoyance, "I am not going to vbit the place. I want to know the mother and sister of the man who must ever be to me the bravest in all the world." Allen wrote the address, and be was•in the act of handing it to her, when the library door opened and Mott Reybold, in full evening dress, walked in. Allen bowed and would have passed out without noticing Reybold, who was evidently surprised and confused by the meeting, but Irene called him to stop, saying: "Mr. Reybold, this is the gentleman who saved my life, and whom I found, though you could not discover him.'!
" Ah, Mr. Gilbert, glad to meet you," said Rey- bold, and he bowed and reached out his hand.
Allen did not see the hancl, but he did see the man.

On the instant his- whole expression changed. He drew himself up, and with flushed cheeks and eyes that blazed till the other's cowed and were averted before them, he surveyed Mott Reybold for a few seconds; then bowed to Irene and left the room.

"You gentlemen seem to have met before," said i Irene, when Allen Gilbert was gone. "I hardly care to have the name gentleman', applied to me in such a connectibn," said Reybold, shrugging his shoulders, and glancing, before sitting down, at the door through which Allan had vanished.
" I—l do not understand!" cried Irene, a glint of anger in the questioning gaze she fixed on Rey- bold.
"And I shall not explain," said Reybold, with,, another shrug, "unless, indeed, your safety should compel me to warn you in time:" "To warn me 7"

"Yes, those were my words." "And, let me say, Mr. Reybold, if your words • were intended to reflect—to cast any suspicion on Mr. Gilbert, taey will not avail.—" "Come, come, Irene." he broke in, "you and I Seem to be only too ready to disagree of late, I'd() not underestimate the services of this man. They redeem much of his past to me. What the past was it matters not now, for he has paid the penalty of his—errors; and Reybold rose and waved his hands, as if he were putting a dis- agreeable subject away fltcvn him in a very magnanimous way.

lint Irene would have persisted in learning more about this matter, if her father had not come in; as it was, she bit her lip, excused herself, and left, the library, full of suppressed indignation. And, strangely -enough, when she found herself in her own room, she exclaimed, as she looked in the mirror at the reflection of her own face:

Lefferts," said Reybold, as he shook the old gentle. man's ha d, and noticed that he was Litt met with the old fatherly manner... "I ant aware of that, Mr. Lefferts, and I can,: truthfully say that im her happiness mine is in- - volved.'''

MR. GLADSTONE'S-ELECTORAL FACTS.

In Monday's "Times," in replfrto a criticism of his article in the "Nineteenth Century" on electoral facts. Mr. Gladstone points out that the figures given in the , article ought to be confined to Great Britain,showing a • Liberal British majority at the next election of 25 in- stead of 46. To that extent he thanksthe correspondent, but says the latter might with advantage have noticed that three other modes of calculating the result of an election gave the figures respectively of 53, 75, and 97, to which has to be added the Irish majority, if in favour of Home Rule. In conclusion Mr. Gladstone says: —" In arguing the question my desire has been to state the case with the greatest moderation. But state it as you will, the result comes out one and the same way. In order to do full justice to the Tories I have computed what would be the effect in reasoning from the numeri- cal excess at the polls of separating the uncontested from the contested seats, and giving the Government credit (surely a liberal act) for the same majority of un- contested seats in 1892 as they had in 1886. A calcula- tion on this basis still produces a British majority a about 90 against the party now in power."

div.head: REVISING BARRISTER'S COURT. WARRINGTON.
div.p: REVISING BARRISTER'S COURT. WARRINGTON.

On Tuesday evening Mr. J. T. Feard, revising barrister, opened a court in the Council Chamber of the Town Hall, for the revision of the list of Parliamentary and,municipal voters for the borough. Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, and Mr. John Clayton, Liberal registration agent, represented the Liberal, and Mr. John Hampson, the Conservative, interest. Messrs..J. L. Tunstall and Gibbon, from the rate office, and Mr. Garnett, relieving officer, were also present. There was a considerable attendance of the public.

LODGER -CLAIMS. A claim advanced by James Dunn, 2, Egypt-st., as a lodger, was submitted by the Conservatives. In reply to Mr. Browne, he said he paid £25 per annum for a bedroom and sitting room, and coal and gas in winter. The rateable value of the house was £24. —Mr. Browne: He pays £1 a year, more than the whole house is worth. I object to the claim.—ln -answer to Mr. Browne, the -claimant said he paid fortnightly for Nis lodgings, 10s. a week in winter and 9s. in summer.—The barrister did not think the claim-a very good -one, but hardly thought he • could expunge it. Heundoubtedly kept two rooms. He thought the description sufficiently accurate. Approximately it was £2s—Mr.Browne : He makes a declaration that that is exactly the amount paid.— The claim was allowed.—Oreste Praeger,42 Lovely- lane, was claimed for as a .lodger by the Con- servatives. -In reply to Mr. Browne, he said he was the son of Herr Praeger, who was a Dutchman, his wife being an Englishwoman. The claimant himself was born in Liverpool. He , paid for a bedroom and a sitting room 7s. a week. He was a professor of music. His father used the sitting room for practice. The claimant occu- pied the bedroom with his two brothers. In answer to Mr, Hampson, he said they slept there by his permission. —The barrister: Thelaw requires that you shall have sole occupation of certainly one room at least. You are described in your declaration as having sole occupa- tion of two rooms, but that is not good enough. I die- - allow the claim.—Frederick Wm. Wood, reporter, 13, Pine-st., submitted claim through the Conservative agent, as a lodger. Mr. Wood said he lodged with his father. He slept in a double-bedded room, and his brother slept with him every night. The house was rated at CIA. The claim was disallowed on the ground taken by Mr. Browne that the complainant had not sole occupation.—The Conservatives put in a claim for Thos. Burton, jun., 82, Liverpool-road. He lived with his father and paid 9s. per week, for two rooms on -the second floor. His brothers did not sleep with hira,,but had separate rooms.—Mr. Browne objected that the form of declaration stated that the rooms were on=the ground-floor and that the claimant, paid -P2.3 a year. Ile now-said they were on the secondloor and that he paid 9s. a- week.—The barrister: Ido not think that is good enough for an objection. The amount is substantially -FM a year,—The statement ,might be incorrect and yetthe claim be a bond ficle one. The claim might be amended. --Mr. Browne: You have no power to amend a declar- ation for a lodger's claim.—The barrister: A clerical error.—The claim was disallowed.
A HST AT SHE CONSERVATIVES.

Richard Crompton, clerk to Mr. Browne, solicitor, claimed as an occupier Sor a house in Legt-st., desiring his nameto be placed entbe list instead.of that of his mother. ":IMr. Browne supported the ,claim. He stated that. he was the sole eupport of the •household, but in reply to Mr. Hampeun admitted that two rooms were occupied by lodgers.:—.ln answer to Mr. Browne, the claimant said the Conservatives had claimed for him last year, but he had never signed..(Laughter.) His Honour avowed the claim.

He said he occupied the best rooms in the house and paid 10s. a week for them.—The Assistant ,Overseer, said the house was lasted at £I2 net.—Mr. 'Browne objected to the claim on the ground that the premises were not of sufficient value.—The revising barrister remarked that the precedent was a bad one, but he had no doubt the claim was Zona fas, and lzie would therefore stretch a point aid admit it, but it was a close run.—The claim of Asthur James 'Titmouse, 504 rWilderspool Causeway, as a lodger, was supported by the Conserva- tives. ;He said he paid 18s. ameek for board sand lodg- ing,but it appeared that he went away at the week end and his rooms were ocoupied iduring his absence. The claim was therefore disaliewed.—Richard Ellin, •23, Liverpool-street, claimed as aiodger. He lived with his father at the above address and had two front rooms. It was elicited by Mr. Browne that the rent of the house was ,only All, and the claim <was, disallowed.

A FELLOW. The revision was resumed on Wednesday morning and continued till late in the afternoon.—Mr. Hampson, on lite court.being opened, complained that en the previous evening, Mr..,Brewne had called him a felloW. Mr. Browne said he. bad not spoken to Mr. Hamps?n after the court had .rises.—Mr. Hampson : It was in-court. He would not have dared to say it nutside. The Revis- ing Barrister said, a great deal depended upon the tone in which the words were spoken. the beat of ad- vocacy things sometimes slipped from ever3tody.,seven from the best regulated men that ought not to be said. One should do, as one did in a scrimmage at footbak4take kicks as they came. He thought Mr. Lampson had teen unnecessarily sensitive on the matter.
