J. Berry, Viinwick-rd., complained that his claim had - been objected to on the ground that he had parish relief, - though such was not the case. Mr. Browne and Mr. Hampson both denied having made the objection. Mr. Hampson on ,examining,his papers said the objection 02ad been made but withdrawn a month ago. Mr. Berry had therefore no need to attend there.—Mr. • Berry said- the objection came to .him time after tame.---The bar- rister : I cannot assist you. A. SOLICITOR'S CLAIM.

Mr. Jenkins, solicitor, made a claim for an occupa- ;lion vote in respect to premises in Winseick-street. -frhe Conservatives supported his claim. In , answer to , Mr. Browne, he said the rentmas £l5 a year, and it was treduced in consideration of his having made .some alterations to the .offices. There were two occupiers, himself, and his partner, Mr.z4,l)nsworth. The revising barrister held that the payment of £l5 rent gave the right to one vote. As Mr.! Unsworth was not on•the list, ' hoallowed Mr. Jenkins's claim. MIS-SPELLING NO BAR ,TO QUALIFICATiON. Kr. Browne brought forward a claim to the occupa- tion franchise on behalf. of ;Absalom Taylor, 239, Winwick-road. Mrs. Taylor 'was present in place of theclaimant, her husband. Mr. Ilampson objected on the ground that the claimant was misdescribed as of Willwieh-road, this being 0. mis-spelling. This ought to be put ,right by declaration.—The Revising Barrister said Lacould not entertain an objection like that, and allowed4he claim.—Mr. Browne. said there were a num- ber of cases in which there were similar objections, and asked hislionour if he would dedl with them in the same way,—Mr. Hampson I don't know that there is one.—Thesbarrister said for such a thing as the obvious slipping of a letter in a name,as such errors were inevit- able, he would not disqualify a claimant. MEAT, OCNSTITUTES sum:toms, OCCUPATION? W. C. Burton,who lives at Grappenhall-rd.,Latchford, made a successive occupation claim in respect to the cycle workaingroundary-st. r. Hampson supported the claim. Mr. Browne said the claimant was already on the list's respect of the house in which he lived and he was COW adding his occupatioa of that to his occupation in Foundry-at. in order to obtain another vote, which he could not do. Re must have left the house and ;lost his first qualification, and subse- quently have occupied the premises in Foundry-st. to establish his present . claim. Mr. }lampoon maintained that there had been successive occupation within the tmeaning of the Act.—Mr. Browns: Mat lathe meaning •of the word successive—Mr. Hampson : don't think .you have much idea of the meaning.—MrLßrowne's objec- tion was sustained, and the claim disallowed.

MIS-SPELLING QF A CHRISTIAN NAME. The Liberals made an occupation claim on behalf of J. Kelly. Garden-st. Mr.HamPson objected on the ground that an his description a Christian name bad been emit- ted. His Honour held that such an omisaion did not Invalidate the claim, and allowed it. Ammon, ,LODOPR'S CLAIM. rittr. Browne claimed on behalf of C. Plinston,ll3,Horse- market-st., as a lodger with his father. The claimant's ,brother appeared, and stated that the house was rated a t £50., and a portion of it was occupied as a shop, in re, nly to Mr. Hampson he admitted that he had only a be( Arnopi to himself. The Revising Barrister remarked that .one room in a house like that might be considered of £-1.0 a year value. The claimant's brother said 7s. a week' was paid fr the room, and £4 to £5 a month for board and lodging,—Mr. Hampson : Afamilv arrange- ment.l (lontend.—The brother, in answer to Mr.l3rowne, said the claimant had a piano and other furniture in his own room.. The claim was allowed. TWO' LADIES CLAIM THE MUNICIPAL TOTE. Mr. Bron,•ne submitted the claim of his two un- married sisteivs, of Crosfield-street, to the municipal vote.—Mr. Browne said that for a number of years prior to his mother's death in April last, they had lived with her. They had then been Yirtnally thy tenots fOae

house, because they were the principal means of support of the house, although it was in his mother's name, until April. After her death he sold his sisters the whole of the furniture and they had lived together there since he was married.—Mr. Hampson : They cannot claim suc- cession from the mother. There is no devise to them. Mr. Browne:. They have paid the rent since their mother's death.—The Revising Barrister: They have paid the rent for a very much longer time than is neces- sary for the qualifieation.—Mr. Hampson : I don't think the claim is good.—The barrister said unless Mr. Ramp- son could show some valid objection the claim must be admitted. Mr. Hampson said he objected that there was a new tenancy. They could not take Mr. Browne's statement that they had been substantially the tenants before their mother's death as conclusive on this point. —Mr. Browne in reply to Mr. Harnpson, said if his mother had been alive now she would not have been ,on the list for that house.—The Revising Barrister remarked that the fact of the house being in the mother's name was no proof that her daughters did not pay the rent. Probably• they allowed this to be so not wishing to hurt her feelings. He would allow the claim.
THURSDAY. EX-ALDERMAN DAVIES' VOTE.

Ex-Alderman Davies, 'who was on the list in respect of his residence, The Old Warps, Latchford, was objected to by the Liberals.—Mr. Browne said he thought it was well known that Mr. Davies resigned his position in the Town Council as he was.leaving the town.—Mr. Davies: No ; I am not aware of it.—Mr. Browne: Was it not published in all the papers ?—The Revising Barrister : What they choose to put in the papers has nothing to de with it. —Mr. Browne: •Do you deny you were •going to reside at Buxton ? Did you see it in the papers P—Mr. Davies: No.—Mr. Browne thought it was well known that his (Mr. Davies's) son came to liveat The Old Warps in his place.—Mr. Davies: Not in my place; stt the farm- house.—Mr. Browne: He occupies the house you formerly occupied.—Mr. Davies.: No.—Mr. Browne,: Was it in consequence of Mrs. Davies being an invalid that you left there P—Mr. Davies; Yes.—Mr. Browne: And went to reside at Buxton.—Mr. Davies: Yes, for two months. —Mr. Browne : At the time you went away had you any intention of returning P—Mr. Davies: I 'simply went to a hydropathic institution.—Mr. Browne.: Didn't your son sell his house at Appleton for the purpose of going to live at The Old Warps ?—Mr. Davies believed he did.— Mr. Browne: And you resigned your aldermanship at the same time.—Mr. Davies said he did, but he paid the rates and everything, and he had made very great structural alterations in the farmhouse o'f his son.-IYLe. Browne said the grounds of the objection were that it was wall known that Mr. Davies had left the town.— The Revising Barrister said they did not appear to have got their information very correctly. What they had put in the newspapers was hardly matter. to be pro- ceeded upon as evidence, he thought It might be very good matter to report, but nothing else.—The objection was overruled, and Mr. Davies, having applied for ex- penses, was allowed a guinea, which he, however, re- turned to the Liberal agent.
A SERVICE OCCUPATION TEZIE'E._

John Oharles-Cummings manager of Mr. J. B. Isaac's shop in Bridge-st., claimed a service occupation of the residence in Bridge-st. In answer to Mr. Hampson, Mr. Cummings said he was not aware that Mr. Isaao was on the voter% list in respect of this house. Mr. (Isaac had never occupied a room or part of a room, though he had slept there one night when he had missed his train.—The Revisingidarrister said that Isaac's name would•have to come off the list in regard to this house.—Mr. Browne: There is no objection.—The Revising Barrister: Well, he must coma off.—Mr. Brewne : You have no power. —The Revising Barrister said he should require a good deal of argument to show thathe had no power. He had been perfectly satisfied over and overagain be had the power to do it. The vote of Mr. Cummings was allowed.
COUNCILLOR PIERPOINT'S PHOTOGRAPHIC 'STUDIO.

Councillor W. Pierpoint claimed a vote in respect to a studio at N, Wash-lane, the claim being opposed by the Tories. . In answer to Mr. Hampson, Mr. Pierpoint said he did not know whether the studio was rated or not.— Mr. Hawkins (assistant overseer for Latchford) said there was no studio rated, 'out Mr. Pierpoint had served him with a notice to have it rated.—Mr. Thompson: Has Mr. Pierpoint tendered you any raoneyl—Mr.:Haw- king : ;No.—Theitevising Barrister said thestudio would be rated with the house.—Mr. Hawklike: With the house and gerden.—Mr. Hampson (to Mr. Pierpoint) Is the studio a wooden building P—Mr. Pierpoint : Yes.— Mr. Hampson : Has it been an old kitchen P—Mr. Pierpoint: ,Old kitchen! (Lauglater4) ;U: - suppose I am obliged to answer this question,--The ,Revis- sng Barrister: 'Yes. (Laughter.)—Mr. Pierpoint: It is not an old kitchen, and never was. lltAvas built for the purposes of a studio by myself, and has.been used as such.--Mr. Hampson asked if it was :not a fact that in that Council Chamber a Liberal alderman had challenged his. right to be there.—Mr. Browne: Oh, really I—The Revising Barrister did not think that was the , question. The question was one of law as to whether or not premises which had not beenrated would .give a person a ,qualification.—Mr. Hampson : You live within a quarter of a mile or so of this studio ? Mr. Pierpoint: Hampson You had got a large house with plenty of room in it .-P—Mr:Tierpoult : I don't know that.—Mr. Hampson : You are only, an amateur photographer and you keep this studio merely for the purpose of getting a municipal :vote.—Mr. Pierpoint: Nothing of the kind.—Mr. Hampson : Will you say on your oath that you do not retain tit for that purpose P—Mr. Pierpoint: Yes, I will.—The Revising Barrister: If he is a photographer he would require a studio.—Mr. Hampson asked Mr. Hawkins what the whole of the premises in Wash-lane were rated at.—Mr. Hawkins : £l4 10s. ; it has been rated at that for. more than, 20 years.—The.Revising Barrister said if the.whole of the premises were rated only at LH riDs.. it•would not give £lO annual-vs/tie for the studio.—Mr. Browne said they only claimed for the burgess vote.—The 'Revising barrister allowed the vote.
.I)R, HISBET AIM THE MEDICAL_ABENKIL&TION.

Dr. J. B. Kisbay, of 13, Palmyra-square, was objected to by the Conservatives. In .answer to Mr. Ilampson, Dr. Kisbe.y . said he was the servant of the Working-men's Medical sassociation. Be had been inthe court before and his vote was allowed by the Revising Barrister. .The house formerly occupied by the Aseocia- Lion onNriar's-green was rented, but their prese4place was owned by them .—ikr.Rampson: And they.reqAure you to live there P—Draisbey : Not necessarily.—Mr.Brawne was proceeding to reacarom the rules of the Medical As- sociation as they related to the duties of Dr.lCisbey.when Mr. Rampson interrupted, and Mr. Browne exclaimed " I wish that man would not chatter so much there." (Laughter.)—The Revising Barris* advised Mr. Raw- son not to get excited, and pointed out that it was no use raisidg questions for discussion which had no :bear- ing on the case. The question was really whether or not it was compulsory upon Dr. Kisbey to live at the house. There was no doubt he was compelled to attend at the dispensary.— Zlr. Hatnpson asked that Dr. Kisbey should be put on his ,oatthand this having been done, Mr. Ramp- son asked him if be would swear that he was not requested to live on the premises by, his employers, the Committee .of the Medical Association?—Dr.,Kisbey : No, there is no absolute condition.—The Revising Barrister decided to allow the vote,,,and,Dr. Kisbey claimed that expenses should be allowed to him as he tad been objected to before.—The Re.vising Barrister said he would allow .a guinea. LLODGline ,VOll4l.

Robert Bruce Fleming who was on the lodgers' list, .was objected to by the Conservatives. He said he lived .with his father, Councillor Fleming at Winmarleigh Lodge, off Sankey-St„ and also worked for him at his tannery. He paid £25 A year for his lodgings, apart from his maintenance. He was paid for his services at the tannery.—Mr. Browne.: your father is not the only partner in the firm 2—Mr. Fleming.: No.—Mr. Hamp. SOU,: Who is the other partner.?—Mr. Fleming: I decline to answer that.—The Revising Barrister did not think a . question like that should be asked. He would allow the vote. Robert Bond Matthews claimed as a lodger with Mr. Grimsha.w, of Gatehouse farm, Sankey Bridges. He had resided there for lour years and had ,paid at the rate of .17s. ed. a week for rooms and attendance. lie asked for expenses to be allowed him against the Liberals who had opposed the vote, but the Revising Barrister pointed out that these could not be allowed as that was only a claim.—Mr. Matthews: Oh, I should like to have had Mr. Browne on the hop. (Laughter.) The Rev. John Davies claimed as a lodger at 8, Cairo- st., and said he paid £.31 a year for the lodgings only. The vote was allowed.,

div.head: EXPOSINO THE MACHINERY.
div.p: EXPOSINO THE MACHINERY.

Ayoung inarned woman appeared in support of a claiin for a voteby her husband. Mr.. Browne opposed the claim, the point in dispute being as to whether the claimant had occupied a house the whole of the qualify- ing year. In answer to Mr. Browne the young woman said they went into residence in the June of last year. Mr. Browne asked,if she had been told to say June by a Conservative agent, and to this the you lig woman re- plied. after a little hesitation, that she had been told to say June by a gentleman, but she did not know who he was. The Revising Barrister did not consider the evi- dence sufficiently good to substantiate the claim.
RESEECTABLE ERROR.

The lodger vote of John Dunbobbin, of 35, Cairo-st., was objected to by the Conservatives. The rateable value of the house was said to be £lo.—The Revising Barrister: That won't d0..-31r. S. Dunbobbin, the father of the voter, said his son had had a vote seven years. The Revising Barrister said a long perpetuation oterror did not make it correct. It gave it a certain respect- ability, of course,

FETYOLOUS OraIrECTIONS. The proceedings on Thursday' were marked by the numbers of what may fairly be termed frivolous objec- tions to Liberal voters who came before the Revising Barrister. The Conservatives seemed to have been on thelook-out for slight clerical or printers' errors in the spelling of names, and wherever these had occurred a notice of objection had been served. Such cases as Firth instead of Frith, Jeffery in place of Jeffers, and other similar minute misplacements or replacements of letters were brought under the notice of the Revising Barrister, and the persons in whose cases tbe srnal)r_mis- takes had happened were under the necessit7 of appearing to defend their' votes. In one instance the only objection appeared to be that the number on the 11007 was painted instead of being in metal. In

almost every case the Revising Barrister sho wed the value he attached to the objections by allowing the vote and awarding the voter his expenses. In consequence of this the treasury of the Conservative agent was at one time drawn upon to an alarming extent. Judging from the voter's estimates of the loss they sustained by missing a day's work, good wages must be the rule in Warrington. Scarcely any of them placed their daily re- muneration at lessthan 55., and 75., or Bs.,was the more frequent figure. Where the wife or a female relative of the voter appeared in his place she was generally awarded 2s. or 2s. 6d., as a compensation for the bak- ing or washing that had been postponed. The court adjourned till Monday when the revised lists will be read over.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 12, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 12, 1891.
THE NEW POSTIEASTER-GENERA.L.

The Duke of Rutland will provisionally accept the duties of Postmaster-General. The Prime Minister does not wish to alter the positions Of the junior holders of portfolios in the Cabinet, and the Duke's acceptance will not create a parliamentary vacancy.

div.head: SHOCKING LOVE TRAGEDY.
div.p: SHOCKING LOVE TRAGEDY.

-eensational and deplorable tragedy took place at Bloemington on Tuesday. Dr. Charles tatland was in love with Miss Bertha Ison, a young girl at school. He urged her to marry Him, but she did not wish until after her graduation. They had several interviews, he being more and more urgent. He left her last week in auger, and returned on Tuesday to ask an interview. No sooner had she appeared than he shot her three times, and then Shot himself. Both are dead.

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE AND LABOUR REPRESENTATION.
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE AND LABOUR REPRE- SENTATION.

A Dundee telegram states that Mr. Gladstone :has written the following letter to a correspondent Tar be it from me to.question the right of labour to 'feral a party for itself. indeed Ido not contest that Tight to every class of the community. If they all exereise•it we shall have a queer Parliament. The practical question in my view is an increase of representation of labour. This increase I have always exerted myself heartily to promote. I shall continue to exert myself, but I be- lieve the Government of this country will continue as heretofore to be carried on by a party combination."

div.head: LINTH. WAITE TRAGEDY.
div.p: THE LINTH. WAITE TRAGEDY.
A CONFESSION.

James Stockwell,who was suspected of the linthwo-ite murder, was arrested on Monday morning. It is stated tbat, tired of being hunted down,he went Otis mother's house at Paddock, Huddersfield, on Sunday night, and that Mrs. Stockwell on Monday morning called in n police Officer and intimated that her son awaited arrest. Stockwell, who presents a pitiable appearance, went quietly to the police station. The prisoner, who is aged 32 years, and described as a teamster, of Miles Bridge, was brought 'before the Huddersfield magistrates,charged with the wilful murder of Catherine Dennis, at Linda- waite. Upon the charge being read to him, the prisoner, amid considerable sensation, pleaded guilty. Hwang at once handed over to the county authorities, taken before two county justices, and remanded to Wakefield tior eight days.
DOUBLE MURDER AND SUICIDE :IN
LONDON.

A supposed double murder and suicide was discovered on Saturday afternoon, in Hungerford-road, Holloway, London': Number fifty-one in that thoroughfare is occu pied by a traveller to a firm of chemical manufacturers, named Ernest Nightingale, his wife, two children, aged sixteen and four months, and their servant. The family retired to rest in the usual way on Friday night, but nothing was seen of them on Saturday morning. At noon, the servant, becoming alarmed, entered the bed- room,and found her master and mistress lying insensible in bed ; the i oelder child was also insensible in' its -cot. She at once raised an alarm, and a doctor being brought to the house-he found that the man, woman, andchild were dead. The police were communicated with, and took charge of the premises, witk-several samples of chemicals,which were found in the room. Late on Saturday night the bodies were removed to Holloway; to await an inqueit. Death in each case is supposed to have occurred from poisoning by strychnine?, as several bottles containing this drug was foundin the room. A fourth death has occurred in connection with the Holloway tragedy. Ruby Florence Nightingale,the baby supposed to have been poisoned on Saturday, died on Tuesday. This makes the fourth victim, and completes the extermination of the family. It was the youngest child of Mr. and Mrs. Nightingale,beinglynt four months old. Though-the doctor is reserving his discoveries con- cerning the deaths for the coroner's jury, it is stated that the deaths resulted from poisoning by sa powerful acid. Regarding Mr. Nightingale's :alleged financial difficulties, it is still doubtful whether the statement has any foundation as he has for many years drawn an an- nual salary of 41400. An inquest was opened a Holloway, on Wednesday. The medical evidence stated that without a minute analysis the cause of death could not bespecifically given and the inquiry was consequently adjourned.

div.head: AN AMUSING DEBATE.
div.p: AN AMUSING DEBATE.
(Supposed to have taken place in a prominent hotel in Wobblington). ElimiNo2sThkS.

In (..:onsequence of some little discussion in the bar parlour of the "Safe Ball-dog," Wobblington, after all the old licenses ha el been renewed at the Brewster Sessions, it was Cecided that, on the fol- lowing Thursday evening, a debate should take I place, bearing on some phase of the licensing ques- tion. 'A small Committee was appointed to make arrangements, and so, at the time agreed upon, a considerable number Of Dot-house favourites met together. Tte gentlemen having assembled in the bar 'parlour ef the "Safe Bull-dog," Mr. Benjamin Mashtub arose, /and amid lcud cheering, proceeded to introduce to the meeting as chairman, the august and impressive personage, knawn to :every an present as Timothy Wind- swell, landlord of the "Safe Bull-dog." Mr. Mash- tub said it would be superfluous for him:to say anything concerning Mr. Windswell, as he was by no means a stranger, his great :virtues and high in- tellectual abilities being well known to all. Gaze, gentlercen,on his manly figure, made noble through the frettuent ate of that glorious decoction, which a certain class:of mean two-legged animals would snatch—(cries of "Shattre.")—yea,gentlemen,would snatch from our loving grasp. 'Gaze upon him, and, as hie eloquent tongue las:lames the activities of debate, and Int the proper moment sums up the whole discussion and presents the true aspect of the-question., remember that ,you are gazing upon, and listening to one, who but for some few hind- rauces 'would be recognized as a :modern Demos- i thenes. Centlemen, realizing that through the over-whelming feelings of :my heart I have over- stepped t4e limits of prudence, ; I now without furthez Otservation beg to introduce to you, one who biscause he is impartial, and to a great extent disinterested in the :question, has 'been chosen for ' this h.CVITC, urable position. (Cheers.) Mr.. Windswell, after he had coughed, adjusted his sprectacles and cast over his audience a sweet, affectionate dlance said=-Gentlemen, (applause)—' frier ;de —(further applause)—brethren,(great cheer- ing; arad tears in many eyes). 'My heart is in the r cast nest therewith (pointing towards a barrel)—with ' —l€ it me see is it FalsticE or Shakespeare? (Shouts and: fdhorus "He's a ,jolly good fellow.") After the chc OfTl3 he proceeded:: We are here for the purpose of disJussing a subject which touches each of use If peeple threatened to take from us our bible, that (v arly tenderly) would be hard. Speaking person- all,y.f I slbould feellt keenly, for I have one that was gi voi to me when a boy. (handkerchiefs appear). I m reer had any other,and I:prize it so highly that I, h• ave. newer allowed it to be opened by anyone, and h av:. never opened' it myself, all these years:; but I have &fisted it:every other week with my own hon- ept andl innocent hands. But, friends, our :enemies KUL at something mere precious they would rob the po or man of his beer, the beverage that has done 9 o much 'to make England great—(hear, hear) --Lae very life-bloddeif thenation. The liquid that encircles ourbeloved island' has done much to pro- tect u s, but not near so much as the delicious bev- erage that abounds in the breweries, distilleries, hotelf ; and beerhouses orti-Lr dear country. The gentleman that introduced me uttered -very kind and c omplimentery :words. Among other things he allud ed to my • impartiality, Gentlemen, friends, and brethren, tr there is enything of which I am eve( :daily proud illia the knowledge that ',I am im- part; Who-ean accuse- me of unduly leaning to- wer( Is one sidEref the question which is to be dis- cuss ed ? 'TeMptcariCe men are bigoted and incon- sistt int; we areenot so. 'They exhibit partiality, but we I ;each tbem better things. (Hear, hear.) The question for debate' is as follows—" Resolved, that a la rge increasein the nuither of licensed houses in this town is greatly to be desired, and =would no doubt make our beloved town more lively than it ' is a t present,andwould thus directly and 'indirectly cre ate greater activity in,many homes?' The prin- cipal speaker for the affirmative is Mr. Peter Nose- flu: ;h, and for 'the negative Mr. Andrew Latecab. Th e Speaker' for' the dErmative will. open the del bate. Mr. Peter'NoSerlush said: Mr. Chairman and Gen- tlE imen,l am:proud of :my position here to-night, pr oud to see: you all, and to feel that you have the pl easure of-seeing me in th:s nursery of-v:rtue and te mperance;prepared to defend the interests of the di slightful and purifying trade inwhich our worthy cl rairme.n is ar-valiant leader and captain. I should h eve 'been pleased to add 'to the words that have b een reed in your hearing—Resolved that-the num- b er of churches in our native town •Siiould be p :reatly diminished. (Hear, hear.) Sometime ago, C a a Saturday titernoon,l ,wes-atrollingout, scarcely I mowing whereto go; within me there wean strange (!raving for something. I could not tell erectly what. In my wanderings I arrived presently at- the door 3f a church. tried to enter, but the odoor was I locked. I knocked and cried out, but reeeived no : answer, .finttwas about to 411epart,‘ when a lady, who 'it seems had come to dust tie pews for- the ap- proaching Sabbath, came and unlocked the door. She said I might enter, so I.l.went in and gazed , around. tfteraitting dawn a few minutes; seeing nothing that I- eared about, and still having the strange cravingwithir, I was about to depart. Just at that moment the lady came and asked me if I would kindly 'move for a moment while i3il6 dusted the seat. lids made me very angry, and as the strange craving had not forsaken me I rushed out .of that inhospitable habitation:,and inless than two minutes .had:reached "The Safe Bull-dog:" After I;aking four glasses of stout, three of whisky and water and a th'op els rum, the :strange craving seemed to be somewhat relieved, and ever since that day, I have, with one exception, strictly avoided &Ideal- ings with cburehes, and have felt myself bound by double ties to the ever-growing charms of the" Safe Bull-dog." I spoke of one exception. I allude to an occasion on which I 15218 basely led into a certain Congregational Church„wh ere the preacher wounded my dignity by actually saying that" the drunkard should not inherit the kingdom of God." I must ask you to pardon me if I have seemed to depart a little from the question as read, but, having heard my experience,lfeel sure that you must agree with me that we greatly need to diminish the number of

churches, and to increase the number of licensed drinking houses, so that poor men like us who are often affected with an inward craving, may without much exertion find such a home of peace as, for ex- ample, the "Safe Bull-dog" affords, where special attention is paid to thirsty souls. (Applause.) Mr. Andrew Latecab was next called upon to speak on the negative side of the question. Mr. Latecab said : Mr. Chairman and gentlemen,l am no great scholar and shall say only a very few words. Flowever, I am proud of the honour :of taking part In this concussion. My enemy on the other side has said very little that amounts to anything; his church story being a bit simple and off the mark. Ile has not done what I expected (a voice—" draw it mild.") lam drawing it as mild as I know how, gentlemen. I thought he would have shown trans- elusively that if there were more drinking places our town would be more lively than it is at present. He has not done so, I therefore say, he cannot prove it (a voice—'" respect the feelings of Mr. Wind- swell.") Where would you find a more lively little town than Wobblington ? You may go from Dan to Beer-sheba and fail to transcover a spot where more life and vigour is shown, not only on Saturdays but all through the week, and not only on the part of gentlemen, but ladies. And what is it I ask, that produces this life and vigour; this desire to walk on both sides of the road at once ; this power to give forth music during a dark and rainy night, even while lying in the gutter; this tendency to raise strange bumps on the heads of the several members of the happy family; it is, gentlemen, the glass that cheers (hear, hear and loud applause) the glass that cheers and conciliates. But still I say we have reached such a perfect state as regards this jollifica- tion point, that we cannot improve upon it. Then let us vote when the question is transmitted for our decision, bearing this in mind, that the increase of licensed houses could not make of our lovely town a more delicious Paradise that it is already. Mr. Windswell at this point gave permission for any member of the meeting to speak on either side of the question. Among the gentlemen who availed 'themselves of the privilege was Mr. Humphrey Diogenes, who said he was a brewer and therefore personally disinterested in the matter. He only spoke from motives of affection for his fellow-men. He had been specially pleased with the remarks of Mr. Noseflash on ecclesiastical points. He had been blessed with a long aud rich experience, in the course of which be had observed that teetotal preachers were of all men the most inconsistent. To his certain knowledge, they would speak against the public-house, and yet would not scruple to receive money from the col- lection box which they knew might possibly have passed from the hotel to the tailor, from the tailor to the cabinet-maker, and thus on en route to the church collection box. To hear such men preach on consistency would be to him indeed like a farce. After several other equally weighty remarks had been made the Chairman said that he claimed the privilege of summing up the discussion before sub- mitting the question to a vote. Among other arse things he said that in preaching against drinking, the preachers had an eye to business, and would not care how much pain they brought to the publi- cans if they could only fill the churches. He. would advise them to spend their strength in trying to pick up the few fallen characters who had ()lice been prominent Christians, and leave the loving drinkseller to deal with the millions of the people who needed peace and comfort. Some shopkeepers were just as bad as the preachers, and while they condemned the man who sold harmless beer to an intoxicated fellowman they themselves would not hesitate to supply him with a stupifying loaf of bread. The man might be staggering, yea well-nigh falling, yet they would withhold from him that for which he thirsted, and would offer him bread. Was that freedom ! Was it liberty !0, wisdom thou art fled to brutish beasts, and men have lost their reason (tears in many eyes). Gentlemen, he con- , tinned, I shall detain you only a few moments longer, but before concluding let me ask this: Sup- pese there had been no public-houses(cries of "Don't mention it ") but gentlemen only suppose such a calamity possible .•(groans and sighs) then what would have become of the troops, the brave defen- , dmrs of our country? When passing through our town some time ago, we took them in, sheltered, nourished, sustained them. But if our business had been swept away by some infernal tornado emanating from the so-called moral atmosphere of the temperance party, those soldiers must surely have perished for want of shelter and general acco- nacrlation. Then let me ask you to collect together in your thoughts the overwhelming evidence which has been presented in this debate, and vote as men of wisdom, and as Englishmen who are determined never to be slaves, but to rise to a grander pinnacle of true freedom and jollification. (Cheers.)—When the vote was taken every member of the meeting voted on the affirmative side of the question, being quite captivated by the irresistible logic of their impartial Chairman. .After the usual votes of thanks the meeting was brought to a close.

CONFERENCE ON THE " FREE" EDUCA-
TI ON ACT. FEE AND FREE PLACI.S.

On Monday afternoon a conference of elemen- tary school managers was held in the Council Chamber, Town Hall, Warrington, to take into consideration the course to be adopted for the car- rying out of the clauses in the new Education Act, as to the provision of free places in the various schools. The Rev. F. W. Willis, rector of Warring- ton, was voted to the chair, and there were a 153 present Rev. Canon Penrhyn (rector of Winwick), the Rev. Morley Stevenson, the Revs. E.C. E. Carle- ton, G. Alton, W. E. Glenn, John Yonge, Thos. Ross, F. Slater, John Gunnell, and J. J. Richards, Alder- man Holmes, Alderman Wright, Mr. Monks, C.C., Councillor F. W. Monks, Mr. E. J. Guest, Mr. R. Garnett, Mr. W. Long, Dr. Gornall. and Messrs. A. Woods, W. Twiss, D. Stansfield, J. D. Buckton, Z. Armitage, Haines, M. Bowden, Winskill, T. Haw- thorn, &c.—The Chairman thanked the meeting for electing him to the chair, and read the circular con- vening the meeting. He stated that there had been meetings of the head teachers and managers of the Parish Church Schools on the matter,and it had been decided to adopt the Act, as advised by the Town Clerk's circular. The first question to be considered was the demand likely to be made for free places. The head teachers of the Parish Church schools thought that if provision was made for five per cent. of the children that would be sufficient. It might be necessary to provide in those schools for more, but they contemplated building additional accomodation for infants to relieve the other schools. The numbers in their schools were 1,200 and they thought that five or possibly ten per cant. of free places would be sufficient.—Mr. Carleton said a meeting of the parents of the Trinity school chil- dren was called a month ago. About a third of all the parents were present, and from the way they received the proposals of the managers he should say there would be no difficulty in getting the parents to co-operate with them, or danger of the demand for free places being met in an unreason- able way. At the same time it was premature to say what the demand was likely to be.—ln reply to the Rev. M. Stevenson, the Cheirman said they gathered that the managers present were prepared to provide free places.—Alderman Holmes said the People's College had decided not to do so.—Mr. F. Monks said the Act would be taken advan- tage of at that college nevertheless, in the way of reduced payments.—Mr. Long said the People's College stood in a different position from other schools. That college had charged higher fees than the other schools, and it would be a greater sacri- fice for them to provide free places.—The Rev. J. Yenge said it was thought there ought to be some understanding as to who should decide which scholars should be free. He thought it would be a most invidious thing for the managers of any one school to have that to do. The best course would be for the School Attend- ande Committee to take the matter in charge.—The Rev Mr. Carleton thought it would be better to delay the consideration of matters for a few months during which time each school might hit upon some plan of action and then a report might be made to the future meeting, and it could decide what was to be done.—Mr. Slater thought it was the wisest policy for each school to provide as many free places as it was thought would be likely to have to be filled, keeping the fact to them- selves, because if there is something to be given there are always numerous claimants,and they are not always thosain need. If they advertised that this and that school were in favour of so many free places that would create a little difficulty.—Mr. F. Monks was in favour of letting each school manager manage his own way. The Department only contributed 10s, a year,and he did not see that it gave any power to control the management of any school. The People's College had decided to take advantage of the Act, and the rate of fees had been ad- pasted accordingly. If there was any difference, that would be deducted at the end of the year. The Roman Catholics, he believed, had already made their schools practically free. He quite agreed with Mr. Slater that before very long there would be a very con- siderable damand for free places, and the ques- tion was who was to provide them. So far as the People's College was concerned they had decided that it formed no part of their duty to do it.

div.head: tl•\IT
div.p: tl•\IT
THE QUESTION OF A SCHOOL BOARD.

Mr. A.G. Jolley said Mr. Monks had forgotten that there was an authority not in existence but looming in the future, a School Board. There was a feeling amongst various schools which was a healthy spirit of emulation, but if they allowed it to run to seed it would be- come a spirit of jealousy; then a School Board would come as a matter of fact in a very short time. He trusted that People's College authorities would not stand aloof if any scheme was propounded that would be for the good of the elementary schools. Without its support they might stand, though he doubted it, but if all of them combined they might avoid the imposition of a School Board upon the town. At the same time when a certain proportion of free places had to be provided if this were not done they would be provided by a School Board un- questionably. Mr. Carleton's suggestion for an adjourn- ment for three or four months met the difficulty. At the end of the time they would be in a position to deal com- pletely and fairly with the question. He, (Mr. Jolley) and his co-managers at St. Paul's would be happy to co- operate most heartily, and he thought the other school managers would be also. If such a school as the People's College was to hold aloof it would be a great blow to the good feeling which should exist amongst them all.—Mr. F. Monks said hedid not lose sight of the fact that there might be such an authority in the future as a School Board in the town. He had always been an ad- vocate for adopting a School Board, because he believed the education of Warrington would be bet- ter carried on under such an authority than hitherto. He had already thrown out a suggestion which he throught might to some extent meet the case if loyally and thoroughly taken up. If such an authority as Mr. Jolley spoke of did step in he (Mr. Monks) did not know that he should be afraid af it ; he should rather welcome it than otherwise. The authorities of the People's College did not wish to stand aloof. They had, he thought, always shown a disposition to work in harmony with other school authorities, and he was Quite certain would in the future.—The Rev. Mr. Carleton proposed: —" That ,a meeting of the manag,ers of the schools be called five months hence to ascertain what is the demand for free places,and to ,learn from the masters and managers how the methods adopted in the various schools for meeting the demand have been successful." The motion was put and carried—The Chairman read the circular letteto of the Town Clerk to the school authorities, which we have previously published. The Chairman observed that the first point in it was as to the adoption of the Act by the schools. He appealed to those present as to whether there was any school not prepared to adopt the Act, and, receiving no answer, said he sup- pesed it might be understood that all the schools would accept it. The next point in the circular was as to the time when the Act would be adopted. It-was thought desirable by several who had spoken to him that it should be at the end of the school year, and that he thought would in most cases be the end of September; and in others at the end of October; but managers thought parents might grumble if in some schools there were free places and in others not, and he thought it would be well if all adopted the Act on the Ist of October.—Mr. Carleton thought some little responsibi- lity might be incurred by managers if they told parents they should not have free education till several weeks hence. On this principle the authorities of Trinity Schools had adopted the Act on the Ist of September.— Mr. Carleton said the great difficulty in the management of the schools was the financial one ; and they wanted some united method of bringing pressure to bear upon a good many people in the town who did not bear their share of the financial burden. Denonainational schools, he thought, were quite strong enough to take care of I themselves under a Board, and he for one was not go frightened of a Board as he once was—(cries of "hear, hear ")—but at the same time they objected to it in the interest of the ratepayers, who would rather demur to the establishment of such an expensive institution. If they could get something like a voluntaryrate--(Dr. Gornall : Too late). Well, it was asuggestion that could be carried out at a small cost—id. in the £, say.

div.head: SCrfOOL ATTENDANCE.
div.p: SCrfOOL ATTENDANCE.

The Chairman pointed out that the attendance of scholars declined very much the week before Walking Day, and the managers of the Parish Church Schools wished to have a school year of 46 weeks, and give three weeks' summer holiday,beginning the week before Walking Day, a fortnight at Christmas, and a week at Easter. It was thought some representation should be made to the mag- istrates and the School Attendance Committee about the desirability of enforcing better attendance of child- ren.--Mr. Guest had some fears that the'attendance at first might not be so good as it had been because parents woad get to know that frt. places were to be provided, and if they were not provided the absence of children would be the result.—Mr. Buckton thought the matter was one for the School Attendance Committee, rather than the magistrates, who could not move until tifeir attention was directed to it by the Committee.—Mr:Jolley thought the school attendance officers worked hard and ener- getically, but to some extent unsystematically. The School Attendance Committee were, he considered, rather out of touch with the managers of the elementary schools in more than one respect. Some magistrates he thought allowed sentimental considerations to sway them in dealing with the school cases. Ffe thought it would be a great advantage if a strong representation were made to the magistrates.—Mr. Garnett thought the school attendance officer and his assistants aid their work very efficiently and energetically. Mr. Riley was a very careful and admirable officer. The very worst cases of non-attendance at school were those in which the Board of Guardians paid the fees. There was a feel- ing that at some of the schools there was a little too much forcing and the children disliked to go to them, and could hardly be driven to them.—Mr. Long, speaking as a Cheshire magistrate, said he saw it notified that in one

retty sessional division not far from Warrington parents would be dealt with much les leniently in the future because they would no longer have the excuse as to pay- ment of fees. He had always thought it hard that poor parents should have to pay for compulsory attendance. —The meeting, after a vote of thanks to the Chairman, was adjourned for live months.

div.head: LABOUR CONGRESS AT NEWCASTLE.
div.p: LABOUR CONGRESS AT NEWCASTLE.

The 24th annual Trades' Union Congress opened at Newcastle, at noon on Monday, when about 54-0 dele- gates attended, representing, it was estimated, some- thing over 2,000,000 of trades unionists from all parts of the United Kingdom. The meetings are held. in the Town Hall, and no efforts have been spared, either by the local or Parliamentary Committee, to ml,ke the pro- ceedings successful. Mr. Harford, chairman of the Parliamentary Committee for the expiring year, occu- pied the chair. The Trades Union Chairman, in wel- coming the delegates, spoke of Newcastle as the cradle of trades unionism, and hoped the result of the week's work would be to secure the amelioration of the condi- tion of the labouring classes. The past year had wit- nessed a severe struggle to obtain shorter hours, and those struggles were not a mere pretext to obtain higher wages. The Mayor then welcomed the delegates to the city. Mr. T. Burt, M. I'., was then unanimously chosen president of the Congress. After long discussion on the method of voting, Mr. George Shipton, of London, was elected vice-president by 185 votes. Mr. John Wilson, M.P., Mr. Tait, Mr. Mawdsley, Mr. Judge, and Mr. Threlfall were appointed the Standing Orders Commit- tee. The report of the Parliamentary Committee was then read, and the Congress adjourned until Tuesday.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

In his address on Tuesday, Mr. Thomas Burt, M.P., the new President, referred to the work and organisa- tion of women, and said wherever a woman did the same work in quality and quantity as a man she ought to ask for the same pay, and the men ought to support her in asserting that claim. It was his opinion that the more powerful the trade unions grew the less they would hear of strikes. He was not there to utter a wholesale condemnation of strikes, but they were ugly weapons, and like the boomerang, unless skilfully man- aged they were apt to come back and hit the thrower. If they could get their disputes settled by the arbitrament of reason they would be fools—almost criminals—to resort to strikes. What they had a right to demand was that the capitalist, how- ever powerful and proud, should receive and listen to their representatives. The probability was that strikes in the future would be on a larger scale than in the past, and if they, representing two million workers, were unanimous and determined, it was impossible to say how much they could accomplish. His leaning was rather in the direction of self-help than State compulsion, and the problem they had to solve was the better distribution of wealth. A lively discussion followed on the method of voting,. The Congress reaffirmed its decision with regard to an eight-hours day.

div.head: WEDNESDAY.
div.p: WEDNESDAY.

An extraordinary scene was witnessed at Wednesday's sitting. The eight hours question was further discussed, Mr. Hall, a Hull delegate, moving an amendment that any bill for the reduction of hours of labour should be of a permissive character, and not put in operation without the consent of at least two-thirds of the organised mem- bers of any trade. The amendment was carried and became the substantive motion. A livoly discussion fol- lowed, many of the delegates being strongly in favour of a legal eight-hours day. Mr. M`Bean, a London dele- gate, opposed the resolution, asserting that at present the workingpeople were simply in a condition of from work to bed and from bed to work. On the other hand Mr. Boyle, a Northumberland delegate, maintained that nothing had been said to prove that an eight- hours day would be beneficial, any more than a foor-hours, a two-hours, or no-hours day. If to work a very short day was good, to work no hours must be the best of all. Mr. Mawdsley, of Manchester supported the resolution, and said they would always have to earn their money. Flowery language would never help them to a solution of the labour question, even though it mightget applause from ignorant mobs. For the next few minutes the hall was a scene of great uproar. Delegates rose excitedly to their feet shouting "Withdraw, withdraw," and asking fiercely to whom ' Mr. Mawdsley referred when he spoke of "ignorant mobs." There was also hooting and hissing and other indignant protests. At the request of the Chairman, he withdrew the expression, but he said the men who started the eight hours movement were the men who wished to take away their work. Let them ask a French- man if he would assist them to get shorter hours. No. He kept his mouth shut about the fraternity business, and he wanted no liberty except the liberty to take our trade. Ultimately an amendment, moved bv Mr. Keir Hardie, enforcing an eight-hours day in all trades save where the majority of the members protested by a bal- lot vote, was carried, and, becoming the substantial motion, was adopted amid a scene of enthusiam by 341 to 73 votes.

div.head: THURSDAY.
div.p: THURSDAY.

At the Thursday's sitting discussion on factory legisla- tion was introduced by a resolution urging that the Act should apply to all places in which women and children worked, that it should be extended to laundries and domestic workshops, and that the age limit for children should be twelve years. The Congress adopted by 265 to 13 votes an amendment fixing the age limit at thirteen years. Resolutions were carried in favour of the pay- ment of members, the appointment of working-men and working-women factory inspectors, the protection of fishermen, the amendment of the jury system, and the withholding of contracts from firms giving unfair wages. The Congress also expressed its approval of co-operative principles. Delegates were nominated for election on the Parliamentary Committee,and it was announced that the Committee, having a balance of £l,lOO, was about, for the first time in its history, to open a banking ac- count.
DREADFUL ACCIDENT ON NORTH BRITISH RAILWAY. FIVE MEN KILLED.

Shortly before noon on Thursday, while a gang of four surfacemen and a fireman were repairing the North British line at Yorkhill, three miles from Glasgow, they stepped from one line to the other, when the Balloch passenger express came up unobserved, and dashed into them. All were killed instantly. The bodies present a dreadful appearance.

The line Was strewn with bleeding limbs, and one of the men had his head smashed to a pulp. The driver of the express stopped at Partick, and examined the front of his engine. The wheels bore marks of blood, and an engine and tender were at once despatched to the scene of the accident, and the bodies were conveyed to Partick, where they are being coffined. The news of the disaster has caused a great sensation.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY. SEPTEMBER 12, 1891.
THE, Trades Congress lias during Labour's Parliament. the week been., holding its twenty-

fourth meeting in Newcastle. Mr. THOMA.3-13IIRT M.P., is the new chairman, and on Tuesday he delivered the pmsidential aiddress.. He referred to the gathering as the largest and most representative body. of Trades Unionists that, had ever net in that or any other county. Conscious of the importance of the occasion,and that his words would be weighed throughout the kingdom, Mr. .BURT was. careful irs his statements. But he. WES as bold as he was careful; and took a,view of the labour 3robleras ef the age which must be pzonounced broad and, manly. Be showed himself, capable of oking ahead when he said that, with the growth of trades unions, there woull be fewer, strikes; but "the pzobability was that strikes in the future)when they did occuriwould be on a larger scale than in the past." This means that,with labour well organised, and as capable as capital of taking care of its. interest,both sides.will weigh the issues at stake and avoid conflict except as to matters of the greatest importance. Mr. Buw recognises that trades uuionists are divided as to the means to the end they have in view, nam.ely, improvement in the lot of the working cktsses.. He said:—

his own leaning was in the direction of self-help, and of associated effort, rather than of State com- pulsion. He did not undervalue the machinery of the State in regard to improving the condition of the working classes, and lightening the burdens of humanity. The problem they had to solve was the better distribution of wealth. They wanted to see th:,`, the worker should have a larger, a more equit- able share in the wealth he produced. They wanted that the poor man's child should have a fair chance in the race of life.
The President's speech met with a hearty re- ception; but when it came to voting on the ques- tion of an international eight hours day, it was

seen that his views as to State intervention were not the views of the majority. The resolution on the question, which was ultimately adopted by 232 votes to 163, expressed it as the opinion of the Congress that the time had arrived when the Government should endeavour to bring about, in conjunction with all foreign Governments, and in- ternational reduction in the hours of labour to eight per day, and demanding the convocation of an international conference for that purpose. It will be noticed that the international character of the resolution is something over and above the bare demand for an eight hours day which was made last yearwhen the Congress was held in Liver- pool. Trades unionists have profited by criticism of their proceedings: It has been frequently pointed out in, this and other journals that it was- hopeless to expect the Parliament of this couatryto look with favour upon a bill malthag eight hours the universal day, so long as very much longer hours were wo.iked on the. continent. This is recognised in the demand which hs. now made for an interna- tional cord srence,and vre cannot bit think that that is the best :node of proceeding. We are doubt.— less far from, the time when the whole civilise world will have adopte4 the eight hours day for all classes of 'Pork ; but sf this we are sure that international action, if firmly an persistently pressed, will eventually lead to a redostion of on-- tinental hours efilabsur to eAsmething :Site the nine, hours system which at present prevails in this. Tountry ; and that this in itsiturn will he followed by Englishmen adopting the eight liscrs day. Whether this will he accomplished. by Ngislative • action, or by coiment as between employers and employed it is prerlature to say ; but th:-.4 it will be accomplished can hardly be deubted b people who read the signs of the times.. On Wednesday thequestion was raised- tifintro- ducing the permissive element in the proposed Eight Hours Bill, the motion reopiring that the measure "should not beput in operation without the consent of at least two-thirds cf. the organised members of any trade." This mode of grappling with the difficulties arising out of mnaltiplicity of trades, and irregularity of hours,is iniown as Tiade Option ; and it is underctsod that it meets with the approval of Lord Itamzormi Cainsturim. • It - led to an exciting debate,, the feeling of those who.aelvocate eight hours as a hard' and fast line being that, if the matter was left optional, the • weaker trades would fail to get the benefit of legislation. It was made cikar, however, that the - representatives of the textile, trades were strongly opposed, to committing themselves out and out to the legal eight hours day, one of them pointedly remarking: that ha objected to• mechanics and miners lictating to factory workers as to their hours of labour. Ultim- ately, by way of compromise, the following amend- - ment was carried, and became. the substantive motion" That legislation regulating the hours of labourto eight per day shalt be enforced in all trades and occupations,save whore the majority of the organised members of any tmdeor occupation protest by a ballot vote against the same." In this form,, the motion was catiled amid great en- thusiasm by 341 votes to 73. The Congress may now be saidto be committed beyond recall on this important issue,and it is a matter-of course to say , that it will soon become a question of practical

To those who are seeking information we re- commend for persual "The Eight Hours. Day" by Mr: SIDNLAY WEBB, L.L.8., and Mr. HAROLD COX, B.AI The work is published, price is., by Mr. WALT= Siam; London, and, as every phase of the question is ably and temperately discussed, it ought to be in the hands of all peliticians and all leaders of- working-men. One important fact to be borne in.mind is that the artisans of Australia have for,3syears had the benefit; ofen eight hours day; and what has been accomplised in Australia, cannot be regarded as uttwrly impossible in Eng- land. The late Professor ROGERS, who was an authority on wages, prices and food in early times, says The artisan who is demanding at this time an eight hours day in the building trades is pimply striving to recover what . his ancestors worked,bylour or five centuriea. ago." It would Seem that we have gone backward instead of for- ward in, this respect, and this, notwitstanding the enormous aid which man has received within the present century—to go no further back-,-from the application of steam, electricity; and labour-saving inventions. We have around mai- it is true, more of the luxuries of civilisation; but we want more leisure .to enjoy them, and thisapplies to employers as well as -eanployed. An eight, hours day by . all means .; but how has it to be obtained? That is still the question.

THE new Education Act con- • Free Schools tinues to be something of a stum- bling block in the path of school managers. Many of thera, as in Warrington, don't know what to do; whether to refuse the fee grant, or accept the: grant and redace fees by the amount of the grant, or make schools free altogether. There is very little likelihood of the fee grant being largely de- clined, although this has been done at Rother- hithe, the parents, it is said, after being consalted, preferring fee schools to free schools. The ease is being cited by the Tories as proof that ther is "a. large body of working-men who ?refer to pay for their. children's education themselves!' We ob- ject,..however, to this way of stating the issue, for • even ,when the money is furnished by the State, . it really comes out .4the poclects of tho,workers. If, as is suggested,. Rotherhithe parents are so.. peculiarly indepeneent as to. reject tha fee grant. because it is a State grant, why do they not refuse the chief grant-in-aid provided by the State? There is certainly no, consistency, in accepting Goaernment aid t. tie extent of two-thirds of the cost of education, and dee.ining it as to the one-third bacause they " prefer to pay for their chiklren's education themselves," We suspect that itwil be found, in,thia•few cascawhere fees continue.to be raid as before, that there is a disposition t. set up a class distinction, in the belief that a better class of scholars will attend, such schools, and that a better education will be ' given. lint it will be seen that such is not the case, especially in School Board districts, where schools can readily ba made absolutely free, through the pmer which is granted to make up any loss out of the rates. It is well-known 'that the accommodation and equipment of J_loard Schools are on the whole, better than that of Voluntary Schools, and that, with an tl.xcellent body of well-paid teachers, az,- cducatior, given is certainly not inferior.

As against the exceptional cours'es taken at Rotberhithe, We may point to the action of the Manchester School Board in making most of their schools free under the new Xct. The result does not show that there is " a large body of work- ing-men" who object to Free Education, and that they have in consequence begun to send their children to the fee schools. It is just the reverse; there are already 800 more children in the Board

'Schools, while the average attendance has increased by no less than 2,150. We have always contended that the payment of fees had much to do with keeping children Out of school who would other- wise be found there, and the new experience in Manchester reduces the matter to demonstration. The fact is one to be taken into account by school managers who have not yet decided what to do. At the managers meeting at Warrington, on Mon- day, it was suggested that the School Attendance Committee should enforce attendance; but the willing attendance which comes of Free Education is far better than that which comes of coer- cion —to say nothing of the relief to the pockets of the poorest of the poor. It is worth mentioning that the 'Manchester School Board have advised the parents who can afford it to allow the pence hitherto paid as school fees to be credited to their children in the School Saving Banks. Acting on this advf se, as many as 4,881 new accounts have been opened with the school pence thus saved. In this way Free Education will come as a double boon—it will ensure better atten- dance, and lead to the formation of habits of thrift which may have important results in after life. The advantages of the School Board system are being everywhere perceived now that Voluntary Schools are at the parting of the ways. There are Tory man- agers even who are beginning to say they are not sure whether it would not be better in the long run to have a School Board; while Liberal mana- gers of voluntary schools are considering, in some towns,whether they should not bring their school's under School Board management by declining to -continue them any longer as Voluntary Schools. 'Soon or late, that will be the way out of present difficulties for all Voluntary Schools, and all who wish to be rid of friction, and rivalry, and was ted effort will say "the sooner the better."

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
We have received coannunications from "A Looker-on," "Blue boy;' and" lona," which are crowded out this week.

The cold wet summer has been hard on farmers and holiday people; but it has been hard, too, on the pestilential microbe; for the Warrington Hospital for Infectious Diseases does not at the present moment contain a single patient. That is something to be thankful for.

"Dear old Sir Gilbert" must have felt flattered, on Saturday, when the ardent old woman sought to kiss him in the public streets. What it is to be a baronet and a brewer, especially when the beer trickles from its lofty height and ends in a lowly kiss! Well, well, as the poet says—" Some men are born great, some achieve greatness, and some have kisses ' thrust upon them."

But the member for Warrington always had "a way with the women." Did he not himself tell how, when canvassing, he offered to turn the mangle whilst the busy wife went to look for the absent husband? Or as the poet again has it : Sir Gilbert once promised to mangle, To humour a woman's whim; But to-day we see a reversion— 'Tis a woman who mangles him.

There is something the matter with Lord Cross. What can it be? He usually makes an exhibition of himself when he proceeds, as he once said, to "reply to Mr. Gladstone," but he went beyond his known worst at Muncaster, on Tuesday. " When people," he said, " make up their minds on a great question they did not change their minds." What a pity Lord Cross cannot change or exchange his mind. The chances are great that he would profit by the transaction.

Lord Salisbury seems to have been afraid of losing another seat in a Parliamentary contest, 80 he has got over the difficulty as to a new Post- master-General by appointing the Duke of Rutland. And who is he, it may be asked ? He was Lord John Manners, who rendered himself famous as a young man by writing those unforgett- able lines : Let wealth and commerce, laws and learning die, But leave us still our old nobility.

Why all this wild talk and wild speculation as to the reported recent agreement between Russia and Turkey? According to a statement made by Lord Salisbury—and as Foreign Secretary he ought to know—" Russia possesses no rights in respect to passage through the Dardanelles and Bosphorus which are not possessed by the other powers also." If this be so, what is there to trouble about? Why prolong the play of "Much ado about nothing " ?

The Cardiff Licensing Bench have refused the renewal of six licenses, one of which was objected to by the police on the ground of its being unne- cessary, and another because the house was the resort of thieves. Convictions were proved against the remaining four. At Cardiff there is one licensed house to every 344 of the population ; but at Warrington there is one to every 250 of tho population; and yet the Warrington magistrates have renewed all the licenses!

Education at 'Daresbury and at Dutton is to be absolutely free. Daresbury and Dutton are small places, but they are possessed of School Boards, and that is "one for the School Boards." The schools too under the Runcorn Board are free; but the Widnes Board are charging a small fee. This is being done because the majority on the Board are denominationalists, whose first thought is to accommodate themselves to the managers of Voluntary Schools.

There seems no doubt, that the outbreak of typhoid fever, at St. Helens' had its origin in the milk supply, the Medical Officer of Health re- affirming his statement that" more than half the cases had consumed milk from the one dairy." It is not pleasant to think of fever coming in with the milk; but the facts should be faced, and special precautions taken. Cleanliness in the dairy is of the utmost importance in shutting off disease germs.

A man named Stockings was brought up at the ingligate Police Court, on Monday, for attempt- ing to commit suicide. It seems he was found sitting on the kerb with an unloaded revolver pointed at his head. He had plenty of cartridges, but didn't know how to load his weapon. Is this a case in which it maybe said—" Where ignorance is bliss folly to be wise ?" Or is it not rather suggestive of " make-believe " ? Stockings might not be " all there" ; but there is reason for think- ing he was "not such a fool as he looked."

The dear, delightful "great unpaid" must be kept going ; they are so very, very funny, at times. On Saturday, two boys were charged at Croydon. with stealing mushrooms, and, after the evidence had been heard, Captain Kemmis (chairman) ad- dressed the prisoners as follows: "Boys, no doubt you stole the mushrooms, but you will have the benefit of any doubt that might exist, and be dis- charged." This is about on a par with that other sapient J.P. who said :—"According to the evidence you are not guilty ; you are discharged this time; but don't do it again."

The Revision of the Voters Lists at Warring- ton, during the past week, has resulted as usual in a great deal of haggling over values and dates of occupancy. When shall we (Yet to the common- sense view that the vote should attach to the citizen apart from any question of property or occupancy? It is something to look forward to that reform in the registration law is one of the chief planks in the Liberal platform. The Tories seem to have made a considerable number of frivolous objections, and have had to pay for the privilege. The Liberals have every reason to be satisfied with the results of the Revision.

Morris, sang several anthems at each service in a manner that called forth much praise. Mr. Grica was at the organ. There were larre congregations.

FIREMEN'S COTTAGES AT WIDNES

The Widnes Local Board have decided that to allot the cottages built in conjunction with the Fire Engine Station in Lacey-st., as follows :—For fire brigade, six cottages adjoining the Fire Station on the Aiforde-st. side, and three cottages on the other side of the Fire Station. For the highway Department of the Local Board, four cottages; and one cottage for the Market Inspector. The rents were fixed at ss. 6d. per week. The Surveyor is to have superintendence of the pro- perty.

and got himself subjected to a fine at St. Helens, by refusing to "move on" when called upon to do so by the police. He would finish his tune, and instead of making • money by it, he is poorer to the extent of "2s. 6d. and costs." He has some- thing to learn. Why not take a hint from the case of a man stone-deaf who was charitably fur- nished with an organ ? A waggish acquaintance played a practical joke on him one day by remov- ing the cylinder. The deaf operator turned and turned unconscious that his instrument was silent. But the best of the joke was he got more money this day than any other. Here's a chance for Carlin, and no risk of being "run in."

Mr. W. C. Jones, of Preston Brook is still woo- ing—vainly wooing—the Leigh Division as a Con- servative candidate. He spoke at a Primrose picnic at Atherton Park, on Saturday, and proved to be an echo of an echo. His name has been men- tioned as the possible Conservative candidate for Warrington at the next election, and so has that of Mr. J. Charlton Parr. But what of Mr. Robert Pierpoint who was referred to at several Tory meetings—some time ago—as the young Obediah who was ready for the old Obediah's shoes? And what of Mr. John Roberts as his backer? Has he too, got to singing— Oh, no! We never mention him. His name is never heard ; My lips are now forbid to speak That once familiar word.

div.head: MARRIAGE AT APPLETON.
div.p: MARRIAGE AT APPLETON.

On Wednesday afternoon at St. Bedes Church, Apple- ton, the Rev. Dean Finegan united in the bonds of holy matrimony Mr. J. T. Singleton, of Victoria-road, Widnes, and Miss Anna C. Parkinson, of Appleton. The bride who was given away by her brother Mr. Abel Parkinson, wore a dress of grey silk, trimmed with cream Bombay silk, and a hat to match. The bridesmaids, Miss Christiana Parkinson and Miss Alice Wright were attired in blue and white cloth dresses, trimmed with Bombay silk. Mr. 11. Singleton was best man. The presents were numerous and costly.
LAWN MOWERS.—Garland, 51, Bridge-st., Warrington. and at Barlestown. .Advt

VOLUNTEER FUNERAL AT RUNCORN. On Thursday afternoon the mortal remains of Mr. Wm. Mason, landlord of the Camden Vaults, Surrey- street, were interred in Runcorn Cemetery with military honours. Mr. Mason, was a volunteer and at the recent encampment, he contracted a cold which took a more serious form, and he died on Tuesday. He was 30 years of age. His corpse was carried to its last resting place on the shoulders of his comrades, and on the coffin were his helmet and his arms reversed. A firing party of twelve, under the coMmand of Sergeant Mort, headed tie procession, then came the Volunteer.band playing the Dead March, and about 40 volunteers. Captain Ashton was in command. The funeral service was read by the Rev. Dr. Prescot, Chaplain to the corps. A large assemblage viewed the proceedings.

div.head: ARCHMASONRY AT RUNCORN.
div.p: ARCHMASONRY AT RUNCORN.

The annual 71,--e:TiiTi-Oi-6;e-iiriciieWa:i-e'r-Chapter (758) of Royal Arch Masons was held at the Masonic Hall, Runcorn, on Wednesday for the purpose of installing the chiefs and officers for the ensuing year. The installa- tion ceremony was performed by Companion Stevenson, P.P.G.5.8., in a very able and impressive manner. The following companions were installed and invested, viz. Companion J. White, P.P.G., assistant Soj, Z ; Compan- ion W. R. Wass, P.P.Gr., assistant Soj, Z.H. ; Companion T. H. Annett, Jr: Companion W. Mellor, P.P.G.P. Soj, treasurer : Companion A. Linaker, P. Soj. : Companion A. Upton S.E. ; and Companion W. Hankinson S.N. The chapter was then closed in due and solemn form, and the Companions sat down to a banquet, when the usual loyal toasts were proposed and responded to. A COLOURED BISHOP AT RUNCORN. Next Friday evening, in Runcorn Public Hall, the people of Runcorn will have an opportunity of listening to a bishop, out of the usual run of episcopal dignitaries. Bishop Hawkins, of the British Episcopalian Methodist Church, will describe his slave life and his escape, and as he is gifted with brilliant powers of description and a , moving eloquence, his hearers will have their reward in la narrative alive with personal experiences of the most thrilling description. The bishop was an intimate friend of Josiah Hanson' the hero of "Uncle Tom's Cabin," and performed the last sad funeral rites at his grave side. Although 80 years of aF,fe,Bishop Hawkins exhibits a vigour of frame and a brightness of intellect that charms all with whom he comes in contact, and the Primitive Methodists of Runcorn are tortunate in secur- ing his powerful aid. RUNCORN UNION SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. The monthly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday, under the presidency of Rev. J. W. N. Tanner.—The clerk (Mr. Ashton) produced the estimate of expenditure for the half year ending Lady Day, show- ing that £llB was required, but deducting a probable balance at Michaelmas of £65, there was only £53 required. A rate of one eighth of a penny would produce a little over this amount, and it was resolved to ask the Guardians to issue a precept accordingly.—The resigna- tion of the three attendance officers, Messrs. G. Ward (Runcorn), T. Riley Frodsham), and W. R. De Prez (Budworth), were considered and it was unanimously decided to ask them to retain their positions, which after some conversation they agreed to do. It was pointed out to them that it was the duty of the teachers to supply them with a list of non-attenders. I RUNCORN AND DISTRICT 406TH STARR BOWEETT BUILD-

div.head: ING SOCIETY.
div.p: ING SOCIETY.

The annual meeting of this Soeiety was held on Mon- day, under the presidency of Mr. James Povah. The tenth annual report stated that during the year £748 14s. 2d. had been received as members' subcriptions and the repayments on mortgages had yielded £B7B 18s. 4d., The total income was £1,659 6s. 9d. The cost of work- ing was £5B lls, 4d., a reduction of £ll 3s. 9d. on the previous year. A nett sum of £Bl7 ss. 7d. had been paid to withdrawing members and £225 had been advanced to members on mortgage on property. The balance i n favour of the Society after writing off the usual amount of depreciation was £96 83. Od. Five appropriations had been made making a total of 57 from the commencement of the Society. Thirty-eight members had withdrawn, the membership now being 290. The report was adopted. At the close of the meeting an appropriation took place,resulting in Mr. S. J. McCarraher of Rock Ferry, being entitled to an advance of £2OO.

WIDNES POLICE COURT

Yesterday, before Mr. T. S. Timmins, Alice Drury and Sarah A. Bate were remanded on a charge of stealing two cwt. of coal, the property of the United Alkali Co. RECOGNITION OF THE WESLEYAN MINISTER AT WIDNES. On Thursday evening a recognition meeting was held in Lacey-street schoolroom of the Rev. W. Pritchard, (formerly of Nottingham), the newly appointed superin- tendant of the Widnes circuit who commenced his ministerial duties in Widnes, on Sunday last. After tea, at which over 200 persons were present a meeting was subsequently held, the chair heinai, ccupied by Mr. S. Davies, senior circuit steward. Aleresses were given by the Chairman; the Rev. G. S. Meek, and Mr. B. Brown. The Rev. A. Pritchard also addressed the meet- ing and received a- hearty reception. Speeches were afterwards delivered by Mr. Robinson and Mr. Orm- royde. DEATH AND FUNERAL OF AN OLD RuNconNTAN. _ _ _ . -

_ The mortal remains of Mrs. Dunbavand of Peel-st., Runcorn, were interred at Runcorn Parish Church on Saturday last. Mrs. Dunbavand had attained the ad- vanced age of 83 years and being a native of Runcorn, she had seen the place grow from a rural village, and a resort of invalids to a busy manufacturing town, and to listen to her reminiscenses was a treat to those privileged to listen to her. Her husband was the late Mr. Richard Dunbavand, formerly assistant pierhead master. The coffin was borne to the grave side by Messrs. Clucas, (the undertaker), Clare, Dykes, and Wakefield, and the mourners were Messrs. J. Pritchard (Manchester), Superintendent Johnson (formerly of Widnes) Wm. Joseph Pritchard (Manchester), Joseph Pritchard (Run- corn), John Hewitt (Barnton), Joseph Ward (Widnes), Messrs. Dunbavand, Wm. Howard and George Ward. The funeral service was read by the Rev. J. Holden. The coffin which was of a handsome description bore beauti- ful wreaths sent by Superintendent Johnson, Messrs. John Pritchard Witham and Joseph Pritchard, Mary Pritchard, Mr. and Mrs. Geo. Ward and Mr. E. Griffiths. _ .
