FREE EDUCATION AT DUTTON.

The members of the Dutton School Board have decided to adopt the Free Education Act, making the Dutton Board School totally free as regards fees, books, &c., commencing on the 28th inst. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. Purros, Sankey-st., Warrington.—i. dvt.
THE DANGERS OF PARAFFIN OIL.-A WOMAN BURNT AT EARLESTOWN.

On Thursday night, about six o'clock, a young woman named Elizabeth Grey, living at 53, Tam- worth-et., Earlestown, was engaged washing, and the boiler fire having burned low, she threw some paraffin oil upon it, in order to rekindle it. She emptied the oil out of a can, and as soon as it came in contact with the red cinders it exploded, and the flames shooting out, caught the young woman, and badly burned her about the face, shoulders, and arms. Dr. Patterson was sent for, and he prescribed for her. Some shelving in the back kitchen also caught fire, but this was soon extinguished. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DuTToN, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt.
EXTRAORDINARY DEATH NEAR WIGAN.

An inquest was held at the Running Horses Inn, Aspull, near Wigan, on Monday, on the body of Ann Ashcroft, widow, Sinam's-square, Aspull. Deceased was blown down by the wind during the severe storm which prevailed on Tuesday last. In the fall her right arm was broken, and she received severe injuries to her legs,and died from the effects of the shock on Sunday. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.
UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. Dirrrox, Sankey-at., Warrington.—Aevt. ACCIDENT TO. THE EARLESTOWN STATION MASTER.

Information has reached Earlestown, that Mr. Yonge, the station master, has received some in- jury, by being thrown from a trap. Be is at present away on his holidays, and on Monday when he arrived at Breedon, he and his wife hired a convey- anceito enable them to reach their destination. On the way the horse either fell, or the shafts broke, but at any rate both Mr. Young and his wife, were thrown out, and received some injury, but to what extent is not known.
StIOP DOOR ROBBERIES AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Patrick Mc- Creese, no fixed abode, was charged with stealing two pairs of trousers on Saturday night, valued at 125., the property of Horatio Syred, pawnbroker, Waterloo-road. Charles Tellett, assistant to Mr. Syred, said he saw the trousers (produced) hanging up outside the shop door on Saturday night about eight o'clock. Prisoner was then standing by the window, and in a few minutes afterwards witness saw prisoner running down Marsh-street with the trousers under his arm. He then gave information to the police. Patrick Kelly, Wellington-street, said pri- soner came to a house where he was on Saturday and asked him to buy a pair of trousers. Witness gave him I a shilling tor the trousers, but he was drunk at the time, 'and did not know what he was doing. P.C. Hough proved apprehending prisoner.—A further charge was brought against prisoner of stealing a coat and vest on the same night from the shop of Mr. W. Miller, Waterloo road. Thomas Haffey, assistant to Mr. Miller, said the coat and vest were hanging up outside the shop door on Saturday night, about eight o'clock, but in a short time afterwards they were missed. P.C. Hough stated that when he apprehended the prisoner on the other charge, he was wearing the coat and vest produced. He made inquiries, and found they had been stolen from Mr. Miller's shop. He charged prisoner with stealing the trousers and also the coai; and vest, but he made no reply.—Prisoner was sent to the Quarter Sessions to take his trial on both charges.
Mr. Heywood secouded.—ln reply to Mr. Brandreth, the Clerk said no rate was levied last half year.
VEGETATION DESTROYED BY CHEMICAL GASES.

, Mr. Parr, (Hatton), complained of the nuisance mired and the damage done by the chemical works of the Alkali Union at Widnes. He had not seen hedges so burned and shrivelled up for years.—Mr. Farrington said on the previous Thursday he saw the gas coming from Widnes and Runcorn in the direction of Hatton.—Mr. Parr said the time he complained of was about three weeks ago. The chestnut trees and the sycamore trees were much damaged. He thought mere care and discretion ought to be used in turning this gas out. It was the biggest nuisance in the Union and yet least notice was taken of it.—Mr. Whitlow said there were trees on the west side that had not a leaf on them, and a farmer on the Aston estate had told him he had had a field of oats spoiled by the fumes.—Mr. Aaron said if Mr. Parr could give the exact date of the escape of gas, Mr. Carey, the secretary to the Alkali Union, would be glad as two inspectors were employed in the day and two at night to see that gas did not unneces- sarily escape and that there was no waste.—Mr. Parr said he supposed there was a law to prevent them from doing this.—The Clerk was instructed to write to Mr. Carey on the subject. • , DEFECTIVE SEWER AT FIELSBY.
—The Inspector reported that he had communicated with Mr. Thornley, of Helsby in reference to this matter, as directed at the last meeting, but he had received no reply.

div.head: ACCIDENT TO A FOOTBALL PLAYER.
div.p: ACCIDENT TO A FOOTBALL PLAYER.

On Saturday afternoon an accident occurred dur- ing the St. Helens v. Ulverston football match on the ground of the first-named at Knowsley-road, St. Helens. Towards the close of the game some scrimmaging took place in the centre, and after one of the packs Greenough, one of the St. Helens for- wards, was left lying unconscious on the ground. Dr. Watson, who was watching the contest, at once made an examinotion, and found that the unfortu- nate man had sustained serious injury. He was carried into the dressing tent, and Dr. Watson sub- sequently stated that Greenough's scull was fractured. The doctor temporarily bound up the bead, and Greenough was removed home in a cab. the injury, fortunately was not dangerous. limninslieN.—lntencling emigrants to IN eW York, Boston Philadelphia, San Francisco, Canaola, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New Z..a.land, should tAlce tickets (lowest, rates) at the " Examiner" Office, by Cunard, Union, American, Aus- tralian, Oriental, and ether lines—John agtmt. div.head: LADY CARLISLE AND THE PUBLICANS.
div.p: LADY CARLISLE AND THE PUBLICANS.

The Brewster Sessions at Brampton haying been found illegal because they were held a day before the statutory period, were held again on Tuesday. The temperance party, headed by Lady Carlisle, opposed five renewals. Mr. Charlton, Manchester, appeared for the objectors; and Mr. Errington, Carlisle, for the publicans. The first urn opposed was the Sportsman, on the ground that the house was unneccessary and structurally unfit.—The land- lord, on being asked what he would do if turned out, replied that he did not know unless Lady Carlisle would give him a job.—Lady Carlisle replied: With pleasure, if you give up the traffic.—The magistrates renewed the license ; and this being a test case, the other four objections were with, drawn.
BAssirrErrFs.—J. S. Garland, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge-st., Warrington.—Advt.
AN EARLESTOWN MAN AND HIS WATCH.

On Monday, a young man named William Shaw, living at Earlestown, visited Manchester, and with several others went to the band contest at Belle Vue Gardens. At night he proceeded to the Exchange Station in order to take the train to Earlestown. He arrived at the station about half past nine, and having some little time to wait, he eutered a wait- ing room, and while reading an evening paper, fell asleep. In the waiting room at the same time were two strangers, and after sleeping for about twenty minutes, Shaw awoke to find that his watch and chain and the two strangers had disappeared. He has informed the Manchester police of his loss, and furnished them with the number of the watch, but it is hardly likely that he will ever become possessed of it again.

div.head: FARM FIRE AT NEWTON.
div.p: FARM FIRE AT NEWTON.

At half-past one on Wednesday afternoon, a fire hroke out in the farm buildings of the Liverpool Re- formatory Farm School. The building is what is called a dutch barn, in which was stored hay, and a quantity of oats newly gathered. The barn is situ- ated near Bed Bank Mill, and the fire was first ob- served by a boy named Penrose. an inmate of the Reformatory. Ile at once gave the alarm, and the offiCers of the school were speedily on the scene,and, assisted by a large number of the boys,took energe- tic measures to subdue the flames. There was a good supply of water at hand, and with buckets this was poured on the burning mass. ,After several hours' hard work, they managed to get the fire under,and to save a good portion of the hay, but what is left will scarcely be of any use, having been damaged by the water. Almost the whole of the oats were destroyed. The damage is estimated at £25, which is covered by insurance. The outbreak is attributed to spontaneous combustion.

MURDEROUS ASSAULT AT A GLASSWORKS, On Wednesday at the St. Helens Police Court, Patrick M`Manus, 22, Hope-st., was charged with unlawfully wounding John Friar that morning.— Chief Constable Wood stated that the prisoner and Friar were glassmakers, and were employed at Bishop's Glassworks. Between two and three o'clock that morning the prisoner went up to Friar and said, "Have you been talking about my wife ?" Friar re- plied, "No l" whereupon the prisoner took up an iron blowpipe and dealt him a severe blow on the head, causing a large wound, from which flowed a great quantity of blood. The man Friar put up his hand to protect his head and the prisoner again struck him with the pipe. Friar was unable to ap- pear, and he asked for the prisoner to be remanded. John Harrican, of 23, Frazer-st., gave formal evi- dence in support of the Chief Constable's statement. He added that after the assault Friar was removed to the surgery of Dr. Reid.—The prisoner was then remanded until next Monday.
UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-St., Warrington.—Advt.
FATAL ACCIDENT WITH A STEAM TRAM.

Jane Alice Norman, three veari of age, daughter of Joseph Norman, collier, 3,801 l Parr, was killed by being run over by an engine attached to one of the tramcars belonging to the St. Helens and District Tramways Company, on Monday after- noon. The girl was playing in the roadway with her brother when the tram-engine, driven by James Massingdale, of 53, Charles-st., approached. The driver rang the bell, and deceased, who was at- tempting to run across the road, stopped clear of the lines three or four yards in front. The engine had then been brought almost, to a standstill, but, seeing that the child was standing clear, the driver again put on steam, and at that moment the girl ran in front of the engine and was knocked down. The engine ran over her, and on being extricated her head and body were found to be badly crushed. She died a few minutes after the occurrence. On Wednesday Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest at the Town Hall on the body of the deceased. Mr. J. MassPy, solicitor, appeared for the driver of the tram, John Thomas Massingdale, and for the Tramways Company.. Joseph Hough- ton, newsagent, John Davies, a bncksetter, and tte tram enginedriver (Massingdale) gave evidence in accordance with the above facts. A juryman pointed out that there were two large day schools within a few yards from the spot, and the jury, in returning a verdict of " Accidental death," completely exonerated the driver from blame but recommended that drivers of the trams should exercise more than ordinary care when the chil- dren were not in school.—Mr. Massey intimated that the recommendation should be conveyed to the directors of the company.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Thesday. Mr. Mclntyre presided and there were present Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. J. Weir, J. Baguley, Edwards, E. Aaron, Heywood, Lewis, Smith, Baxter, W. IVhitlow, Brandreth, Pickering, Kirkham, Parr, J. W. Bagu- ley, Bretherton, J. Ashton (clerk.)

div.head: TEE SEWERS OF THE UNION.
div.p: TEE SEWERS OF THE UNION.

The Clerk reported that he had accompanied Mr. Wells, the engineer, to the Authority along the line of the Ship Canal, from Twenty Step Bridge, Appleton, to Weston, and had examined the outfalls. The work to be carried out by the Ship Canal Company seemed to be going on in a satisfactory manner, and according to agreemen t. At Weston a question arose about differ- ent sewers, and no one seemed to know where they were except Mr. Aaron, and it seemed to him that the Autho- rity ought to have a plan not only of these sewers but of the sewers throughout the Union.—Mr. Aaron said this was a very serious matter to the ratepayers, and he pro- posed that Mr. Wells be asked at what price he would sup- ply plans of the sewers of the various townships.—The Clerk said the sewers could be marked upon the ordnance map —ln answer to Mr. Brandreth, the Clerk said the plan was wanted in the case of pipes which were hidden and not open ditches.—Mr. Brandreth said it looked rather bad that they had not a plan of the sewers when they had spent so much upon them.—The Clerk said he had no plans except of Overton Sewers.—The Clerk was instructed to make inquiries as to what plans were avail- able.
THE POLLUTION OF KECIEWICK BROOK.

Mr. H. I.—Longton, solicitor, Warrington, acting on behalf of Messrs. Earp and Co, wrote respecting the alleged pollution of Keckwick Brook. Personally, he said, he felt very much surprised atter the facts elicited at the inquiry at Preston Brook that proceedings shoull lee threatened and he felt sure that the members of the Authority were under a misapprehension of the real state of the case. There was to doubt the case came within the latter portion of section 4 of the Rivers Pollution Act and this being so he could not see why proceedings should be taken, when in fact Mr. Earp, who is an expert in these matters is using "the best practicable means to render harmless the liquid carried into the stream." Mr. Earp, had told him that he was quite willing to adopt any reasonable means that the Authority might think an improvement on what he was doing, though he felt confident with his experi- ence, that there was no other means as applicable as his own to reader the liquid harmless and to minimise the alleged nuisaace.—The Clerk said he had replied that the Authority would be sorry to have to institute proceed- ings and he would suggest that his clients avail them- selves of section 6 of the Act, and if he would ask for an opportunity of being heard against such proceedings being taken he would get the Authority to appoint a meeting at which Messrs. Earp could he heard.—The Clerk said he had not received any reply to that letter.

div.head: NUISANCE INSPECTOR.
div.p: THE NUISANCE INSPECTOR.
Mr Aaron proposed and Mr. W. Whitlow seconded the re-appointment of Mr. J. Farrington as inspector of nuisances, and the motion was carried unanimously.
FRODSHAM WATER SCHE'3IE.

_ Mr. Edwards had given notice of his intention to move that the resolution approving of the proposed water scheme for Frodsham be rescinded,and he explained that he had called a meeting of ratepayers for the previous evening to discuss the matter. Mr. H. G. Linaker took exception to the legality of the publication of the notice, and as he (Mr. Edwards) did not wish to form one of the noble army of martyrs in an appeal case, the meet- ing stood adjourned until it could be legally called. He therefore wished that his notice of motion should be adjourned for a fortnight.—No objection was raised. THE COST OF SEWERAGE. In reply to Mr. Brandreth the assistant clerk said Frodsham Lordship had not paid their calls.—Mr. Bran- dreth said unless these calls were paid at once the author- its' would over draw their balance if they paid accounts due. He moved that on loan account the Bank of Eng- land be paid £303, made up as follows :—Frodsham sewerage, £lB4 17s. 3d. ; Appleton Sewerage £59 18s. sd. ; Frodsham Lordship, £5B 10s. 2d. There was still owing Frodsham £3,200, Frodsham Lordship, £1,400; and Appleton £1,351 58. It was strange that after 1 spending all this money they should not have plans.—Mr. Heywood seconded the motion. Carried. Mr. Brandroth, chairman of the Finance Committee, pre- sented the estimates for the half year ending Lady Day, 1892_ The probable balance at Michaelmas was £348. The probable expenditure for the ensuing half year was £4lO ; including salaries, £135 ; sundries, £25 ; balance and contingency fund, £250. There was thus only £62 required from the rates and as the rateable value of the authority's district was £163,272, a rate of one-tenth of a penny would produce £6B 7s. Od. He moved that a rate of one-tenth of a penny be levied.—

div.p: IMPROVEMENT OF PUMP WELL AT SUTTON.
Three tenders were submitted for this work, and, after some consideration, it was decided to accept one sent in by Mr. De Prez, of Moore.
PROPOSED NEW HOUSE AT STOCKTON HEATH.

Plans were submitted for a new house proposed to be erected at Stockton Heath, but as the same were not in conformity with the by-laws, they were rejected, and the Inspector was directed to confer with the owner with respect to the matter.
WATER SUPPLY TO COTTAGES AT PRESTO-&-T'-HILT,
The InspEctor stated that operations had commenced for the provision of a water supply to certain cottages situate at Preston-o'-th'-nill, which was considered very satisfactory.
This wai all the business.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF IMPROVEMENT – COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF IMPROVEMENT - COMMISSIONERS.

A special meeting of this Board was held at the Town Hall, on Thursday. Mr. H. J. Grice.the chair- man presided and there were present Messrs. Taylor, Pritchard White, Dobson, Coward, Wass, Abel, Bis- brown, Lightburn, Wiswall, Lake (law clerk), Marshall (secretary), and Barker (surveyor.) The business of the meeting was to appoint the committees which were constituted as follows: Highways and Buildings: Consists of all the members of the Board. Health: Messrs, Lightburn, Taylor,Wass, , Bisbrawn, Fisher, Meadowcroft, Humphreys, Wiswall. Finance: Messrs. Fisher, Speakman, Meadowcroft, Hankinson, Pritchard, Taylor, Lightburn. Parliament- ary: Messrs. Lightburn, Taylor, Pritchard, Speakman, Meadowcroft, Wiswall, Humphreys. General Purposes: Messrs. Hankinson, Wass, Fisher White, Taylor, Abel, Dobson, Coward. Waterloo Bridge: Messrs. Pritchard, Fisher, Timmins, Speakman, White, Wiswall, Smith, Taylor. Library: Rev. Canon Wood, Messrs. Riley, Sowerby, Handley, Hankinson, Humphreys, Dr. McLennan, Messrs. Pritchard, Simpson, Taylor. THE BAHTS.—A discussion arose on the baths question and it was decided to allow the Committee to lapse, but it was intimated to the members that it could be re- formed when any member cared to move in the matter. PLEASURE GROUNDS.—It was stated that there was a strong public opinion in favour of making the common land into pleasure grounds, and the members agreed that it would be well to keep the Committees on this subject alive if only to act as a vigilance committee. It was constituted as follows: Messrs. Hankinson Wiswall, Dobson, Pritchard, Abel, White, Taylor and Humphreys. REVISION OF BYE-LAWS COMHITTEE.—The Chairman of the Standing Committee with Messrs. Humphreys, Wiswall, White, Timmins, and Coward. VEHICULAR BRIDGE ACROSS' THE MERSEY.—A Com- mittee for carrying out this purpose was formed of Messrs. Pritchard, Taylor, Wiswall, Fisher. and Light- burn.
SCIENCE AND Anr.—Messrs. Grice, Wiswall, and Humphreys, were elected the representatives of the Board on the Science and Art Committee.

A POINT OF Law.—The question as to whather Mr. P. Smith was entitled to retain his seat on the Board, that gentleman having failed to attend six monthly meetings of the Board was discussed. Eventually the Law Clerk gave his decision that Mr. Smith was still entitled to sit.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly hiBeting of this Board was held at the Town Hall, Widnes, on Tuebday afternoon. Mr. F. H. Gossage presided, and there were also present Messrs. D. Wright, B. Brown, J. Midwood, H. Cook, G. I. Nield, S. Sadler, J. Taylor, J. Tilley, J, Hough- ton, and H. S. Timmis ; H. S. OppenLeim (law clerk), T. Craik (law clerk's assistant), J. S. Sin- clair (surveyor), I. Carr (engineer), S. Hoyle (accountant), and W. Lowe (inspector.)

ACCOUNTS OF THE BOARD.— THE AUDITOR'S CRITICISMS. A communication was read from Mr. Hazlehurst, the district auditor, in which he directed the attention of the Board to several defects, as he considered, in the method in which the Board's accounts were kept, and suggested improvements. In other respects the accounts ,were reported to be satisfactory.—The Chairman said there appeared to be nothing essential in the report. The accounts were, on the whole, acknowledged to be very well kept. There were details which those gentlemen always very reasonably pointed out,and he haa no doubt when these were put into the hands of their accountant he would see his way as far as possible to coincide with the auditors' suggestions. He thought the report ought to be referred to the accounntant and the Finance Com- mittee and it was quite possible they should be able to do away with all the points which the auditor raised. As to surcharges, the Local Government Board always took those things into consideration, and if there was a reason for the charges the surcharges were always re- mitted. He thought they were very much in the position they had always been in except that they had got an excellent report as to the state of their accounts.—lt was agreed to refer the report to the Finance Committee and the accountant.

div.head: TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION GRANTS.
div.p: THE TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION GRANTS.

Communications were submitted froin-iiie-lancashire County Council with regard to the grants in aid of tech- nical instruction.—The Chairman said the portion of these grants to which Widnes was entitled was £4BO. —lt was decided that the Clerk be instructed to take the necessary steps for obtaining payment of the amount ant to which Widnes was entitled under the conditions made by the County Council ; and also to take the best means of ascertaining the probability of the grant being continued permanently ; and that the Technical Instruc- tion Committee of the Local Board be requested to pre- pare and submit to the Board a scheme of dealing with the amountof such grant or grants.
A LETTER FROM THE RATEPAYERS' ASSOCIATION.-THE

BOARD THINKS IT WILL RUN IT A OWN BUSINESS. A letter was read from Mr. W. Christie, secretary of the Widnes Ratepayers' Association, stating that he had been instructed by the members of the Association to ask the Board to refuse to confirm the appointment of James Toole, as clerk of works under the Board's sur- veyor, on the ground that, were the appointment neces- sary, the situation should have been advertised when men in Widnes would have had an opportunity of apply- ing for the vacancy.—The Chairman said it was very nice to receive suggestions from outside bodies, but the Board must "run its own business,," as the Americans said. He thought the letter might lieon the table.—This was agreed to.
TILE WE LLS .-A BI ti RAI NFA LL. -WI LF CIL BREAKING OF LAMPS.

The Water Engineer reported to the Gas and Water 1' Committee,in connection with the Netherley boring con- tract, that the first hole had been sunk to a depth of 230 ft. Boring had again been suspended for about a ' fortnight awaiting the delivery of a shield bracket for ! the protection of the shoulder of took at the bottom of the 301 n. hole. This had now been fixed in position, and ! the hole would, it was expected, be completed in three , weeks' time. The work in connection with the second borehole was well in hand. The two bottom lengths of tube had been fixed in position, and the space behind I filled in with concrete. He had been obliged to reject one of the top lengths of tube on account of a small crack in the body of the pipe close underneath the up- per flange. Stock's well :—The smaller of the two cav- ities alluded to in his last report had been filled in with , concrete. The bottom and sides of the brook had also been lined with concrete, so that the work was now completed. The work of concreting the brook was finished the day previous to the heavy rainfall of the 25th inst., when the water in the brook rose 3ft., at which level a very considerable quantity used to find its way into the well. There was still some little percolation going on, but very slight compared with that previons to the alteration. Burst Main : On the 13th inst., the 16 inch rising. main gave way at the back of the flange on the first Joint at the outlet of the air vessel. This would appear to be due to a slight settlement of the engine house, consequent upon the subsidences alluded to, from underneath the foundation footings. The re- pairs were effected upon a stoppage of 43 hours. The total rainfall for the last three months had been 12.115 inches as compared with 7.15 inches for the correspond- ing peripd of last year. The effect of this had ly.!en to increase the working level of the water in the well at

Netherley by 10 feet, and that at Stock's Well by 8 feet. The illuminating power of the gas during the month had averaged 17.58 candles. The Committee recommended that the tender of Joseph Turner and Co., Ld., for the purchase of tar produced at the Gas Works during the period ending 30th September, 1892, at 31s. per ton be accepted. It was further recommended that notices be issued offering a reward of 10s. to any person giving such information as will lead to the conviction of any person or persons wilfully or maliciously damaging street lamps in the district, also that the Clerk be instructed to investigate the cases of break- ages now reported by the Engineer, and to pro- secure any offenders whom he may think fit.— Mr. Wright moved the confirmation of the minutes,and, referring to the damage to lamps, said there had been 189 different lamps damaged, and the damage done amounted to £4O. He thought the public ought to render assistance in putting an end to this dam age to their pro- perty.—The Chairman said he was very much afraid Widnes was sinking into a bad way as far as juvenile offenders were concerned. There were cases continually coming before the Bench, and to have to adjudicate upon these cases, more particularly of juvenile offenders, was one of the saddest parts of his life. If the public could only be enlisted to morally assist the police, he thought a great deal could be done, but as it was they were sinking very low indeed.—The minutes were then confirmed.

div.head: STREET MAKING AND BUILDING_ PLANS,
div.p: STREET MAKING AND BUILDING_ PLANS,

The Highways Committee recommended that the Sur- veyor take the requisite steps for the making of the fol- lowing private streets, viz.:—East-st.; Edward-st. from Warrington-road to Castle-st. ; passage betweed War- rington-road and Castle-st. Plans of the following were submitted by the surveyor :—Three houses and one shop in Birchfield-road, for Robert Hurst,approved ; amended plan of warehouse in Marsh-st., for W. Farrant, ap- proved ; streets and passages on the land belonging to Robert Hurst, off Birchfield-road, approved.—The minu- tes were confirmed on the motion of Mr. Sadler.
SWING BOATS IN THE MARKET.-THE MEDICAL OFFICER-
SHIP. -S LA LTG lITE R-HOI7SES , &C.

The Health Committee's minutes contained the fol- lowing items :—The Clerk submitted and read report, which he had prepared in accordance with the resolu- tion passed at the last Board meeting, and the same was considered and the Market Inspector instructed as to the letting of the market ground for the erection of swings, kc.—The Clerk reported that the Local Governmentßoard had not yet replied to his application re the salary of the ' Medical Officer of Health, and it was recnmmended that ' in case the office of Medical Officer of Health be not filled up by the expiration of Dr. Cooper's term of office on the 30th September instant, Dr. Cooper be temporarily, appointed Medical Officer of Health until a regular ap- pointment can be made. Accident Hospital: Patients at last meeting 8, patients admitted since 6, patients dismissed 3, patients died 2, patients still in 9. Infec- tious Diseases Hospital: Patients at last meeting 3, patients admitted since 6, patients discharged since 6, patients still in 3.—The Medical Officer reported that the birth-rateha,d been 4010 per I,ooo,and the death-rate 20.12. It was recommended, upon the application of the occupiers, that the following premises be registered as slaughterhouses for a period of twelve months, viz :-69, Mersey-road, John Bower, pork butcher; 47, Waterloo- road, Louis Pfister, pork butcher; 15, Ann-street ; Chas. Henry Bill, pork butcher; 63, Widnes-road, Mrs. Most, pork butcher ; Junction of Widnes-road and New-street, James Fletcher, butcher; Near Moorside terrace off Lowerhouse-lane, George Coupe, perk butcher. The receipts from the market for the month were £20195. 6d; being a decrease of £4 6s. 3d. as compared with corres- pondinc, month last year caused by loss of hawkers' tolls, .&c. Mi.. Wright, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said they had instructed the market inspector that when he could let the land without swing boats he was to do so, and no swing beats of a dangerous character would be allowed.—The minutes were confirmed.
APPOINTMENT OF CHIEF LEDGER CLERE.-MORTGAGES.-

div.head: RECOVERY OF WATER CHARGES
div.p: THE RECOVERY OF WATER CHARGES

The Finance Committee reported that there were 75 applications for the appointment of chief ledger clerk, and they unanimously recommended the appointment of Mr. James Woodeud, at a salary of £llO per annum. It was recommended that the clerk prepare,and the Board's seal be affixed to the following mortgages, viz.:—Humph- rey Wroe Roberts, £l,OOO at 31 per cent. for five years, on general account • Herbert Phillips, Jos. Broome, and Reuben Spencer, £4OOO at 3i per cent. for 10 years on general account; Elizabeth Naylor, James Knowles, and Jonathan Cunliffe, £6OO at 3i per cent. for 10 years on water account ; Sarah Ann Ashworth, Thomas Robert Peel, and John Watson, £l,OOO at 3i. per cent. for seven years on water account. Recommended that the collec- tor be instructed to take legal proceedings for the re- covery of the various accounts owing to the Board, as shown on lists submitted by the accountant.—Mr. Mid. wood moved the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Wright remarked that many ratepayers were dissatisfied with the charge of ss. per quarter for water in addition to their meter, and they considered they ought not to be charged for what they did not get.—Mr. Neil agreed with Wright's remarks; and Dr. O'Keeffe said that had he been present at the Committee meeting when the resolution as to the recovery of arrears was adopted he would not have agreed to it. He moved that the matter be re- ferred back to the Committee.--Mr. Midwood pointed out that the Finance Committee had simply to collect the charges made by the Gas and Water Committee.— Mr. Brown spoke against the amendment ef Dr. O'Keeffe which on being put to the vote was rejected by seven votes to three.—The minutes were accordingly adopted. '

THE VERWIILAR TRAFFIC BRIDGE, &C. The General Purposes Committee's minutes contained the following s—Recommended that Mr. and Mrs. 'rhos. Whittle ne appointed to the office of Town Hall care- taker, at a joint salary of £2 ss. per week, with man's uniform, subject to the terms of the printed definition of duties attached to their application .—Vehicular Traffic Bridge: Letter, sth August, from Mr. Fred Lake, Law Clerk to the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners read: Resolved that this Committee again meet the deputation from Runcorn to further discuss the question.—Fire Sta- tion and Cottages: Recommended that the allotment of the cottages be as follows :—For fire brigade, six cot- tages adjoining the fire station on the Alforde-st. side, and three cottages on the other side of the tire station ; for Highway Department four cottages ; and one cottage adjoining Alforde-st. to be alloted to the Market Inspec- tor. That the rents be Si. 6d. per week (clear), and that it be a condition of tenancy that no part of a cottage shall be sub-let, also that the Surveyor shall have the supervision of the whole of the property.—Ferry Ap- proach : Recommeaded. that the Surveyor prepare an estimate of the cost of his proposed scheme, and that the Chairman and Mr. Sadler with the Clerk and Sur- veyor be appointed a deputation to interview the direc- tor,: of the Ship Canal Co., with a view to carrying out the scheme.—Adooted on the motion of Dr. O'Keeffe.

TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION COMMITTEE. This Committee reryimmended that Mr. John Mac- Mahon be appointed Art teacher on the following terms, viz. : Salary, twelve shillings and sixpence per night, and a fee of three shillings per student for the ordinary classes and ten shillings per student for the higher grade art classes ; that Mr. John Angell be appointed Science teacher. on the following terms, viz. : At a fee of three shillings per student in each class and the Goverment Grant earned by each student in his classes ; that Mr. Samuel Cook be appointed assistant secretary at a salary of £l2 M. per annum ; that J. Shone be appointed care- taker at a remuneration of 4s. per week. Resolved that the following members of the Committee be and are hereby appointed a sub-committee, viz. : Dr. O'Keeffe, Dr. Hurter, Messrs. H. Wade Deacon and J. Morrison, with power to make such arrangements as they may con- sider necessary for carrying on the work of the ensuing sessioa.—The minutes were adopted on the motion of DT. O'Keeffe. This was all the business.
RUNCOR-; BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. Present—Mr. Mclntyre (chairman), Bev. J. W. N. Tanner; Messrs. S. Taylor, J. W. Lightburn, T. Lea, J. Weir, J. Baguley, E. Aaron, Lewis, Kirkham, J. W. Baguley, Bretherton, Heywood, Brandreth, W. Whitlow, Smith, Baxter, Pickering, and J. Ashton (clerk).

APPOINTMENT OF VACCINATION OFFICER. 4' The first business was the appointment of a vaccina- tion officer for Runcorn district in place of Mr. Coletwn, resigned. The applicants were Mr. E. W. Humphreys, solicitor, Mr. R. Moore stationer, Mr. T. Cook insurance agent, and Mr. G. Ward relieving officer. —Mr. Whitlow moved, and the Rev. .1. W. N. Tanner seconded, the ap- pointment of Mr. Ward.—Mr. Lea proposed Mr. Moore, and Mr. Parr seconded.—Mr.Brandreth suggested that the other candidates should not be left out iti the cold and Mr. Taylor then proposed Mr. Humphreys, Mr. Kirkham seconded.----Mr. Heywood proposed Mr. Cooke. The voting was as follows Ward, la Moore, 3; Humphreys, Cooke, 2.—On the motion of Mr. Brandreth seconded by Mr. Taylor, Mr. Ward was then unanimously elected to the position. It was stated that the payment would he by fees, and that the amount would beabout £l5.

_ _ _ _ ...... ....._ COUNTY COUNCIL A.GAIN. The Clerk read the following letter :.--" Cheshire County Council,Clerk's Office,Chester, 31st August,lll9l. Dear Sir,—As lan informed, by the county accountant that the amount of £1,64a Ss., being the balance due from the Runcorn Union upon the precept issued for county and police rates, and which was made returnable on the 30th June last, still remain unpaid, I have to re- quest that you will be good enough to remit a cheque forthwith to the county treasurer. I shall be further obliged if you will in future pay the amount of the pre- 1 emits as they become due, and in one sum instead of by instalments. (Signed) REGINALD Parrs, Clerk of the Council."—The Clerk said a cheque was sent to the county treasurer a week before that letter was written. —Mr. Lightburn : Had Runcorn to advance the money again? (Laughter.)—The Clerk : No.—Mr. Aaron: If he would attend to his business and send us a balance sheet, it would look better of him.
THE ESTESIATES.-IMPORTAN.T FACTS.
Mr. Brund—ret—C;Lniiied the estimate tor the half year ending Lady Day, 1892. The estimated expenditure was: Common charges, £3,961; county rate, £3,293 ;

balance and contingency fund, £2,288 ; total, 29,542. The probable balance at Michaelmas was £3,183, and deducting this, left the amount required from the rates at £6,359. The rateable value of the Union was £219,660, being an increase of £Bl9 as compared with last year. A rate of 7d. in the £ would meet the requirements. Ihe rate in the corresponding period last year was sd. in the £, and last half ycar 10±d. 111 the L. The proposed rate was therefore 3id. less titan i n March last. He thought that in future they would have less rates than the had had. The Clerk had drawn up a table comparing the rates from 1886 and it was as follows: 1886, 5-4-d. and 61-d. ; 1887, 6d. and Bd. ; 1888, 51d. and 8k;; 188.9, 6d. anu Bd. ; 1890, 4d. and 9d. ; 1891, sd. and lOid. Tie Clerk had also prepared an analysis of payments to the county since 1886, and he found that main roads had cost most money. In Sept. 1886, the item for main roads was £16,931 133., ,and on the 31st. March, 1890, the item for the same purpose was £43,353 (exclaimations of astonishment). He supposed, how- ever, that the local highway rates were now practically nil.—Mr. Aaron : Not a farthing less.—Mr. drandreth said they ought to be. he wont on to say that the Clerk had also prepared an interesting comparison of the rate- able values in the Union, and while some townships had increased others had decreased. Land must have gone down in value, as it seemed to him that nearly all the decreases were on farms.—The Chairman: That is so. —Mr. Brandreth said the Assessment Committee, on which farmers were well represented, was responsible for the diminution. He was astonished that the Assess- ment of Runcorn had decreased from £60,000 in 1883 to £56,399 in 1890, while in the little village of Helsby the assessment had increased from £5,623 to £7,870, or about £1,200. —Mr. Lighburn pointed out that the reduction in Runcorn was due to a re-assessment of the Ship Canal property —Mr. Taylor said the increase in Runcom during the last half-year was £9OO as compared with the previous half-year.—Mr. Lightburn said those gentlemen who had the fight with the Ship Canal Company were responsible for the reduction of the assessment of Runcorn, which was a permanent loss to that town of £l5O a year,—Mr. Brandreth said the Committee fought to maintain the valuation.—Mr. drandreth reported that the townships of Bartington, Budworth, Kingsley, Kingswood, Pres- ton-o-th'-Hill, and Whitley Inferior had not paid their calls. He moved that the overseers be pressed for pay- ment .—Mr. Aaron seconded .—Carried.

div.head: TREE EDUCATION ACT.
div.p: THE TREE EDUCATION ACT.

The subject of the Elementary Act having been intro- duced by Mr. Brandreth, the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner said all the schools in Budworth were free.—Mr. Taylor said the Board Schools in Runcorn were free, and the Denom- inational Infants' Schools were also free. A small fee was charged in the higher standards.—Mr. Aaron said the schools at Weston were free.—The Clerk: The schools are free at Frodsham, and at Kingsley the Aat was adopted on Monday.—Mr. Brandreth asked if the Relieving Officers still paid fees.—The Clerk said he had written to the Local Government Board, asking what should be done with respect to the Inquiry Officers, for if the Board paid no fees they required no Inquiry Officers. He had, however, not yet received a reply.— Mr. G. Ward, Relieving Officer for Runcorn, said he had stopped paying fees since the Act came into opera- tion.—The Clerk said the other Relieving Officers had also stopped paying fees.—Mr. Brandreth : I believe we can allow extras yet?—The Clerk: Yes.—The subject then dropped.—A vote of thanks having been accorded to the Rev. A. Jameson, of Weston, for flowers sent to the Workhouse, the meeting ended.
WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS,
THIIRSDAY.—Before Messrs. A. Fletcher (chairman) and
W. Lees McClure.

WOUNDING HER MOTHER-IN-LAW.—Mary Ann Noon, Nelson-st., Widnes, was charged with wounding Mary Noon on Wednesday night.—Mary McLoughlin, residing at 54, Wellington-st., stated that shortly before ten o'clock on Wednesday evening she saw prisoner strike prosecu- trix on the head with her clog.—Dr. Hutchinson said the prosecutrix's wounds were so serious that she would be unable to appear that day.—Prisoner was remanded in custody until Monday. SERIOUS CHARGE.—Dominick Dovitch, Water-st., and Charles Martin Kevitch, 18, Hope-st., two Poles, were brought up on remand, charged with wounding Ann Surmen, another Pole, by throwing a piece of coal at her, which struck her in the stomach, rendering her in- sensible.—Dr. Hutchinson said the prosecutrix was still in a dangerous condition, and was unable to appear that day.—Prisoner was further remanded for a week.

STRIKING WITH • CLOTHES PROP.—Andrew Gorman, Victoria-st., was charged on remand, with wounding a man named James 'robin by striking him on the head with a clothes prop on Saturday night. After hearing the evidence of prosecutor and Dr. Hutchinson, the charge was reduced to one of assault, and a fine of Zs. 6d. and costs was imposed. IMPORTANT TO SWINE KEEPERS.—Patrick Leonard, Catherine-st., was summoned, under bye-law eleven of the Widnes Local Board, with unlawfully keeping swine within 501 t. of a dwelling-house, and also Lr deposit- ing swine dung within a like distance.—Mr. J. Malkin (Oppenheim and Malkin), St. Hel ' ens prosecuted on be- half of the Widnes Local Board, and Mr. J. W. Knowles defended.—Walter Lowe, nuisance inspector, admitted that he had given defendant permission to keep the pigs in the sty until they had littered.—The Chairman: The case will then be dismi:.sed.—With regard to the dung being within the required distance, the inspector said he did net give permission for it to stop there too.—For this offence defendant was ordered to pay a fine of 2s. 6d. and costs.
A Fkaocrous Doa.—Samuel Eyes, lodging-house keeper, Lugsdale-road Widnes, was summoned fer keeping a ferocious dog on the 23rd ult.—An order was made for the dog to be kept under control. _ .

DRUNICENNESZ-JOhrt Lawler, Pitt-street; James W. Bank, Lugsdale-road ; Mary Hannon, Water-street; and Patrick Murray, Liverpool-road, Cronton, were each fined 2s. ad. and costs for being drunk, and Mary Ann Tobin, Water-street, and James Farrell were fined ss. and costs each for having been drunk and disorderly. BREACH OF Tan PEACE.—For this offence, Margaret Boyle, Walmsley-street, was ordered to be bound over three months in £lO and one surety of £5. _ _ _

As-sAul—Ts.—Mary Ann Beresford, Irwell-st., was sum- moned for assaulting Mrs. Alderton, Beaumont-st., on Saturday night. The case was dismissed, on defendant promising to pay Ns. and costs.—Margaret Brown pleaded guilty to having assaulted Margaret Dwyer, and the latter was also summoned for having assaulted Margaret Brown. Brown was ordered to pay a fine of 2s. ed. and costs, and the case against Dwyer was dis- missed.

THEFTS BY CHILDREN.—Robert Keating (12), Mary Ann Keating (9), both of 18 Lea-st., and Joseph Flood (11), Pleasant-st., were charged with stealing a quantity of timber from Messrs. Dennis's works, Widnes, on Wed- nesday.—P.C. Davies deposed that shortly after six o'clock on Wednesday evening he saw the children coming from Messrs. Dennis's works with the :wood staves pro- duced. When asked what they were doing with them, the boys said they were going to make bats with them. —The two boys were each ordered to receive three strokes of the birch rod, and the girl was discharged. THEFT FROM A FLAT.—William Crank (14), and Robert Hunt (17), were charged with stealing a quantity of paint and tar from the flat Lone, lying in West Bank Dock.—The prisoners pleaded guilty, and were ordered to be locked up until next morning, when they were re- leased.
SIR GILBERT GREENALL'S SUP- PORTERS;
PUBLICLY EMBRACED BY A LADY ADMIRER.

An amusing scene was witnessed opposite Bank- chambers, Winwick-street, Warrington, on Satur- day, the parties interested being Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., M.P.' for the borough, and Mrs. Gorse, Factory-yard, Bank Quay, who is said to be one of Sir Gilbert's most ardent supporters. This lady was overheard to make the remark that she would" kiss dear old Sir Gilbert." She watched her opportunity, and. as Sir Gilbert stepped from the office of Messrs. Greenall and Buckton towards his carriage' which was standing at the door, she ran towards him, flung her arms round his neck, and tried to carry out her desire. "You dear, kind old gentleman," she exclaimed, as Sir Gilbert good- naturedly tried to free himself from her embrace. Sir Gilbert's coachman and Mr. Greenall, solicitor, also endeavoured to restrain the aged baronet's ad- mirer, but she was not easily put off; and at length Police Constable Turner had to interfere. Mrs. Gorse resented the policeman's interference, for she said, "You have prevented me kissing Sir Gilbert." Sir Gilbert bore his part of the ordeal with calm submission and evident good nature, and Mrs. Gorse said to the bystanders that she was better pleased than if she had had a ten pound note put into her hand. She did not forgive Constable Turner for preventing her carrying out her heart's wish. The incident was witnessed by a large number of inter- ested spectators.

The Earl of Northesk died early on Thursday nsorninL. at his seat, Longwood, from the rupture of a blood vessel George John Carnegie, ninth earl, was a representative Peer for Scotland. He was born Deceinber, 1843, and succeeded to the title in 1878. He was formerly Lieut.- Colonel of the Scots Guards, and a Commissioner of Sup- ply for Forfarshire.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
SUPPOSED THEFT OF SHAWLS.

On Wednesday, at the Warrington Police Court, John Carney was charged with being found in possession of a quantity of shawls supposed to have been stolen, on Monday night.—Detective-Sergeant Monaghan said the prisoner was a new recruit at the barracks, and on Mon- day night, Sergeant Craythorne, of the barracks, saw him with a bundle containing the shawls and 40 tickets belonging to the London and North-Western Railway Company. The shawls were supposed to be samples be- longing to a commercial travellcr.—Sergeant Craythorne said the prisoner had been taken before the military authority.—The prisoner said he had found the parcel, but Sergeant Monaghan said that was the first time he had made that statement. He was remanded till Saturday.
PRACTISING FOR GUY FAWKE'S DAY.

Samuel Boan, a respectable-looking boy, was charged with letting off in Bridge-street, on August 29th, certain fireworks, to wit Chinese crackers.—The case having been proved, Police-Sergt. Chandlev, for the edification of the magistrates, discharged a Chinese cracker in court, which made a pretty loud report.—Mr. Hunt said he had got the constables to go round among the dealers in fire- works, and warn them not to sell such things to young boys. He would rather reach those who sold them.— Major Pickmere : They ought not to be allowed.—Mr. Hunt: They are downright dangerous. We shall have some serious accident.—Sergt. Chandlev said there were some a deal louder than that he had exploded.—The deputy magistrates' clerk said the law prohibited fire- works being sold to boys under 12.---Defendent was dis- charged on payment of 3s. 6d. costs.

div.head: THEFT OF A JACKET.
div.p: THEFT OF A JACKET.

At the Borough Police Court on Thursday John Garrity abet James Pickett were charged with stealing from the person of William Smith, in Scotland-road, about 20 minutes to 12 on Tuesday morning, a man's jacket value 10s. 6d. They pleaded not guilty. Smith, it appeared, was sitting down in Scotland-road, opposite the herb beer shop, with the jacket on his knees, when Pickett who was in the company of Garrity, took it and ran away with it,the complainant pursuing him but being un- able to catch him. Smith complained to Inspector Bowen of the theft and as the result P.C. Wood was soon on the alert,and caught Garrity pledging the jacket in Tunstall's pawnshop, Pickett being outside. Garrity then said Pickett had given him it to pawn. It transpired that Garrity was seen to give it to Pickett, and that he had given it to a man named Johnson to pawn, who had offered it at Murphy's in Scotland-road. The prisoners were committed for trial.

div.head: BEARDING THE LION IN HIS DEN,
div.p: BEARDING THE LION IN HIS DEN,

John Moran, employed at the lead works, Sankey Bridges, and Jane Moran, his wife, were charged at the Warrington police court, Gn Monday, with being drunk in Irlam-street on Saturday night, and John was charged with assaulting P.C.'s Corbett and Phillips on the same occasion.—P.C. Corbett said he was in the police station, on Saturday night, when the female defendent rushed in and claimed protection from her husband. Witness went out and saw him in the street wanting to fight a man, and asked him to go away, but he refused. He became very violent, struck at several bystanders, and rushed into the police station, where he was very violent, and was rough with witness.—P.C. Phillips said the male prisoner kicked and struck him and Corbett several times, and he and P.C. Corbett had to put him into the cells, whereupon his wife flew at them like a tiger.—The male prisoner at first said he recollected nothing of the affair, but now stated!: that he was kicked by Phillips as be was going into the cell.—The Chief Constable: I thought you said you recollected nothing about it.—The man said he had not wanted to mention it, but he was obliged.—He was fined 10s. and costs, in default 14 days, and his wife ss. and costs, in default 7 days. A ROUGH SHIP CANAL LABOURER.

At the borough police court, on Tuesday, Andrew Ennis, ship canal labourer, was charged with refusing to quit the Golden Lion Inn, St. James's-street, the previous moreing, and with assaulting Police-Sergeant ' Taylor and P.C. Cooper, on the same occasion. P.S. Taylor deposed to being called into the inn, and finding the prisoner there drunk and using very bad language. He requested him to go out upon which he became very violent, and had to be put out. In the street he was very disorderly and tried to force his way back into the public-house. Witness then took him into custody and he became like a madman and struck him. P.C. Cooper, who was in plain clothes, came to his assistance, and was kicked by him, and P.C. Corcoran afterwards helped them. The prisoner came quietly until he got to the bridge, then threw himself down and kicked Cooper again on the legs, and it was with con- siderable difficulty he was got to the police station.- -Cooper and Corcoran gave evidence, the latter stating a that he had to strike the prisoner across the legs with his staff to keep him quiet.—The landlady of the inn also testified to his misbehaviour in the house. He was fined 10s. and costs ; in default 14 days. SHAMMING A POLICEMAN TO GET A WATCH AND CHAIN. John Cobb, formerly of Wellington-st., Warrington was charged with obtaining by false pretences, from Abraham Cohen, of the firm of A. and D. Cohen, jewel- lers, Rylands-st., on the 7th of July,a silver lever watch, and a silver albert chain. Mr. Forshaw appeared for the prosecutor. He said the prisoner on the 6th ult., called on the complainant, and said he was a member of the Warrington borough police force, and Mr. Hunt had sent him to buy a watch, and he wanted a silver lever. Mr. Cohen said he had not one in stock, but would wire for one. The prisoner said he must have a watch that night, as he was going on duty, whereupon Mr. Cohen lent him one, and told him to come the following morn- ing for the lever. He did so and was supplied with a lever watch and chain, value £7 Bs., on which he paid LI 15s. on account.—Mr. Cohen gave confirmatory evi- dence, and said the prisoner got the watch and chain and a jubilee shilling, for which witness charged £7 Bs., and stated that he gave his address as Wellington-St. He paid £1 15s. and arranged to meet him at the police station every Friday and pay him ss. or 103. till the debt was cleared off. He said that week was his first on the force, and that the Chief Constable examined every man before he went on duty daily to see if he had a watch.— Mr. Garnett thought the complainant had not shown much of the characteristic cleverness of leWs.—The com- plainant : He told me all particulars about the police. —Mr. Garnett: Just the very thing that ought to have made you suspicious.—The complainant : He seemed. such a quiet decent man.—The prisoner said hebargained to pay the complainant on the Wednesday, and he never mentioned Mr. Hunt's name.—Mrs. Cohen having given evidence, Mr. Samuel Hunt, the Chief Constable, de- posed that the prisoner was never in the borough police force, and had never been sent by him for a watch. It was not his practice to examine con- stables to see whether they had watches.—The defend- ant said he had applied to the Watch Committee for a situation as constable,and Mr. Hunt had in his possession three good testimonials of his.—Mr. Hunt said he did not know the defendant but remembered a man named Cobb applying two or three months since to the Com- mittee with good testimonials. —Detective-Sergeant Monaghan said the prisoner used to be employed by the ' London and North-Western Railway Company. The sergeant also deposed to apprehending the prisoner at Retford, and obtaining the watch from him. The criain he said he had sold in the train on his way from War- rington. He had not been in the town since the 7th ult.

He replied on being charged by him that he had nothing; to say.—The prisoner said he was willing to pay ex- penses and so much a week for the watch. On his tak- ing back a wringing machine, on which he had paid 245., to the Jews in Sankey-st. they refused to return him any money. He supposed they were connected with the prosecutor's firm, and so thought he would have a watch and chain from them to recoup himself for his loss. When he found there was no connection between this firm and the other Jews he was very sorry, and in- tended to pay for the watch and chain when he got into good work.—He was committed for trial to the Quarter Sessions, the Bench at his request, consenting to accept bail in two sureties of £lO each.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON-:BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Holmes (in the chair), and
Mr. John Geddes.

AN UNLICENSED PEDLAR.—James Casey was summoned for unlawfully offering for sale a quantity of spectacles, without having a license, in Buttermarket-st., on the previous afternoon. The defendant said that he had until recently been working on the Ship Canal, but had hurt his arm. He did not know he was doing wrong. A fine of ss. and costs was imposed. DRUNICENNESS.—Joseph Muiphy was charged with be- ing drunk and disorderly, in Bridge-st., on Friday night, and was fined ss. and costs.

MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman R. W. Fran- comb), Aldermen Harrison, and Wright, and Major Pickmere. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Stephen Collins, in Bridge- st., on the 29th ult., Sarah Bird, in Buttermarket-st., on Saturday night, ss. each, Thomas Holmes, in St. James's- st., the same night ss. and costs.—John Rafferty was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Butter- market-st. on Sunday afternoon.—P.C. 20 Cooper said the man was walking about behaving very noisily for three-quarters of an hour, and asked why the man was allowed to do so for so long, said it was to allow him a chance to go away.—The defendant was fined ss. and costs the Mayor remarking to constable: You allowed him time to get sober.—Frederick Farney, a Scotchman, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Butter- market-st., and assaulting an old woman named Mary , Wilson on Saturday night.—P.C. Bell said the man was drunk and the woman complained to him that the de- fendant had struck her with a cane which he carried. , He refused his name and address, asd ,became very abusive, and it took two policemen to bring him to the station.—P.S. Chandley also gave evidence, and said the prisoner gave several false names and addresses.—The prisoner denied the assault.—He was fined ss. and costs; in default seven days' imprisonment.—Hannah Chad- wick, a married woman, drunk and disorderly In Lime- st., on the 29th ult. ss.—Margaret Stokes, married woman, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Howard-st. and doing wilful damage to the cape of P.C. Rylatt, on the 31st ult. She bit him across the arm through the cape. . 10s. including costs. VAGRANCY.—Mary Ainsworth charged with sleeping out in the Market Place, at a quarter-past one that morn- ing, and having no visible means of subsistence, was dismissed on her stating that she was going to Earles- town. DRUNK IN CHARGE OF A HORSE. Jonathan Finch, confectioner, Bewsey-road, charged with being drunk in charge of a horse and phaeton, and with furious driv- ing in Sankey-st., on the 30th ult., was fined 10s., includ- ing costs. A PROFANE WOMAN.—Binnery Hinds, widow, of 8, Hill-st., was fined ss. for using profane language in that thoroughfare on August 29th. OBSTRUCTING THE STREETS.—AIbert Mynekyne, pork butcher, Market-st. ; Margaret Massey, greengrocer, Lower Walton; Thomas Pickering, greengrocer, Bryn, near Wigan; and George Flannaghan, hawker, of Widnes, were fined ss. each for obstructing Market-st., on the 2nd just, by allowing their horses and carts to stand there longer than necessary.—Henry Woods, carrier, Ashton-in-Makerfield, for similarly obstructing Winwick-st., on the same date, was mulcted with costs. —Evans Thomas Evans, draper, Sankey-st., for exposing certain goods for sale so as to cause an obstruction, was ordered to pay costs.—Edward Bate, of Hoyle-at., charged with obstructing the footpath in Tanners-lane, by wheeling a barrowful of bread thereon, on the 31st ult., was dismissed. A GANG OF STREET GAMBLERS. William Farrell, Martin Callaghan, Thomas Glavin, 'Patrick McGarth, John Belly, and Peter Callaghan, all young men, and William Cunningham, a boy, were charged with playing cards for money, in Bank-st., on the 30th ult. P.C. Amson proved the case and said the game they were playing at was called " banker " ; and the boy was the worst of the lot. It was mentioned that this lad had previously been brought up for being drunk and dis- orderly. They were fined 10s. and costs, or 17s, in all, each. TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. R. Garnett, E. J. Guest, and E. M. Crosfield. WIFE ASSAULT.—Thomas Healy, army pensioner, was charged with assaulting and beating his wife Alice on the 6th of August. The complainant said on Saturday morning the prisoner when he went to work told her he was not coming back because she was keeping her eldest son. Ile came home in the afternoon, drunk, and quar- relled with the son, who struck him. On Sunday morn- ing between one and two the son was in bed, and the defendant came to him with a boot and told him he would beat his brains in. Witness interfered, and he seized her by the hair of the head, and dashed her seve- ral times on the floor, and kicked her repeatedly in the stomach. She did not want him to go to prison, but wanted a separation,and would be content if he paid for her support in the Workhouse. The defendant said his wife was an habitual drunkard, and she had driven him three times from the town, and he was twice brought back and had to pay the penalty. The son was dose upon 18 years old, and she was keeping him in idleness in spite of him (the defendant). He never assaulted her, and nobody ever saw him drunk. The Chief Con- stable, P.S. Chandlev, and D.S. Monaghan gave the de- fendant a character for steadiness,but said the complain- ant was a drunken woman, and had been there both for drunkenness and stealing. The defendant agreed to allow his wife Ss. a week and £1 a quarter from his quarterly pensipn of £5, and to keep away from her, and I on this understanding the case was dismissed. DRUNK AND DlSORDERLY.—Christopher Simmons drunk and disorderly in Bewsey-st., on Monday night, and whom, P.C. Amson said, it took four men to carry to the Police Station, was fined ss. and costs, in default seven days. SCHOOL CASES.—The following persons were dealt with at the instance of Mr. G. Riley, school attendance officer.—Alfred Birehall, forgeman, Silver-st., ss. ; Leah Briars, labourer, Bewsey-road, 23. 6d. each. Hannah Flynn, labourer, Catherine-st., 3s. 6d., and ordered to send her daughter to St. Anne's School.—John Mahoney. ' forgeman, Pierpoint-st., 23. ; James McKean, Ship Canal labourer. Pierpoint-st., sa; Pat Sheening, tanner, School Brow, 2s. 6d.; Samuel Smith,moulder,Cheetham- st., ss.
WEDNESDAY.—B efore Alderman Holmes (Chairman), Alderman Chandley, and Messrs. J. Geddes and John Fairclough. -

SCHOOL CASES.—Peter Hinds was charged under a warrant with not sending a child to school and fined ss. James Travis, forgeman, Silver-square, was similarly charged. The mother had been ordered to produce the boy but did not. A fine of 10s. was therefore imposed. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—CharIes Williams, a negro, for being drunk and disorderly in Bridge-st., the pre- vious night, was fined ss. and costs. TMIIRSDAY.—Before Major Pickmere (chairman), Alderman Sutton, and Captain Ridgway.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY. —Thomas Mitchell, ship canal worker, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Scotland-road, the previous night, and assaulting Edward Gibbons, in Orford-street, on the same occasion. Mr. Gibbons said the defendant came to him drunk and asked if he wanted any men. He replied that he wanted no men of his description, and several times requested him to go away, but he would not, and started mauling him about. Witness went back into the yard and as he was going through the gate the defendant struck him, and got hold of him by the shoulder, ripping up the sleeve. A constable deposed to the man's drunkenness, and to his using bad language to a woman in Scotland- road, and he was fined 10s. including costs.—Frances Higinbotham, a stranger in Warrington, drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-street the same night, was discharged on her promising to leave immediately for Chester, whither she said, she had been on her way. VAGRANCY.—John Colt was charged with being found sleeping in the straw shed of Elizabeth Monks, at Arpley, at a quarter-past one that morning. The officer who proved the case said Mrs. Monks complained of a lot of damage being done by men who slept in the shed. They were continually breaking the lock off the door to get in. ss. and costs, or seven days.—Alfred Bell was charged with sleeping in hay at the foot of a stack belonging to Mr. John Cross, Arpley, that morning, at a quarter to two. The constable in the case said the stack stood on the spot where a former stack had been which had been set on fire by some one. ss. and costs, or seven days.
FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Chandley (chairman) Alder-

man Wright, and Dr. Oornall. DRUNK.—James Keogh was charged with being drunk in Wilderspool-road, at 20 minutes to 11 the previous night. A constable proved the case, and said the defen- dant had annoyed two ladies from Wilderspool to St. James's Church, begging coppers from them. A cabman interfered with him for using bad language to them, and the defendant quarrelled with him. He was sent to prison for 14 days. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—John Rooney was charged under a warrant with being drunk and disorderly in Shepherd's-yard, on the 15th ult. Fourteen days' im- prisonment with hard labour.—Thomas Flannery was charged under a warrant with a like offence in Butter- market-st., on the 24th ult. 55., or 7 days. WIFE ASSAULT.—Edward Clare, spring mattress maker, of 33 Ashton-st., was charged with assaulting Mary Jane Clare, his wife, on the 7th inst. Mr. Davies appeared for the complainant, and Mr. Browne for the defendant. —Mr. Davies asked for a judicial separation in case of proof of the assault. The defendant as a rule

behaved well except when under the influence of drink. 1 He was in the habit of going with other women, and really it was through his being caught by the wife with a woman of bad character that the assault occurred. He had been in the habit of locking her and her baby in the house.—The complainant said on the evening of the 7th ult. she found her husband with his arm round the waist of a young woman in the fairground. She told him he had better be at home in company with his wife and child. He slapped her face then and on her reaching home he was there and threw the meat off his plate at her, but it hit the wall not her. He knocked her head twice against the wall and thumped and bruised her arm.—Margaret Forshaw in giving evidence for the com- plainant, and stated that she was an industrious hard- working woman. Witness was in at the time of the alleged assault but heard nothing.—Mr. Browne said the complainant had aggravated the defendant by her lan- guage to him on meeting him with the young woman whose only fault was that she had had a bastard child. A crowd collected and cried shame on the complainant. He never struck her, and the bruise on her arm might have been caused by pushing the door to as she went out. He was in a hornet's nest among his wife's relatiens to whom she was always going.—He was bound over in the sum of £2O to keep the peace, and mulcted in costs.

CRUELTY TO HORSES.—The following persons were prosecuted by Inspectors Dowty and Wilson, R.S.P.C.A., for cruelty to horses :—Richard Martindale and Thomas Rowley, 333, Knutsford-road, the latter the owner of the horse, were fined, the former 3s. 6d. costs, and the latter 10s. Edward Roberts, carter, Widnes, and Ellen Rigby, owner, greengrocer, Widnes, were fined, the for- mer ss. 6d. costs, and the latter 10s. Thomas Evans, greengrocer, Earl-st., Earlestown, and Thomas Wright, korsekeeper, 5, Edgeworth-st., Warrington, Bs. 6d. costs each. Enoch; and George Boswell, horse dealers, 10s. and costs each.

WILFUL DADlAGE.—Margaret Curran, of Derby-st. , was charged with assaulting Bridget Ready, her mother, also with wilfully damaging her window, on the Bth inst. She was fined costs and damages.—Thos. Price, a boy, son of John Price, 27, Winwick-st., was charged with wilful damage on Tuesday morning, in Winwick-st., to a bill hoarding, the property of the Warrington Bill Post- ing and Advertising Co., Limited. 25.6 d., 7s.in all.—Ann Donlan, 24, Silver-st., for wilful damage to a window frame, the property of Thomas Hill, in that street, was mulcted in costs,
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.

div.head: MONDAY. —Before Dr. Steele (chairman), and Mr. G. L.
div.p: MONDAY. —Before Dr. Steele (chairman), and Mr. G. L.
Davies.

TEMPORARY AUTHORITY .—Ellen Powell, Frodsham, applied for temporary authority to sell intoxicating liquors under the license now held by Mr. Brookes, Castle Hotel, Halton.—Superintendent Large said he had no objection to the application being granted, as the applicant had held a license at Frodsham for 12 years without. any complaint.—Granted. BAD LANGUAGE.—John Moores pleaded guilty to mak- ing use of obscene language in Trinity-st., Runcorn, on the 31st ult., and was ordered to pay a fine of ss. and costs, or go to prison for 14 days. DRIINKENNESS.—Thomas Heyes and Martin Ward were each ordered to pay a fine of ss. and costs, or in default seven days for being drunk and disorderly on Saturday last.-A middle-aged married woman named Agnes Heyes, with a baby in arms, residing at Ince, was charged with a like offence in Bridge-st., on the same night. Prisoner denied the charge, and said she had only had two glasses of beer. Superintendent Large said a number of people came to town for marketing purposes on Saturday, and having got drunk created a disturbance. Runcorn then got blamed for it all. Prisoner was ordered to pay a fine of ss. including costs, or in default 9f payment go to gaol for seven days.—Margaret Molineaux pleaded guilty to being drunk and disorderly at Weston on the 31st ult. She was ordered to pay a fine of ss. and costs.— Michael Moran and Edward Brady were similarly dealt with for like offences in Weston Village. John Molineaux pleaded not guilty to being drunk and disorderly at Weston on the 31st ult. Jessie Molineaux supported the defendant's plea, and said she was in his company the whole of the day, and he was not drunk. The case was dismissed.
WIDNES POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Mr. T. S. Timmis.

DRUNKENNESS.—Ed ward Carney,hailing from Garston, was charged with being drunk on the highway at Widnes, on the previous day, and was fined ss. and Costs. STEALING RAGS.—Joseph Lynch ,who said he came from St. Helens, was charged with stealing a bag, containing a quantity of rags, valued at Is. 6d., the property of Samuel Eyes, lodging-house keeper, Lugsdale-road, Wid- nes. Prisoner was remanded in custody until Monday. On Monday morning the prisoner said he had sold the rags, but did not steal them. There were numerous convictions against the prisoner, and he was committed to take his trial at the Quarter Sessions. MONDAY.—Before Mr. F. H. Gossage.

DRUNKENNESS.—Andrew Cosgrove, Marg-aret-street ; Patrick Tancey, Wareing-st. ; and George McLean, 55, Victoria-st.,were charged with being drunk on the high- way at Widnes, and were fined ss. and costs each, or seven days in default.

Total 5l Total WIRRAL IST v. WARRINGTON 2r.—Played at Rock Ferry, on Saturday. Warrington batted first on a wicket that had suffered considerably from the recent heavy rains. The start was most unfavourable, four wickets being quickly down for 25 runs ; the next three wickets added 30 runs, but as the visitors had only nine men, the total only reached 61.. Reynolds, Jolley, and Bibby were the only ones to get into double figures. The wicket, though terribly slow, was not difficult, and if the visitors had used a little patience whilst batting, the score would have been considerably more. Graham and Harden bowled very steadily, and kept a good length all through the innings. On Wirral going in to bat runs came at a good pace, and 30 runs were up ere the third wicket fell, the sixth wicket also added 21 runs. The home team, who were also three men short, finally won by 12 runs. The visitors' bowling was very weak, none of the five bowlers who went on to bowl being able to get a good length. Isherwood was the most successful, but his three wickets cost 24 runs. Score :

PEARSON AND KNOWLES (IST), WARRINGTON, V. RUN- CORN (IsT.)—The former's last match of the season was playea on the home ground on Saturday. The Warring- tonians beat a strong team of the visitors by 21 runs. Although the visitors came with a strong team to try again to defeat the home team, they made a poor show against the excellent bowling of Hampson and Beaman, ampson taking five wickets for 10 runs, and Beaman Three for 10. Harding, batting with his old form, punished Wright severely, making a nice score of 21. Gately bowled well for the visitors. Score :

WARRINGTON V. PRESTON.—Warrington brought their season to a close on Saturday with a brilliant victory over Preston. The narrow margin by which the latter club had won the first engagement lent additional interest to the match,but the large gate was undoubtedly attributed to the fact on this occasion Clark. the junior profes- sional and wicket-keeper, was taking his benefit. The Warrinc.,rtonians won the toss, their side being weakened by the absence of their captain, Mr. S. M. Crosfield. R. Smith and W. H. Podmore were the first batsmen, Hewitson and Grubb being the bowlers. The first four overs produced as many runs, all from Hewitson, but eventually both began to hit out, Podmore despatching the slow bowler to the boundary. With 21 runs on, Grubb beat him with a fast one, and Lee followed. Two runs only had been added, when Grubb effected an easy catch in the slips, which disposed of the amateur. With J. J. Crosfield and Lee as partners runs came steadily, but the professional had only made nine when he was bowled by Grubb. Crosfield was content to score by the aid of singles, but the monotony was not relished by Clarke, who hit out freely, knocking together ten in quick time, but being tempted to hit out to Hewitson, missed, and paid the penalty, the board reading-50-4- 10. Belland Crosfield stayed together till lunch, when the score was 55. On resuming, Bell was smartly ruq out by Leigh, whilst seven runs later, Clark was caught at short slip. Yonge was almost stumped first ball,but he had a short career, as hitting out at Hewitson, he skied one to Addie. Crosfield and Voisey now became partners,and the finest cricket of the day was witnessed. Voisey hit cut brilliantly, playing each bowler with con- fidence. Runs came freely, but with the score at 88, Crosfield was completely beaten by Hewitson. Brown joined Voisey, and another slight stand was made,East- wood meanwhile displacing Grubb. With one short of the century Brown was bowled, and Griffin whipped in. The century was hoisted amid cheers, and at 110 Voisey's grand innings was brought to a close, Eastwood bringing off a smart catch. Voisey was loudly cheered for his fine display, his contribution of 29 coming just when runs were required. On Preston sgoing in to bat, they were first represented by J. Leigh and P. Addie, and Crosfield and Smith bowling. Addie should have been caught first ball, but only two runs had been notched when Leigh called his partner for a short run. The batsman had not reckoned the capabilities of so smart a fielderas Podmore, for a fine return to the wickets sent the Preston captain to the pavilion. Best came next, and aided by a wild throw, a single was made into five,!and then Smith beat him. Eastwood returned a ball tamely to Crosfield, whilst Eccles was dismissed by s fine catch at short leg by Bell. Addie was dismissed in a similar manner to Eastwood, and half the wickets were down for 23 runs. Blacow shaped poorly at Smith, being dismissed without scoring, but Hazlewood and Ladyman made a short stand. Bell relieved Smith, who changed over to Crosfi,;ld's end, but both batsmen, however, were dismissed by the aid of smart fielding, and Grubb being soon bowled, the ven- ture closed for 50, the Warringtonians being loudly cheered for their brilliant victory. div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.
RUGBY.

WIDNES ST. MARY'S V. MR. LAW'S (LIVERPOOL TEAM.) —This match was played on Saturday afternoon, on St. Mary's ground, in fine weather. Mu'linger started for Law's team; Clarke returned, and the home team attacked, a minor resulting. Diractly afterwards Clarke received a pass, and after a good run scored a try. M'Gurl failed at goal. Mason added a second try, and Howard a third, no goals resulting. Half time score : St. Mary's 3 tries, Law's team nil. Final result : Widnes St. Mary's 1 goal 7 tries 1 minor ; Law's team 2 tries.

TRANMERE WANDERERS V. RUNCORN.—The Tranmere Wanderers having had their ground in Wilmer-road enclosed during the recess, boldly ventured on a big undertaking, by making their opening fixture with the formidable Runcorn team, who on Saturday afternoon met with a capital reception at Tranmere. Runcorn started and P. Hancock returned, the home forwards at once rushing off, and but for a very plucky save by Houghton would have scored well. The home halves were smart in their work, and smothered several attempts of their opponents, till Crompton got hold of the ball, and he made off, only to be hauled down after going a few yards. Scrambling play brought the ball to the home 25, but a pass to J. Davies gave the latter a chance, of which he took full advantage, and dodged over the line. Crompton kicking an easy goal. Snape retrieved his name with a really clever get away from the throng of Runcornians, and punting to the opposition 25, gave his forwards a good chance, which brought about a try to George Headou, after a scramble with Houghton. No goal resulted from the kick. Crompton got away, and, the full back being away, he simply walked over and kicked a goal from his easily gained:try. The kick-off saw play resumed at the home end, where the pressure was considerable. Opposite the goal Crompton got hold, and ran straight through, a poor attempt at goal bringing about half-time with the score : Runcorn, two goals one try ; Tranmere Wanderers one try one minor. E. Jones re-started against the hill for the home team, W. Hancock and G. Headon at once being useful ; and J. Williams put in a most excellent dribble,to which Houghton responded with a strong run. The Runcorn forwards rushed down the field, and one of the home three-quarters having run back over the line with the ball, a scrimmage at five yards ensued. From a nice pass back Ctomptom dropped an easy and com- fortable goal. Houghton made a spendid shot at goal from the touch line, but failed to score. Following the drop out, Davies darted over, but was collared and a maul ensued. Houghton got hold from the next drop, out, but Brown secured him finely,. Then three of the Runcorn men had a scramble among themselves for the ball, when it was over the line, but a dead ball only re- stilted. Soon after J. Davies got a try, and then Hough- ton made a magnificent drop from the touch line, just grazing the post about thirty feet from the ground. Crompton next got over again, but no goal accrued. Final result: Runcorn 3 goals, 4 tries. 3 minors; Tran- mere Wanderers 1 try, 2 minors. After the match the home team entertained the visitors at the Castle Hotel, Birkenhead.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION V. SUTTON VICTORIA.— These teams opened their season at Sutton, in grand weather. The visitors were minus three of their selected team, and, of course, were severely handicapped, the home team having their full strength. The Warring- tonians scored their first goal two minutes from start, following up with another point one minute later, the half time result being Warrington 2 goals, Sutton none. After change of ends the home team led the attack, but Davies and Lewis were too many for them. Warring- ton now had several tries at the Sutton goal but were unable to increase their score, while at the other end Sutton managed to notch their only point after hard work. Final result : Warrington 2 goals, Sutton Vic- toria 1. Davies and Lewis played a good game for War- rington.as also did John Mather arid Jones.—Warrington team : Goal, Jones; backs, Davies and Lewis; half- backs, Ayling, substitute, and Jas. Mather; forwards, Clayton, Cornforth, Phillips.
