div.head: TORY GATHERING AT LEIGH.
div.p: TORY GATHERING AT LEIGH.

On Saturday afternoGn, a meeting of Conservatives was held in Atherton Park, Leigh, when Mr. Whitley, M.P., Liverpool, was expected as the principal speaker. The honourable gentleman, however, writing from Rhyl, said he had caught a severe cold, which had brought on great weakness, and his medical man would not hear of his moving about for a short time, as the consequences might be serious. There was only a small attendance of the public, the meeting beng preided over by Mr. 0. P. Lancashire. Mr. W. C. Jones, of Preston Brook, the Conservative candidate for Leigh, moved a resolution expressing entire confidence in the Government, and con gratulating Lord Salisbury on the peaceful and prosper-- ous state of the country, both at home and abroad. Mr. J. Hill-Smith, barrister, of Armagh, seconded the resolu- tion, which was carried unanimously.

div.head: HAMMERSMITH MURDER.
div.p: THE HAMMERSMITH MURDER.

At West Ham London Police Court, on Saturday, William Alexander Wynne, 39, a dispenser, was further charged on suspicion with causing the death of his wife, Clara Elizabeth Wyune, 27, supposedly by administering crystal chloral, of hydrate, at 42, Golborne-road, North Kensington, on the 11th August. Dr. Dunn, who made the post-mortem examination, said there was a scalp wound, but the skull was not fractured, and he could not discover the cause of death. The brain was decom- posed. The appearance of the brain was compatible with poisoning by chloral, or with great excitement, caused by ill-treatment. After hearing other evidence, the magistrate said it would be for the jury to say whether the deceased died from chloral or excitement through ill-treatment, and he committed the prisoner on the capital charge, and also on the charge of doing grievous bodily harm.

div.head: TRE LATE SIR PHILIP GREY EGERTON.
div.p: TRE LATE SIR PHILIP GREY EGERTON.

On Saturday afternoon, the mortal remains of the late Sir Philip le Belward Grey Egerton, Bart., of Oulton Park, were consigned to their last resting place, in a new vault, in the burial ground connected with Little Budworth Church. Tke place of sepulture is on the north side of the sacred edifice, and immediately adjoins the tomb in which are interred many members of the Egerton family, including the parents of the late departed baronet. In accordance with the wishes of Sir Philip, the funeral was conducted in as quiet and unostenta- tious a manner as possible, but still it proved of an im- posing character. The tenants from far and near arrived in quick succession, in Little Budworth, attired in black. They as well as others who visited the village, found signs of mourning on every hand, for there was not a single house which was not darkened by the draw- ing of the blinds. " Truth " says—Sir Philip Grey Egerton, who died last week, after a long illness, was a most popular land- lord, and will be a very great loss to the Cheshire Tories, of whom he was one of the most shrewd and most active leaders. Sir Philip, who was for many years in the Coldstream Guards, greatly distinguished himself during the Crimean War. During the last ten years of his life Sir Philip principally devoted himself to looking after his large estates in Cheshire, and until his health failed, he took a prominent part in county business. He was a most devoted Churchman, and his comparatively early death will be deeply regretted by a very wide circle of friends.

PUBLICANS AND OTHER CITIZENS: A REPLY TO " SHAREAOLDER." Sir,—Perhaps you will allow me space to make some sort of reply to the letter of "A Radical teetotal share- holder in a Warrington Brewery "—what an aggravat ing signature—which appeared in your last issue. Like Mr Lawrence Flood, he is evidently a man of feeling, hopelessly endeavouring to be somewhat logical and con- sistent. But I'm prepared to admit that a gentleman who can combine radicalism, teetotalism,and beer brew- ing ought to be an authority on matters of consistency. Will he be a little more merciful. Only a few of us can hope to have such a faculty of unifying contradictions. May I suggest to Mr. Flood and " Shareholder " that inconsistency and hypocrisy are two very different things. Inconsistency is oftentimes mere mental weak- ness; hypocrisy always intentional vice. Hypocrites are among the most consistent men alive; and for all hypocrites whether publicans or preachers I have the supremest contempt. But I trust that I shall be saved from deeming every inconsistent petson a hypocrite. I have no doubt " Shareholder " has taken much pains with his lengthy letter and lam quite willing to give it the attention it merits. If he should consider what I have to advance worthy of a reply, perhaps he will reserve his " strong language" for such occasions as it is likely to serve him as argument. "Shareholder's' arguments may be grouped under two beads, firstly the beer interest in its relation to com- mercial life, and secondly, in its relation to religion. The objection that the religious and temperance class are not free from criminality comes with such ill grace from a representative of the class which provides three-fourths of the crime of the country that one is quite justified in ignoring it. Now I should lay it down as a principle, that, unless there be a direct benefit derived from the Liquor in- terest, temperance tradesmen are not false to their colours in having commercial relations with publicans and others, nor are teetotal employers dishonest—as " Shareholder " says they are—in their employment of non-temperance workpeople. " Shareholder" appears to have such an inflated opinion of the importance of "The Trade" that he needs to be reminded that a pub- lican or a brewer is not conferring any special advant- age upon a tradesman by the purchase of a loaf, a coat, or a load of coals. He buys as a citizen, and not as a publican and pays no more for his purchase than any- one else. Then as to the employment by teetotallers of men who take drink. Anyone can tell " Shareholder " that for the employers as a class it is indisputably to their disadvantage. The commercial prosperity of the Empire is not founded upon Beer but upon Brain. And the men who put an enemy into their mouths to steal away their brains are not as a class the men who are of the most value to their employers. So then neither to temper- ance tradespeople nor the temperance employers does any peculiar benefit accrue from the liq or trade. This being the case there is no principle of morals involved, and we have no desire to boycot our fellow citizens, the publicans and their friends at the instance of " Share- holder " and Mr. Lawrence Flood. But there is a simpler reply to "Shareholder's " soph- istry. If a teetotal employer is dishonest in employing men who drink,then the non-teetotal employer is equally dishonest in employing the services of men who don't drink. If a temperance tradesman is inconsistent in supplying goods to a publican, then it is equally true that a publican is likewise inconsistent on every occasion he takes money for the first glass of beet, whenever he supplies non-intoxicants and refreshments to non-drinkers; and also at such times as he receives money for drink from men who have not earned it them- selves but abstracted it by questionable methods from the earnings of their temperate and abstaining families. , To put the matter briefly—lf teetotallers are to shrink 1 from dealings with brewers and publicans because they consider their trade a calamity, the representatives of the Beer interest, if they would act consistently, must boy- cott the adherents of a teetotalism which threatens their trade and which they cannot but regard as intolerable and highly fanatical. " Shareholder " has seen only one side of his argument. The teetotal grocer is a hypocrite for serving the publican with groceries. That is the side he has seen. May I suggest the other ? The publican is a hypocrite for going to a teetotaller for his groceries. Both sides of the argument are equally true or equally false. "Shareholder "may hold which opinion he likes. The argument is worthless. With "Shareholder's "views on the Beer interest in relation to Religious life and work, I find myself in more

accord. Clergymen and others who denounce " the ' trade," and nevertheless derive from it direct pecuniary benefit in the shape of gifts either for personal use or church work can lay but little claim to consistency of conduct. But then so few have any desire to be incon- sistent. Does not " Shareholder" see that they have a powerful incentive to consistency. But perhaps he means that it is a shameful, a blasphemous thing, that Religion which seeks to save men should receive any benefit what- ever fnm a traffic which is ever ruining them. If so, I heartily agree with him. They who receive the brewer's gifts for such a purhose sell afresh the Crucified for paltry silver pieces.—Yours truly, ODED.

div.head: DRINK QUESTION IN WARRINGTON.-AN
div.p: THE DRINK QUESTION IN WARRINGTON.-AN
APPEAL.

Sir,—About a year ago you did me the honour of in- serting a letter of mine, in your paper, on a question which has been engaging the attention of the magis- trates, and the public of the town, at the Brewster Ses- sions. I should esteem it a favour if you would accord me the same privilege again, on the same subject. I read your leader on August 29th, and I also read the speech of Rev. Mr. Yonge, and Mr. R. Davies's defence of the publicans. Whilst not agreeing with all that your article contained, or all that was said by the above two gentlemen, I was very much pleased with a good deal that was written and said on the subject, and it ap- peared to me a very good case was made out to deal drasticly with some, if not all the seven houses that were attacked.

Now,l don't want to deprive a man of his" pot of beer," or the publican of his living ; neither am I likely to say very hard things of the publicans as I was once closely connected with the trade, having married the daughter of a licensed victualler who conducted his business with honour and respect for more than thirty years in Bridge- street; hut there are limits of endurance, and the public voice has a right to say—" thus far and no farther." If a man indulges his appetite by imbibing intoxicating drinks to such a degree as to become a nuisance and an annoyance to his neighbours or his fellow citizens, then I say the public have a right to step in, and curtail the facilities for the sale of such drinks. Nor can the publi- can with any degree of fairness object to the power being exercised of suppressing some of the houses that I are far too numerous for the public weal. Has it never struck you,Mr. Editor ?—it has me—that as a whole they are a very greedy and selfish lot ? They are everlastingly harping upon their vested interests,and to shut up one of their houses without giving compen- sation would be nothing less than confiscation, and I public robbery. They seem to think that they are the I only people that have any vested interests in trade. What about the butcher, the baker, and the grocer,— have they no vested interests in their trade •, and have , they no claims to public protection ? "Oh !" but some will say, " we do interfere with them or their trade ;" but I maintain that the trade of the publican does in- terfere with the trade of these people. When there are an inordinate number of public houses in a confined area, as is the case at the Market Gate end of Butter- market-street. I have seen these houses send forth the frequenters of the orgies held within their walls until the street has been well nigh impassable. I have heard their blasphemous and vicious language, and I must say that such scenes as I have witnessed and the language I have heard prevent respectable tradesmen from carrying on their business "without let or hindrance," when people have to push their way through such a surging sea of vice and immorality. Yet, I am not a willing advocate of repressive mea- sures; I would rather convince a man by moral suasion than by coercion, as I believe his repentance would be of a more real and lasting character. For after all I am often driven to the conclusion that the remedy lies in the hands of the working classes, for there is no blinking the fact that they art lie great drinking class of the age, and the working class of Warrington proverbially so. I would implore my fellow townsmen to make an effort to shake off the evil reputation that attaches to the town, to pursue a wiser course, by pursuing a more sober course. I would ask them of what use are they to the community in this utilitarian age, if their whole life from the cradle to the grave is to be given up to the "demon drink." During the last 15 years when enjoying my holidays, I have visited different parts of England, and have come in contact with all sorts and conditions of men. I have always avowed myself a Lancashire man' and, as I love my native place with all its faults, I have generally claimed Warrington as my home. The response I have been met with has sometimes not been of the most plea- sant kind.—" Oh! you belong to drunken Warrington." I have at times felt a tinge of shame and remorse come over me at my indiscretion for making known the place of my nativity, and have at times attempted to repel the charge, but only half heartedly, knowing that it was only too true. I wish the men, aye,and the women too could see themselves as others see them ; then there might be some hope,that in the future they would eman- cipate themselves from the drinking habits which they seemed almost to have imbibed from their mother's breast. If we could only prevail upon them to eschew this evil and to take more legitimate pursuits, many of the ques- tions which are now waiting for Solution would soon be- come matters of history ; a perceptible change would be manifested in a more orderly appearance of 6the people, and would lead to a more active participation in public affairs.

As an ardent Radical, I have been actively employed, in the town of my adoption,in political warfare for more than a quarter of a century, in helping to carry those measures that have been for the benefit of the working classes. Much has been done ; much remains to be done. I have ever found in my experience that the most apathetic and indifferent and yet the loudest clamourers, and the greatest grumblers at the present state of things, are found in that class who have surrendered themselves body and soul to the drinking customs of age. Next year, I hope to visit the old town again, to witness the completion ol the great undertaking in the immediate neighbourhood—" The Ship Canal." What a pleasing reminiscence of my visit it would be if, on my return, I could convey the intelligence to my wife and family that there had been a marked change for the better in the social habits of the people since my former visit, induced by more attention being paid to the moral and intellectual improvement of the masses, and less to the habits and customs that have kept them enslaved for so many years, and which still exercise so baneful an influence on their comfort and happiness. It can be done. They have the power. That they may exert the will to bring about so desirable a chanze is the earnest wish of
AN OLD WARRINGTONIAN. Birmingham, Sep. 5, 1891.

div.head: FATALITY TO AN OLD MAN AT EARLES-
div.p: FATALITY TO AN OLD MAN AT EARLES-
TOWN.

On Wednesday morning a man named Brian O'Toole, 58 years of age, of 79, Legh-st., Earlestown, met with an accident whien resulted in his death two hours later. O'Toole, who was lame, and walked with the aid of a stick, was employed by Messrs. R. Evans and Co., as a horse driver on the canal bank. On Wednesday morning about half-past ten, the foreman over Evans's coal tip, on the canal side, brought the deceased's horse from the stable and hooked it to an empty wagon, for the purpose of drawing it off the tip. The horse, however, turned stupid, and would not move, and O'Toole then got hold of its head, asking Collings (the foreman),to bring him a piece of rope. Col- lings brought the rope, and O'Toole struck the animal with it, when it suddenly started and swerving to one side, pulled the deceased with it, and he fell across the rails. Before he could recover himself,one of the wheels of the wagon came against his body and badly crushed him. Dr. Valentine was sent for,and after examining the man, ordered his removal. He was taken home on the ambulance litter, where he died at 12 o'clock.

div.head: DEAN LEFROY UNPOPULAR.
div.p: DEAN LEFROY UNPOPULAR.
"Truth makes the following reference to Dean Lefroy who was formerly Archdeacon of Warring- ton :

An indignant clamour is rising at Norwich against Dean Lefroy, who is credited with the intention of spoiling the ancient and picturesque Close by building in it. The Council have remon- strated vigorously against the scheme, and everybody in the city is protesting against the proposal to spoil the meads and gardens, for open Spaces are nGt numerous in Norwich. It may be hoped that the dean, who is becoming very unpopular in the city, will drop his building speculation, for it is clear that matters must have come to a serious issue when the leading "Church and State" organ in the city announces that "Norwich people have never been used to these huckstering manceuvres on the part of the church, and do not take kindly to them," and this journal truly adds that even if the capitular income be diminished," yet the work is not laborious, and if a balance-sheet of the Cathedral revenue were published, most of us would agree that on the theory that the labourer is worthy of his hire, all the functionaries inside the precincts are fairly well provided for." This writer is quite correct in his ideas, for, even after allowing for the results of agricultural depression, the dean of Norwich has £1,200 a year, with an excellent house ; and each of. the four canons has £6OO a year with a good house' to which it may be added that one of the residen- tiaries holds a valuable London living, another is master of a college at Cambridge, and another is Archneacon of Norfolk, a sinecure office which increases his stipend by £2OO a year.
Two children on their way to school were on Wed nes- day killed at Stanningley, near Leeds, through the sudden collapse of a wall.

div.head: ITT E EX k M ER, SAT HR .•'. Y, SEPTEMBER 12, 1891.
div.p: ITT E EX k M ER, SAT HR .•'. Y, SEPTEMBER 12, 1891.
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c. BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

I learn that the Runcorn District Fund is in a very flourishing condition, and that the finances show a great improvement upon last year. The " Negro Nomads" entertainment, organi/ed by Mr. Light- burn cleared profit of £l6, and this on an evening when everything conspired against the success of the project. The annual meeting of the fund will be held some time next month.

The estimates presented to the meeting of Run- corn Board of Guardians on Tuesday last, will be grateful and comforting to the ratepayers. The poor rate has fallen from 10i in the to 71., and there is the assurance of Mr. Brandreth that the rate is likely to become still further reduced. May he prove a true prophet.

Mr. Brandreth created quite a sensation amongst the members when he gave an extract from a return prepared by the clerk (Mr. Ashton) showing that from 1886 to 1890 the cost of main roads had in- creased from £16,931 to £43,353. He argued that the rates levied by the local highway hoards must be reduced in a corresponding degree, but Mr. Aaron said they were not one farthing less. we have it on the authority of Mr. Speakman, however, that the magistrates when in power had starved the roads, and we are now reaping the result of a cheese paring policy. I have never yet seen any denial of this impeach ment,but there is no getting behind the fact that the county expenses are expanding very rapidly.

Dr. S. Taite Beckett, assistant to . Dr. McDougall of Runcorn, has been appointed assistant surgeon to the North Liverpool dispensary, and in a few weeks will sever his too brief connection with the town. The good wishes of many Runcornians will follow him.
In Runcorn and Widnes churches on Sunnay prayers were offered for tine weather, and judging by the glorious sunshine of the past few days they have been very efficacious.

Although the excitement of the Commissioners election has died away it is still a topic of conver- sation and one can hear on many sides expressions of regret that Mr. Stubbs did not succeed in obtain- ing the coveted seat after all his hard work. Had those arrayed against the temperance candidates spared a few out of their abundance he would have been elected and the defeat of the teetotallers complete. I congratulate Mr. Bisbtown upon his return, however, and hope he will introduce that " higher tone of municipal life "to which he refer- red in his election speech. I would ask him as a new member to investigate one subject and ascer- tain by what law and under what principle large property owners are enabled to compound and have a reduction of 25 per cent. on their rates. Would not 15 per cent. be ample for the purpose?

div.head: BRIMSTOOAN AN' TRAYCLE.
div.p: BRIMSTOOAN AN' TRAYCLE.
(MIXED.) BI Tum O'DicK O'Boß's.

Footbo' times here ageean ! Id seems to me as th professional leather- punchers nobbut get abeawt a fortnit's halladay every year, though they could affoord a lot longer; aw suppooase their bosses think two week long enough for th' ambulance chaps an' coroners to rest, an' bizness to be slack at th' hospitals an' infirmaries. Well, there'll soon be plenty o' young chaps ready to occupy o'th' new wings as booatii hes bin an' is bein' added o' through th' country, an' them under- tekkers as lies bin lookin' so glum sin' th' Intlooenza cleared off will rub their hands an' chuckle aboon a bit. A w've done a tooathri years herd labour on th' footbo' field mysel', an' abeawt th' middle on't aw eased mi mind o'th' followin' lines:— A HALF BACK'S SONG. When I was a lad I played as a " sub " In a football match with a local club;

I played half-back, and I played so rough The newspapers said I was proper stuff. Yes, the papers all did mention me As the risingest young player in the town of B—. I played again, and I played so well I again " came off" as the papers tell, I took no notice of the sphere at all, But went for the player, and not for the ball; Through going for the players so heavilee, The doctors made their fortunes in the town of B—. As a half-back player I made such a name
The committee-men soon from all parts came, To ask me to leave the mill—what cheek ! _
And play for their clubs at a pound per week, But their tempting offers did'nt much tempt me, As I'd got a better thing on in the town of B—.
I smoke and booze, I train and play,
And enjoy myself in a general way; And better than all—my stars I thank— I've a tolerable balance in the Savings Bank! _
And all through supplying the Infii-maree With patients every week end from the town of B Now youngsters all, whatever you may be,

_ If you wish to become as snug- as me, And if you're clever at the simple trick Of knocking fellows silly with a running kick, Be content at first to play as a" sub," And yo'll subsequently find yourself inside a" pub."

Aw'm capt as somebody hes'nd floated footbo' afoore this; med id into a Company yo' know, wi' so mony theawsand shares at five peawnd apiece. They could easy werk id, au' bi hevin' a " pub" attached thered be a chance o' geddin' th' players' salaries back, an' payin' abeawt twenty-five per cent. every hafe year. If th' company geet a big greawnd, wi' electric leet, they could werk id like a circus, an' hey per- fo-mances every neet, beside th' Setterda' after- roon's game; ov coourse to do this th' company wod hey to own seven good teams, an' bi' buyin' up o' th' Welsh an' Scotch internationals they'd manidge. Id wodn'd do to let a player do moore nor eighty minutes werk or play a week, becos he mut hort hissel ; onyway id wodn' leeaye him a reasonable time ta devote to boozin', an' heaw could he keep up his form witheawt ? But we'll hey another tawk on th' subject later on.

Aw see " Dagonet's " bin rompin' reawnd Blackpool, an' boomin' id a bit; he were capt to see sich a sees, " a sea that there is no standoffishness about, a sea that Isn't ashamed of being a sea, but comes right up to you and shakes hands with you." Aw wonder wod he'd ha' said iv a big slice off th top ov a big wave bed bin moore familiar still an' set on his knee, but happen there were no heigh tide on when he were theere for him to ride through. He's rayther o'erdone id abeawt th promenaid bein' gay wi' green gerdens an' fleawer beds, an' bein lit up fro' one end to th' other we lectric leet. Id strikes me as he's nobbut kept aside o'th' north pier, or else he'd ha' getten some rare gam eawt o' th' Salvayshun Army, th' bumpologists' an' quacks, an' lazy men an' wimmen o' every des- cription. But th' weather hesn'd bin th' reight soort for showin' " Dagonet wod Blackpool watter 1 con be; just thee gooa deawn Merch, owd cock, when th' spring tides are on, an' th' sittin' room windows are puddled up—or iv they're nod then th, fooak want rafts to knock aheawt between th' kitchen an' th' perla —iv nod life belts. Tek a twenty nine feet tide, we a strong wind fro' ayther th' north-west or th' seawth west, an' gooa on th' front abeawt two heawrs afoore th' tide's at th' full, an' there'll be enough copy to fill a ledger. See 'oth' wimmen torn eawt r cricket caps an' footbo' shoon to enjoy id; watch 'em tack abeawt for ten minutes to reych a lamp pooast ten yerds away, an', when they do reych id, nooatice heaw tight they clip id, just for o'th' world as iv id were their young chap. Yigh, an' varra soon after they've ayther to leeve id, or else climb to th' top, iv they want to keep fro' bein' dreawned. For moore nor two heawrs there's as grand a scene, an' as mich fun as onybody clapt een on, an' iv " Dagonet " nobbut sees id wonst he'll fotograff id for his papper, beside stickin' id i' one ov his plays, or else aw'm mist'en.

Welly everybody as aw know hes getten th' amateur fotograffy craze; o' as they keer to tawk abeawt is exposures, an' hypo, apertures, etsettera. lv aw ax a mate wheere he's werkin' neaw, he tells me " at FB," aw'—well, aw'm one on 'em mysel,'th' wife says hoo olez thowt aw were a bit wrang i'th' top stoory, but hoo He'er thowt aw were so far gooan as to wear welly a month's wage i' sich turn- foolery. Thad dampt mi spirrits a bit, aw con tell yo', becose aw'd gone hooam i' rare glee, an' towd her wod a pratty picter aw'd mek on her, an' heaw nice id wod look framed an' hung up o'er th' peeano ; hoo said aw should ne'er tek her likeness, for we'd no rooam far a chamber o' horrors, an' as aw owt to be hung up, but nod o'er th' peeano. Aw've done mi best to ged her to sit, but aw've getten a negative fro' her every time—at leeast ciw've missed geddin' a negative; hoo says hoo isn'd a hen, an' hoo'll nod sit, an' bribery 'll nod mek her. Aw mon come hooam some neet wi' a bit ov a saycret abeawt one o'th' naybers, an' then mek terms. Amateur fotograffy is rayther moore respectable nor pigeon-fiyin', an' it's nod as rough as footbo'; it's healthy. too, an' there's plenty o' gam in id, especially iv yo' tek a picnic perty twice on one plate, an' aw've heeard o' wedgeheyds as hes dole thad silly trick. An' he's getten laughed at aboon a bit, becose he bragged wod a splendid picter id wok mek, an' t'en orders for a tooathri dozen. Another chap as aw know went seven mile specially to fotograff a varra owd cherch, an' after he'd t'en id he see a keaw suppin' eawt ov a trough, sooa he geet his tackle ready an' took a shot. (N.B. His tackle weighed thirteen peawnd, an' th' sun were ninety seven i' th' shade). When he deve- loped he'd a picter o' th' cherch, wi' a keaw stood on nowt, wi' id heyd deawn thi' teawer as iv id were suppin', an' he'd trudged fourteen mile, on a boilin' hot day; wi' at leeast a ton weight o' tackle for thad! Th' langwige as he used were a tooathri degrees i' th.' shade hotter nor th' sun wor. Iv owt o' thad soort happens to me depend on me lettin' yo' know; id'll be put i' writin' to be oppened fifty year after mi berryin'.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY SPEECH BY LORD CROSS.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY SPEECH BY LORD CROSS.

On Tuesday, Viscount Cross was present at a Unionist demonstration at Muncaster Castle, the seat of Lord Muncaster, M.P. Replying to a vote of confidence in the Government, Lord Cross said it was all very well for Mr. Gladstone to talk about a. few by-elections. It was rather a pity Mr. Glad- stone had been an Oxford man, because if he had been brought up at Cambridge,as he (Lord Cross) had been, he would have learned a good deal more of mathematics, and he would not have fallen away to calculations of chance as he had done. It was all very well to talk about the bye-elections, but wait till the general election. When the people made up their minds on a great question they did not change their minds. Home Rule had been before the country now a long time. The country had pro- nounced emphatically against it, and when the general election came Mr. Gladstone would find that the country was determined there shall not be Home Rule, but that the empire must remain united. The members of the Government could go to the country with the certainty that they would be kept in power. A great deal had been said lately about free education and Lord Salisbury's action en that question; but he might tell them Lord Salisbury's view had always been since 1870 that the moment they made it compulsory to send children to school that moment it was an absolute necessity that the country should pay for education. It was not a matter that had come upon Lord Sqlisbury sud- denly; it was not a question to catch votes. They had done that which they had been bid to do, and he firmly believed when the general election came the country would do its part and return the Union- ist Government to another lease of power.

div.head: CATHOLIC BAZAAR AT RUNCORN.
div.p: CATHOLIC BAZAAR AT RUNCORN.

On Wednesday a four-days bazaar was com- menced in Runcorn Public Hall with the object of reducing a debt jf .£7BO which at present burdens St. Edward's Roman Catholic Schools. The hall which had been newly painted, was decorated with Japanese fans, screens, ana umbrellas, and pre- sented a very bright and charming appearance. The stalls were arranged around three sides of the hall were laden with a choice assortment of fancy and useful articles. Miss Hughes, a lady philanthropist, well known in Catholic circles was the superintendent of several of the stalls, Whose contents excited the admiration of the visitors. There were clerical vest- ments of most costly material, and decorated in the most artistic manner with gold lace and other expensive laces, the chief portion being Miss Hughes' own handiwork. Her assistants at the stalls were Mrs. Eastwood, Miss Julia Hughes, Miss Rutter Hughes, Miss Smith, Miss Arnstein, Miss Jones, Miss O'Leary, Miss Louisa Arnstein, Miss Marlow, and the Misses Comerford. A stall containing a variety of articles useful and ornamental was in charge of Mrs. Byrne ; Mrs. Costello, assisted by Miss Costello and Mrs. Nickson assisted by Miss Katie Nickson and Miss Foulkes were also in charge of stalls. The refreshment stall was in the small hall and presented a most attractive appear- ance. The walls were decorated with fans and screens and on the tables were tastefully arranged beautiful plants from the conservatories of The Grange. This de- partment was under the control of Mrs. Mutch, who , was assisted by Mrs. Roberts, Mrs. Barnes, Miss Heyes (St. Helens), and Miss Leigh. The general decorations had been carried out by Mr. Kitchen, of Liverpool. The opening ceremony should have been performed by. Dr. Commins, M.P., of Liverpool, but Dr. Gastaldi ex- plained that at the eleventh hour he had received a telegram from Dr. Cummins saying he could notpop.sibly come, at the same time wishing every success to the bazaar. Dr. Gastaldi said he had been fortunate in se- curing at the last moment the services of Mr. Francis Murphy, pf Liverpool, and he had great pleasure in introducing him to open the bazaar. The debt upon the schools was a serious burden to the missions, and although it had not been contracted in his time, he was no less anxious to clear it away for his own sake and the sake of his successors. The payment of an annual in- terest of £4O was a burden upon the people. - -

Mr. Murphy, who had a cordial reception, sympathised with the audience at the absence of Dr. omnains, and went on to say that bazaars were always arranged to aid some benevolent object, and this was no exception to the rule. Nothing could be higher or nobler than clearing off the debt upon these schools. At the present time there was great sympathy between all denomina- tional schools. A few weeks ago no one would have thought that the moment for Free Education had come but now it was the law of the land. Free education in principle was obtained but not in fact. It was quite impossible to expect children to be educated free if there was a debt upon the school. He therefore urged them strongly to clear off the debt on St. Edwards Schools and be in a position to thoroughly support the educational system in order to keep themselves free from still greater debts. (Applause) As a matter of economy it was necessary that this debt should be removed and they owed a debt of gratitude to the ladies for their noble aid.—Mr. P. Smith proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Murphy for opening the bazaar. They might think it strange that he should appear on that platform but he did so fearlessly, not as a Roman Catholic but as a good citizen. (Hear, hear:)—Mr. John Lyons seconded the motion which was carried, and Mr. Murphy suitably replied. The fair stallholders then commenced the sale f their wares. In the evening concerts were open for the entertainment of visitors and the serio comic recitations of Mr. Nicholls, of Liverpool, was a source of great attraction. The bazaar on the second day (Thursday), was opened by Dr. Robinson, in the absence of Mr. Bancroft Cooke, C.C., of Liverpool.—Dr. Gastaldi, said although he was disappointed at the absence of Mr. Cooke, yet he rejoitged at the presence of Dr. Robinson,who was a true Samari- tan and a noble woiker for the poor people of Runcorn. I (Applause.)—Dr. Robinson said he felt in a delicate posi- tion, never having addressed such an assembly before, but he was glad to Eee the ladies engaged in such an ex- cellent object as that of endeavouring to give the chil- dren a better Christian education. He wished success to the bazaar, which to formally declared open.—On the motion of Mr. Vincent Casolani seconded by Mr. P. Smith a vote of thanks was accorded to Dr. Robinson for his kindness.

pliThe third day's proceedings were opened yesterday by Mr. Doughan, a menberof Liverpool School Board, who said the position cf a priest who was the manager of a poor school was oae deserving sympathy.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.
GOOD TIMIPLARS \FISSION VAN.

On (Tuesday) evening a meeting in connection with the Good Zmaplars' Mission Van No. 1 was held on the land adjoining Brookfield-terrace. A large number of people assembled to hear the speakers. The meeting was addressed by Mr. Morris Jones, of Liverpool, Sister Frisk, who is in charge of the yan,Bros. Frain, Mantle, and Roberts. All the speakers urged upon those present the necessity of total ibstinence, and showed the great evil strong drink is doing in our midst. At the conclusion of the meeting a collection was taken. At intervals between the speeches hymns were sung. A number of pledges were taken at the close.

div.head: SUSPENSION OF LIVERPOOL ATHLETES.
div.p: SUSPENSION OF LIVERPOOL ATHLETES.

There was almost a wholesale suspens ion and disqualification of Liverpool athletes on Thursday night at the meeting of the Northern Counties ' Athletic Association. The first to come under the ban was R. L. Kennedy, who was declared ineligible to compete under amateur rules, and the association instructed the secretaries of the Burnley and Rain- ford clubs to give the prizes won by him to the man who finished next to him. It was decided also to order the permanent suspension of R. W. Ray, of Walton, and J. Clarke, of Blundellsands. R. Saunders, of Bootle, was suspended until June Ist next year. A Cheshire man in J. Leather, North- wich, was permanently suspended, and 11. Webster, of Warrington was cautioned as to his future con- duct in consequence of unbecoming demeanour in 300 yards handictp at the Liverpool Masonic sports.
A FEARFUL HAILSTORM IN VENICE.
DESTRUCTION OF MR. H. WOODS' STUDIO.

The following is an account, which appeared in the "Gazette of Venice," of a hailstorm, and which caused fearful havoc to property; it occurred one day last week. About three o'clock in the afternoon the sky be- came obscured, and the darkness was so intense as to indicate that a storm of some violence was approach- ing. The wind raged and the rain fell, followed by hailstones as large as nuts, and sometimes as large as eggs. On the roofs of the houses, the contact of the hail gave one the idea of an invisible army of blacksmiths at work on their anvils. Window panes were broken and tiles blown about and shivered in thousands of pieces. The rattling of the hail on the Piazza of St. Mark was like the rumbling of an iron plate rolling mill. The small steamers which ply on the Grand Canal ceased to run, and the glass coverings of their engine rooms were smashed, although protected with gratings of brass rods. The trees on the Riva of the Schiavoni were uprooted; and the windows of the Municipal offices sustained great damage, as well as the windows of many other palaces. ' The most serious effects of the storm were to be seen at the residence of the English painter, Sig. Henry Woods, who resides in Celle del Dose, San Ma,urizio. This gentleman has erected from the side of the house into his garden a fine studio, covered in with large panes of plate glass, and this was thickly covered with vines. Out of 75 panes of glass only 2 remained; many of the panes represented the curious appearance of spiders' webs, the hailstones having "cut clean through" them. Fortunately, Mr. Woods, who anticipated a severe storm., and having had some little previous experience, removed several valuable paintings from his studio, and so they escaped any damage; but his studio was left a wreck; glass and vines had disappeared ; there remained nothing but the wooden frame work. The storm will certainly prove a harvest for the glaziers. In the windows of the Municipal Offices about 250 panes of glass were broken, and such was the force of hail- stones that they chipped off pieces of the columns in the Piazza, and off the steps along the Lido. At the Rima Baths the confusion was indescribable one of the attendants swooned through fright. The glass-covered entrance of one of the theatres was smashed to pieces. The storm seems to have travelled across Lombardy, commencing at Turin, then at Milan, and onwards, ter- minating, but with redoubled energy and with worst effects, at Venice. In the island of the Giudecca the vines were totally destroyed. Telephonic communica- tions were completely interrupted ; about 150 wires were cut as if by strong flippers; and the damage done amounts to some thousands of pounds.

div.head: CADISHEAD.
div.p: CADISHEAD.

THE WABES.—Cadishead wakes commenced on Satur- day, and, as last year, occupied the Recreation Ground and the frontages of the Lion Hotel and the Coach and Horses. On Tuesday the scholars of the Wesleyan Sun- day school had their annual tea party and procession. WESLEYAN CHAPEL.—On Sunday the anniversary ser- vices of the Sunday school were held in the above place of worship. The Rev. A. Kent, of Leigh, preached both afternoon and evening. The attendance in the afternoon was moderate, owing to the rain, but in the evening the place was crowded. The collections for the day amounted to a little over £24.

div.head: L IMAI.
div.p: L IMAI.

DAY ScHoors.—The managers of the Lymm parochial schools have decided that the schools in all departments and standards shall be free. They have accepted the Government fee grant under the. recent Education Act. THE POPULATION.—There were mn the last census day 1,057 separate families in Lymm, living in 997 houses. There were 84 houses unoccupied and six in building. There 2,423 males and 2,572 females, making a total of 4,995 of a population. The populatipn in 1881 was 4,665, being an increase of 330. THE REV. R. COWARD.—The Rev. Richard Coward, curate of St. Mary's Parish Church, Lymm, has been offered and has accepted the living of Luxulyan, in the diocese of Truro, which will shortly fall vacant, owing to the Rev. J. K. Rashleigh leaving for another cure. Mr. Coward will not leave Lymm until November, as there is at present no Bishop of Truro, and Dr. Gott will not be consecrated until September 29th.

div.head: LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: THE LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of this Board took place on Thursday night week. Present, Mr. Cameron (chair- man), Messrs. Dutton, Rogers, Harrison, Brazendale, NA'hitelegg, Holt, Swallow, and Thomason; Mr. T. J. Ridgway (law clerk), Mr. W. Mullard (clerk), Mr. J. Mort (surveyor), and Mr. W. Severs (gas manager). TECHNICAL EDUCATION.—The Law Clerk stated that the clerk had received a cheque from the Cheshire County Council for £ll9 as a grant under the Technical Educa- tion Act.—The Chairman said the Board had about £2OO to spend in technical education, and it was for them to consider what was to be done with it at an early date, as the winter was coming on. After a long discussion it was decided to issue a circular addressed to the clergy, ministers, schoolmasters, and others interested in don, also the governors and trustees of all the existing schools in the district, inviting them to a meeting to be called in the evening on some day to be fixed after an interview with the rector. A wish was expressed by the Board that the money should be spent for the benefit of the district to the largest advantage, and with that aim the opinion should be had, if possible, of young men likely to take advantage of the education afforded under the Act, which it was thought would materially assist in settling the questiAn. LIGHTING.—The Surveyor reported that the Lighting and Road Committees had had two meetings during the month, and they suggested that there should be laid down 16 new lamps, including nine Bray's, and that 7 present lamps be removed, throughout the whole district. Further consideration of the matter was de- ferred to a special meeting, and Mr. Brazendale gave notica to bring it up then.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

INGENIOUS FRAUD BY A BUTCHER.—WiIIiam Palm, butcher, Frodsham, appeared in answer to a summons charging him with travelling on the London and North- Western Railway, between Liverpool and Runcorn, without having previously paid his fare, and with intent to defraud the above company.—:Defendant pleaded guilty.—Mr. W. J. Bland, of the solicitors' department, Lime-street, prosecuted. The facts were reported last week. Defendant was tined 20s. and 10s. costs, also 21s. costs of seven witnesses,. a total of £2 lie. 6d., or one month's imprisonment with hard labour. PAROCHIAL COMIAITTEES.-1.1. Meeting: of the Prod- sham and Frodsham Lordship Parochial Committees was held in the Town Hall, Frodsham, yesterday week, when Mr. Thomas Davies presided, in the absence of the Chairman. The Clerk reported that he had received from Messrs. Timmins,the estimate of the probable total cost of the proposed water scheme,including the purchase of land and wayleaves, which amounted to £3,575 ; and further, that he had written to Mr. John Higson, and Mrs. Perrin's trustees as to the sale of the lands re- quired, but that no reply had as yet been received. The Inspector of Nuisances reported on several cases of typ- hoid fever, which were of a mild character; also on cases of overcrowding ;in one instance, in a small cot- tage, two families resided, there being seven children and five adults. Orders were given that if the notices calling for the statement of the overcrowding were not attended to, summonses would be taken. RATEPAYERS' MEETING.—A meeting of ratepayers of the township of Frodsham was held in the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Monday evening, for the purpose of tak- ing into considmation the proposed scheme for supplying the township with water. There was a ,large attend- ance. Mr. John Pollard, sen., occupied the chair. Mr. James Edwards, junior overseer, and Mr. George Jones, assistant overseer, were also present. The Chairman having read the notice calling the meeting, Mr. Edwards inquired whether any ratepayer questioned the manner of calling the meeting, whereupon Mr. H. G. Linaker stated that the meeting had not been arranged for in ac- cordance with instructions laid down in the overseer's manual. Mr. Edwards did not concur with this opinion, and, on referring to the manual, quoted therefrom cer- tain portions which, he considered, proved beyond doubt the legality of the meeting. When he handed the book to Mr. Linaker, that gentleman maintained his contention. After further observations, Mr. Win. Youd moved, and Mr. Linaker seconded, that a meeting of ratepayers be called for Thursday, the 17th inst., to take the water scheme into consideration. This being carried, the usual vote of thanks was given to Mr. Pollard for presiding.

At the SOuth-Metropolitan Gas Works, London, on Thursday, a girder, weighing ten tons, fell and killed Charles,-Smith. On Tuesday the licensing justices at Cardiff declined to renew six licenses in that town, one on the ground that it was unnecessary.

....... ... ..... On Wednesday night, Patrick Connell died at Ros- keen, from injuries received during the faction fight on Sunday last. Three men have been arrested. Three Grimsby smacks which have arrived at Shet- land from the Iceland cod fishing,report the wreck on the coast of Iceland of the Grimsby smack Lyons, and the loss, it is feared, of all her crew, numbering twelve hands.

James Elwell, a minor, residing at West Coseley, near Dudl9y, has been shot dead while standing on his door- step. A party of volunteers were firing at the 600 yards range at Wren's Nest Hill, when one of the bullets went far over the range, whizzed past three women, and killed the miner.

Two brothers, sons of Mr. W. Mullett, school master, Barrow Island, Barrow-in-Furness, were on Thursday night fishing in the timber pond at Ramsden Dock when the youngest fell off into the water. The elder brother, aged nine attempted to save him and jumped in for that purpose. He made a gallant attempt at rescue, but failed and both were drowned. The father on hearing of the fate of his lads was taken home insensible.
LATEST NEWS.
GREAT EARTHQUAKE IN SALVADOR.
HEAVY LOSS OF LIFE.

The following telegram from San Salvador, of Wed- nesday's date, has been received by the" New York Herald" :—Millions of dollors' worth of property has been destroyed and many lives lost by an earthquake to- day. Whole towns have been wiped out, and hardly a city along the coast has escaped. There have been in- dications for several days past that a serious disturb- ance might be expected. The volcanoes of San Salva- dor, 80.11, Liguel, and Izalco have been unusually active, and deep subterranean rumblings with slight earthquake tremors have been frit, but no great alarm was experienced. At 11 -15 this morning the earth began to shake. The wave had a strong vertical and oscillatory movement. The inhabi- tants rushed into the streets in their night clothing, and although the shock lasted only twenty seconds, yet be- fore it had passed a panic-stricken mob was making its way to the open country. The walls of the houses cracked and then tottered and fell. Meanwhile there was a deep and continuous rumbling like heavy thunder, while the sky became overcast and the air filled with a fine penetrating dust. While the shock lasted the earth rose and fell in long waves,and even strong men were un- able to keep their feet. As soon as possible after the dis- turbance temporary shelters were thrown up outside the city, but nearly all the men, women, and children had only the sky for a cover. Through the morning the:e have been slight shocks, and the inhabitants are afraid to return to their houses. President Ezela is doing his utmost to stop the panic. The towns have sufferedmost severely. Anaquilto and Comasanga have been com- pletely destroyed, while Coutepeque, San Pero, Santa Tekla, and Wasahuet are practically ruined. The shock was also felt at Santa Ana and Susimtepegue, sixty miles from here. Two persons have been killed in this city. It was impossible to estimate the number of tatalitie elsewhere, but it is feared that there are many.

div.head: ANOTHER ACCOUNT.
div.p: ANOTHER ACCOUNT.

NEW YORK, THURSDAY MORNlNG.—Special despatches from San Salvador, state that the Republic has once more been devastated by a terrible earthquake. It is already known, however, that several towns have been levelled with the ground, that hundreds of lives have been lost, and that the damage to property will amount to many millions of dollars.
THE TERRIBLE HURRICANE AT NEW BRUNSWICK. SEVENTY WRECKS.

HALIFAX, THIIRSDAY.—Further particulars have now come to hand of the destruction caused by the terrific storm which lately visited the Maritime Provinces. Seventy vessels were wrecked, and several lives lost. Three bodies, wreckage, and a lifebuoy marked, " Cam- illa, St. John's, Newfoundla.nd,"have been washed ashore at Scateria Island. 30 per cent. of the apple crop has been blown down.
THE SHIP CANAL.
SUDDEN DEATH IN A RAILWAY CARRIAGE.

John Valentine, 46, captain of No. 1 canal dredger, belonging to the Ship Canal Company, and who resided at 42, George-st., Urmston, near Manchester, died in a London and North-Western Railway carriage on Satur- day morning. The deceased had been working at Pres- ton Brook up to 10 a.m., and after paying the men who worked under him, he left Preston Brook, in , company with two other workmen named Samuel Inglefield and Joseph Jepson, for the purpose of going to Norton Rail- way Station. When they arrived at the station they took tickets, deceased booking to Warrington. As he was stepping into the carriage he fell back on to the platform as if in a fit. His companions put him into the train, but soon after it started Valentine died. When the train reached Warrington the body was removed to the Patten Arms Hotel. An inquest was held on the body on Monday afternoon, at the Patten Arms Hotel, before Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner. Mr. W. J. Bland represented the London and North-Western Railway Company. Sarah Valentine, wife of the deceased, stated that she lived at Urmston, near Manchester. Her hus- band worked on a canal dredger. He was 46 years of age.—Samuel Inglefield said that he worked with the deceased. On Saturday they walked from Preston Brook to Norton Station. They had barely time to catch the train. Deceased had always appeared to be in good health. When the train came in he saw the deceased suddenly swerve backwards, and fall into the arms of a man who was standing near. They then put him into the train. Between Norton and Daresbury deceased ap- peared to be very quiet. Witness opened his coat and put his ear to deceased's heart, which was still. Witness left the train at Daresbury, but let the deceased be taken on to Warrington, thinking that was the best thing to do. He had known deceased for three or four months. Deceased was a very steady man. A verdict of "Death from natural causes" was returned by the jury. OPENING OF THE SECOND SECTION.

The second section of the Manchester Ship Canal, the first having been successfully flooded two months back, is in an advanced stage of preparation for filling. Large gangs of men are working day and night, and it is expected that the water will be run in one day next week.
The woman Owen, who attempted suicide near Llan- fairfechan after a futile effort to take her husband's life, is said to be out of danger, but the man is in a critical condition.

'FETE EXAMINER SATURDAY SEPTEMBER 12, 1891. NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. CYCLING. In connection with the Crewe Cycling Club, a 50 miles road handicap took place on Saturday afternoon. A start was made from Crewe Green shortly after two o'clock, when 19 competitors faced the starter. All being in readiness, Mr. H. Townley, secretary of the club, set the limit man, Harry Astley, on the long journey which lay from Crewe Green, Sandbach, Holmes Chapel, to Dunham IE4, and then back to Crewe Green. The first to arrive bpi was L. Townley, quite a lad, who, with a start of 40inin., accomplished the distance in 3hrs. 55min. The second arrival was Saunders, who had 22min. start, and came in three mins. behind Townley. Rigby was awarded third place, and it is only fair to say that he rode the best, finishing in three hours and a half. Woolridge, with 15 minutes start, came in fourth, and the fifth man was Patin. Gottberg, the scratch man, gave in on reaching Altrincham, and returned by rail. The last fifty miles mem- bers' handicap for this season held by the North-road Cycling Club was run off on Saturday afternoon over a newly chosen course still less frequented than the well-known quiet routes discovered by this club. The winner turned up in H. J. Howard, who this year deserted the tall machine for the safety. His time for the full distance was 2hrs. 33mins. 57secs. S. C. Houghton on an ordinary bicycle beat the record by 25secs., doing 2hrs. 45mins. 55secs. Two hundred and twenty cyclists assembled on Sun- day morning to take part in a long-distance contest or- ganised in France by the" Petit Journal," and the scene outside the offices of that newspaper prior to the open- ing of the race was one of unusual animation. The cyclists, who were received by M. Thomas, president of the Union Velocipedique de France, ranged themselves in 20 rows, and a bugle being sounded at seven o'clock precisely as the signal for 'the departure, they set off for the official starting point at the entrance to the Bois de Boulogne. When opposite the Rne Pergolese, on the signal for the official start being given, they dashed off at full speed into the Bois de Boulogne. Large crowds had assembled at various points along the route between the Rue la Fayette and the Port Dauphine, leading into the Bois, and the start was watched with great interest. It was subsequently reported that several bicycles had been slightly damaged by pieces of broken glass and sharp nails that had been scattered across the road by, it is believed, some evil-disposed persons, just beyond St. Cloud. The broken glass was fortunately noticed by some of the foremost riders,who warned their comrades, otherwise the tyres of many of the machines would pro- bably have been cut to pieces. Numerous prizes, rang- ing from 200 to 2,000 frances, will be awarded to those who most speedily cover the distance. Great indignation is everywhere expressed at the dastardly attempt at St. Cloud to disable the machines, and every effort will be made to trace the miscreants who planned it. --- FOOTBALL. An informal openingof the Warrington•football season took place on Saturday, when the first 15 met the next 18 on the Cricket Club ground. Judging from the form displayed, the teams are in capital conditicn. During the first half the juniors gained a lead of two goals, the tries being obtained by Buckley and W. Warburton. The Ist team, however, pulled themselves together in the latter stage of the game, and gradually wearing the juniors down, ran out winners by two goals (one dropped by Lawless, an improved try by the same player) and a try (Evans) to two goals. This week end the Warrington first team will take a trip to the Isle of Man, there to meet the leading club, Douglas. They will probably stay till Tuesday, and next Saturday they will engage on their own ground in a contest with their old and formidable rivals from Swinton. There will be a splendidly attractive opening of the home programme, and it can safely be predicted that there will be a big crowd. In the premier team which Warrington will this year put in the field there will be a few if any changes from last year. Ashton captains the combination, and this in itself is an omen of success. In addition to this it is said all the players are in • first-rate condition, and there is, therefore, every prospect of a brilliant season. Mr. B. G. Roscoe, the well-known Rugby half-back, who is now in Africa with the English team, is settling down there. He has received an excellent appointment at the hospital of the De Beers Mining Company, at Kimberley, and will in all probability play with the Kimberley Club. In a letter to a friend at Bolton, Mr. Roscoe describes the narrow escape of the team by drowning, owing to their tug being nearly run down. Widnes have, says the "Athletic News," a clinking good lot of forwards this season, who, perhaps with an undue tendency for vigorous tackling and a rather undesirable mode of standing a trifle offside, seem to be cut out for their work. The attendances at the - League matches on Saturday were something enormous, and so far as we can make out were as follows ,—Notts v. North End, 11,000 ; Ashton Villa v. Blackburn Rovers, 10,000; Sunderland v. Wolverhampton Wanderers, 8,000 ; Accrington v. Burn- ley, 8,000; Darwen v. Bolton Wanderers, 7,000 ; West Bromwich Albion v. Everton, 6,000; Stoke v. Derby County, 4,000. , In connection with the St. Helens Recreation Club on Thursday, a cricket match between the Recs. (with Walter Robinson, Arthur Mold, the Lancashire fast bowler ; and Alec. Watson,all of Lancashire county) and a strong district team from Clubmoor, was played on the Boundary-road ground. This was followed by a foot- ball match between the Recs. F.C. and Mr. T. R. Sut- ton's county team. Tne matches were arranged for the benefit of Walter Robinson,the highly respected " pro." of the Recs. C.C., and some thousands of spectators at- tended. The cricket match was won by the Recs.,who scored 228 for 7 wickets (Robinson 93, and Watson 70). against 96 by Clubmoor (12). In the football match the county team scored one goal (kicked by Crompton from a try by Brownbill) to three tries (Fildes, Reynolds, and Dolan) by the Recs.

A SERIOUS CHARGE. Henry Jonas, chartered accountant, was committed for trial yesterday, at Birmingham, charged. with de- frauding the Patent Axle Box and Foundry Company of £30,000. SUICIDE OR MURDER? On Thursday night, a caretaker named William John Connolly, about 65 years of age, was found in a field at Ballygowan, near Newtownards, with his throat cut from ear to ear. An open razor was lying by his side. It is not known whether the case is one of suicide or murder. FATALITY AT A RIFLE RANGE. At Pirbright Camp, yesterday, an inquest was held on the body of William Harper, Ist Battalion Coldstream Guards, who was shot dead at the shooting range whilst engaged in painting the bull's-eye of the target with other men. A verdict of "Accidental death" was re- turned. THREE MEN DROWNED. On Thursday night, four men, Edward Rousham, Joseph Hopwood, Robert Waring, and Robert Wilkins, compositors, rowed from Blackfriars to Richmond. On the return journey they stopped at Isleworth, where they partook somewhat freely of refreshment. Shortly after reembarking, the boat was upset. Wilkins saved himself with difficulty, but the other three were drowned. THE TRADES UNION CONGRESS. The Trade Union Congress resumed yesterday, at Newcastle, when a resolution was adopted, calling for the appointment of additional workingmen and women inspectors, and extending the scope of the resolution to India. A discussion took place on the miners legal eight hours day. An amendment averring that further parliamentary interference was undesirable was defeated by 237 to 59. Glasgow was chosen as next year's place of meeting by 259, against 227 for Norwich. THE LATE EX-PRESIDENT GREVY. PARIS, FRIDAY.—It has been decided that the body of M. Grevy shall be accorded a State funeral at the public expense. KILLING A POLICEMAN. SAN FRANCISCO, FRIDAY.—A well known actor named Curtis, while under arrest for drunkenness to-day, fatally shot a policeman. TERRIBLE COLLISION AT SEA. A STEAMER SUNK AND GREAT LOSS OF LIFE. ATHENS, FRIDAY.—A collision took place last night, off Cape Sunium, between the steamer Taormina, be- longing to the Italian Messageries line, and the Greek steamer Thessalia. The former sank almost immediately, and about forty cabin passengers perished, including the captain. The second officer and several passengers who were on the bridge at the moment of the collision were saved by boats from the Thessalia.
